I

BRUCE R. GALLOWAY
Grand Master – 2017-2018

Most Worshipful Bruce Robert Galloway was raised a Master Mason
in Reading Lodge No. 254 in Redding on August 21, 1986. He served as
Master of that lodge in 1992 and again in 2007. His lodge honored him
in 2008 with the presentation of the Hiram Award.
Bruce has served in various capacities for Grand Lodge. He was a
District Inspector, and for six years served as the Assistant Grand Lecturer
for Division II. Bruce was a member of the Ritual Committee for six years
and has served as a Facilitator at the Leadership Retreats. He has served
on each of the constitutional boards.
Bruce is active in York Rite Masonry and is a Knight of the York Grand
Cross of Honor. He is a member of Saint Francis Conclave – Knights of
the Red Cross of Constantine and is a 32nd degree Scottish Rite Mason
in the Valley of Sacramento, Orient of California. He is also a member of
the Sacramento Chapter of National Sojourners.
After serving in the U.S. Army, Bruce spent 26 years as a manager
with AT&T. He then went on to work as a consultant and executive in
the wireless industry.
Bruce lives in Redding with his wife Gay. They have two children. Their
daughter Bonnie, and her family live in Colfax. Their son Scott, a Master
Mason, and his family live in Fullerton.

BRUCE R. GALLOWAY

Grand Master
October 15, 2017 - October 21, 2018

3

One Hundred Sixty-Ninth
Annual Communication
Friday Afternoon, October 19, 2018
The 169th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand
Master Bruce R. Galloway on Friday, October 19, 2018.
Worshipful Brother N. Uriah McBroome, Master of Reading Lodge
No. 254, raised the opening session of Grand Lodge. The gavel used to
raise Grand Lodge was presented to the Grand Master at the Five Way
Reception in Corning, and was crafted by Worshipful Brother David
Sokol, a Past Master of Vesper Lodge No. 84.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand
Marshal to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of
California at the Altar. The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past
Grand Master, and the Grand Master and Deputy Grand Master personally
greeted each one. The Grand Master asked the brethren to join him in
saluting our Past Grand Masters by the battery of three times three. The
Past Grand Masters were then escorted to seats reserved for them in
the auditorium. The Grand Master then directed the Grand Secretary to
send to each absent Past Grand Master the usual letter of greeting from
the grand lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge
Officers, Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain
if a constitutional number were present to convene the Grand Lodge of
California. The following were present as indicated by their response to
the calling of the roll:

Memorial Service
The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend Jeffrey M. Schimsky,
Grand Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed
brethren. His remarks were as follows:

The Grand Master then asked the brethren to pause in the deliberations
for the annual Memorial Service.

To quote A.A. Milne: “How lucky I am to have something that makes
saying goodbye so hard.”
It is our honor and duty to set aside this time to remember those who
are now with our Great Creator, to remember their service to our Maker,
and to raise our thoughts from this earthly work to our eternal rest. It is
a holy time, a sacred time, a time when the sweet spirits of our departed
fill our hearts with thoughts of comfort, knowing that they are now at
peace with our Creator.
The Hebrew word for funeral service is “Levaya,” meaning “to escort.”
The deeper meaning for this service to our brother is to assist him in
making his way to his final resting place, to escort him to the eternal. In
this way, we have a shared responsibility to recommend our brethren to
our Creator through our memories of their work here on Earth.
In addition to the men we eulogize here this morning, there are other
pieces of our Masonic family that we have lost during this last Grand
Lodge year. Over 1,300 of our dear brothers set down their working tools
and 400 of our wives/partners have passed on since last we held this
service. While we cannot honor them all here today, we can honor a few
who have had a profound effect on our Grand Lodge. One of those men
was a mentor to me, personally, and a Former Grand Chaplain, Worshipful
Brother Micky Roth of blessed memory.
Another such brother is Worshipful Christopher Putnam, who served
nine terms as our Assistant Grand Organist. His gift of music to our
beloved Craft will live on in our hearts. It is fitting to quote a musician
to memorialize this brother who was so dear to many of us:

Shadows are fallin’ and I’m runnin’ out of breath
Keep me in your heart for a while.
If I leave you it doesn’t mean I love you any less

Keep me in your heart for a while.

Keep me in your heart for a while
—Warren Zevon
May his memory be for a blessing.
To honor the dead in the Jewish tradition, we recite the Mourner’s
Kaddish (or prayer), translated:
Glorified and sanctified be God’s great name throughout the world,
which He has created according to His will.
May He establish His kingdom in your lifetime and during your days
and within the life of His entire House, speedily and soon; and say,
Amen.
May His great name be blessed forever and to all eternity.
Blessed and praised; glorified and exalted; extolled and honored;
adored and lauded be the name of the Holy One, blessed be He,
beyond all the blessings and hymns, praises and consolations that
are ever spoken in the world; and say, Amen.
May there be abundant peace from heaven, and life, for us and for
all our people; and say, Amen. He who creates peace in His celestial
heights, may He create peace for us and for all; and say, Amen.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

15

It is a tradition of the Hebrew people to place a stone at the grave of a
loved one. Although there are many explanations for this practice, one
is particularly poignant. One of the greatest Mitvot (or commandments)
that you can perform is the burial of another person. Why is this such a
kindness? Because it is a debt that the dead can never repay. It is a good
deed that is done with the purest of intentions and without the hope of
ever being returned. As a recreation of that good deed and that burial,
we leave a stone. This morning, as we honor those that have passed on,
as we eulogize and speak kind words in memory of those who are no
longer with us; as we, with our hearts and minds, “escort” them to their
hereafter—I place this stone.
Most Worshipful Frank Loui, Past Grand Master, then delivered a eulogy
for the late Past Grand Master Donald Burns McCaw.

EULOGY
DONALD BURNS MCCAW
Most Worshipful Donald Burns McCaw entered into the Celestial Lodge
on December 5, 2017. He was a local Bay Area product. He was born on
April 20, 1928 in San Francisco, California to David and Enid McCaw.
He attended public schools here in San Francisco before crossing the
Bay Bridge to continue his education at the University of California in
Berkeley, where he earned a Bachelor’s Degree in Science majoring in
Business Administration. Upon graduation in 1949, he was commissioned
a Second Lieutenant, Infantry Branch, United States Army Reserve. His
business career commenced with the nationally-recognized insurance
brokers, Cosgrove & Company. However, Most Worshipful Brother Donald
had an ambition to become a lawyer. So, in 1954 he returned to school,
attending classes at night while still working full time in the insurance
brokerage business. He graduated from Golden Gate University School
of Law in 1958 with a degree of Doctor of Jurisprudence. In 1960, he
became a founding partner in the San Francisco law firm of McCaw &
Barnum, from which he retired in December 31, 2003.
On March 25, 1950, he married the former Camilla Burbank, who is
known to her friends as “Skip.”
Most Worshipful Donald was a third-generation Mason. He was raised a
Master Mason on August 15, 1963 in Park-Crockett Lodge No. 139, which
is now San Francisco Lodge No. 120. He served as its Master in 1971.
He served with distinction as the 112th Grand Master of California
and Hawaii in 1977-1978.

Donald Burns McCaw

Past Grand Master
April 20, 1928 - December 5, 2017

On September 29, 1994, Most Worshipful Donald became the fifth
member in the history of our Grand Lodge to attain the rank and status
of Mason of the Year. Brother Donald’s past service to the Grand Lodge,
to the Masonic Homes, to Jurisprudence, to this Memorial Temple, and
to the California Masonic Foundation was more than sufficient to qualify
him for this award. But the epitome of Don’s contribution and service was
his role in the formation of Nob Hill Masonic Management Inc., which he
also led during the incorporation’s early years. Nob Hill was conceived,
formed, chartered and functions today as a for-profit corporation in the
operation and management of the Masonic Auditorium, Exhibit Hall,
Parking Garage and Pine Street Properties. He served as its first president

18

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

and guiding spirit.
Most Worshipful Donald was a member of Asiya Shriners, National
Sojourners Association and Scottish Rite in the valley of San Francisco
where he was coroneted a 33º Inspectors General Honorary.
Donald is survived by Skip, his wife of 67 years and son, Daniel, a
fourth generation Master Mason, who belongs to San Francisco Lodge
No. 120 and Fairfax Lodge No. 556 and is also Past Master Councilor of
Ross Valley Chapter, Order of DeMolay.
Donald will be sadly missed by all. Until we meet again – farewell, my
brother.

Warren J. Blomseth
Past Grand Master
April 30, 1929 - January 6, 2018

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Most Worshipful John L. Cooper III, Past Grand Master, then delivered
a eulogy for the late Past Grand Master Warren Jennings Blomseth.

Freemasonry was at the center of Warren’s life, but it was not all of it.
His love for his wife, Dee, was an inspiration to those of us who knew
how deep and profound their relationship was. His Masonic duties did
not cause him to neglect his religious and civic duties. He was an active
member of the Covenant Church, and attended the famed San Francisco
Bible Club whenever he was in the City. That club was virtually a Masonic
institution, having been founded many years before by Most Worshipful
Brother Chester R. MacPhee. Warren was also a loyal Rotarian, and an
active member and supporter of many other community organizations.

EULOGY
WARREN J. BLOMSETH
It is a privilege to be asked by our Grand Master to deliver the eulogy
for Most Worshipful Brother Warren Blomseth, the 129th Grand Master
of Masons in California. It is especially meaningful for me to be asked
to share this last tribute of our affection for my brother and my friend. I
served him as his Grand Secretary for the Grand Lodge Year 1993-1994,
and we became close friends – a closeness that death can never dim, for
his vision of Freemasonry more surely shaped my own than almost any
other person, Mason or non-Mason.
Brother Warren was born on April 30, 1929, in North Dakota. When
he was six years old, his family moved to California, and his love for his
adopted state was unbounding. His introduction to Freemasonry came
in 1944 when he became a member of the Fruitvale Chapter of the
Order of DeMolay in Oakland. He entered the portals of Freemasonry
on November 14, 1951 in Diamond Lodge No. 603 in Oakland. In 1962,
he served as Master of that lodge, which by that time had become known
as Tri Square Lodge No. 551. In 1963-1964, he served as Senior Grand
Deacon and 1965-1966 he was our Grand Orator.
His 33-year employment with the San Francisco firm of J.H. Pomeroy
caused a pause in his Grand Lodge career until his retirement, when his
talents were once again recognized by our Grand Lodge. In 1990, he was
elected as Junior Grand Warden, progressing through the Grand Line
until his installation as Grand Master on October 13, 1993. He brought to
that position his enormous business and financial expertise, and after his
term as Grand Master, he served our Grand Lodge as Grand Treasurer
for three more years.

Warren was also a meticulous writer and speaker. As his Grand
Secretary, I often had the opportunity to read early drafts of his speeches
and papers, all carefully written in longhand in beautiful blue ink with
one of his favorite fountain pens. If he did not revise a speech or a paper
at least eight times, I knew that he was pressed for time! Accuracy in
the spoken and printed word was important to him, as was a sense of
humor. That characteristic came out in his Grand Master’s Message to
Grand Lodge in 1994, a part of his message that I will never forget. This
what he said:
“In preparing this message, like all of my messages, I gave considerable
care to the choice of words. This was done in an effort to communicate
in the clearest and most concise manner possible. The exact word is
important if one’s true meaning is to be conveyed and readily understood.
My favorite story in this regard is no doubt a favorite of everyone who
has heard it –
Noah Webster’s wife came suddenly into the pantry and caught Noah
embracing the chamber maid –
‘Mr. Webster,’ she exclaimed, ‘I am surprised.’
The great compiler of our most famous dictionary gave his wife a look
of reproof –
‘No, my pet,’ he replied. ‘You are amazed. It is we who are surprised!”

22

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Warren’s meticulous dedication to everything he undertook was
matched by his broad vision of the outcome. That vision was shaped, as it
is for many a Mason, by his experience in the Order of DeMolay as a young
man. He and I talked often about the inner meaning of Freemasonry, and
his vision of our Ancient Craft still inspires the things that I do. That was
his effect on all those whose life he touched.
He laid down his working tools on January 6, 2018. Those of us who
remain can only use them in a way that would have made Most Worshipful
Brother Warren Jennings Blomseth proud.

M. William Holsinger
Past Grand Master
November 12, 1932 - December 1, 2017

EULOGY
M. WILLIAM HOLSINGER

One of Bill’s greatest accomplishments was signing the contract with
Live Nation. At the time, many of us wondered if this was a good move
for our Grand Lodge. What would the neighbors think? How would they
adjust to increased activity in our building? What kind of programs would
Live Nation bring to Nob Hill and the City of San Francisco?

A booming voice, a gentle demeanor, a man dedicated to his family, these
qualities all describe our friend and colleague, Marvin William Holsinger.
Better known as M. William Holsinger, or just plain Bill.
Bill was born in San Bernardino, California. He graduated from San
Bernardino High School, attended San Bernardino Valley College and
studied real estate at the University of California Extension.
Bill served our Country as a member of the United States Army at Fort
Leonard Wood, Missouri. During this time, he was an x-ray technician,
an ambulance driver, and the company clerk at the 54th Field Hospital.
After the completion of his tour of duty, Bill returned to California. He
worked for the County of Orange as a Junior Right-of-Way Agent, which
included appraising and negotiating the purchase of real property for
public purposes. Three years later, he moved to Riverside and joined the
Riverside County Flood Control and Water Conservation District, where
he performed similar work. He eventually joined the City of Riverside,
retiring in 1993 as their Real Property Services Manager. No matter
the location, title, or the job assignment, Bill was instrumental in the
appraisal, purchase, use and sale of property for the benefit of the public.
He was a member of the American Right of Way Association and a past
president of the Riverside Society of Appraisers.
Bill began his Masonic journey in Evergreen Lodge No. 259 in 1963
where he was Initiated November 13, 1963; Passed to the Degree of
Fellow Craft on January 22, 1964; and Raised to the Degree of Master
Mason on April 15, 1964.
Bill has served our Grand Lodge and Masonry for over 50 years. After
serving as the Master of Evergreen Lodge in 1971, Bill went on to serve
as the Grand Marshal in 1972; the Grand Tiler from 1974 to 1976; the
Grand Orator in 1978 and the Grand Treasurer in 2005 and 2011.
During his journey through the Grand Line—between 1999 and 2002—
Bill served on all of the constitutional boards of Grand Lodge. He served

After several contentious years, working with our neighbors and a total
renovation of our auditorium, this move has proved to be very successful
for everyone.
The quality of entertainment available is second to none, and the fears
of those of us that thought Live Nation only booked rock concerts have
been laid to rest. Thank you, Bill, for your foresight.
As with many of our members, Bill belonged to several Masonic
organizations. He was a member of Southern California Research Lodge;
Southern California Past Masters Association, where he served as their
President in 1985; and the Scottish Rite in Long Beach, where he served
as the Master of Kadosh of the Consistory. He was honored with the
rank and decoration of Honorary Inspector General of the 33rd Degree
in 1987. He also served the San Bernardino Scottish Rite as Wise Master
of the Chapter of Rose Croix.
Bill was a member of Al Malaikah Shrine Temple, the Riverside High
12 Club, and National Sojourners. He and his wife, Jean, were members
of Ungava Chapter No. 106, Order of Eastern Star, which meets at the
Evergreen Masonic Center.
One of the highlights of Bill’s Masonic journey was his service as
Associate Bethel Guardian of Bethel No. 264 during the time his daughter,
Leslie, was Honored Queen.
Bill and Jean were members of Magnolia Presbyterian Church during
the time they lived in Riverside. He was an ordained Elder, a member of
the Endowment Committee and a member of the Property and Finance
Committee.
Several years after Bill concluded his term as Grand Master, he and
Jean moved to San Jose to be closer to Leslie and her family.

26

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Bill was a great asset to this Grand Lodge as he was always willing to
lead the way, to find solutions to difficult issues and to ensure Freemasonry
was truly a way of life. His motto “Making Good Men Better” is still
relevant today.

Saturday Afternoon, October 20, 2018

We will miss our brother. We will miss hearing his booming voice and
gentle counsel. We will miss his ability to lead our Craft.
The brittle thread that bound Most Worshipful M. William Holsinger
to his earthly life has been severed. His ship has sailed from this life
to Eternal Life. He watches over us, guiding our gentle Craft from that
home, not made with hands, Eternal in the Heavens, where we shall all
meet him again.

Presentation on Freemasonry and Civil Society: A Report on the
Partnership Between the Masons of California and the University
of California at Los Angeles
The Grand Master called upon Most Worshipful Larry A. Adamson,
Past Grand Master of California, to deliver a report on the partnership
between UCLA and the Masons of California.
Most Worshipful Sir and Brethren All:
I sincerely and fraternally thank you for this opportunity to address
the assembled here at this the Annual Communication, 2018.
One decade ago, this Grand Lodge and the masons of California boldly
and enthusiastically joined with the then Grand Master to support the
expansion of Freemasonry’s commitment to public education and the
development of a new and ambitious program. This program centered
on supporting higher education’s study and discussion of Freemasonry,
with emphasis on Freemasonry’s role in the worldwide development of
civil societies.
First named “A Partnership to Advance the Study and Understanding
of Freemasonry,” the program was later formally named “Freemasonry
and Civil Society at UCLA.”
If you will permit me to digress for a brief moment, I will remind you
of the drivers behind this bold step by California Masonry. In the decade
preceding the partnership, American Freemasonry sat back passively and
quietly and watched as others defined the image and perception of our

Your leadership felt it was time that we became proactive—rather
than reactive or, worse, silent—in how the image and perception of our
institution was portrayed. The best way to achieve this was by expanding
our involvement in public education. In a letter to our Craft, the Grand
Master said, “We must support dedicated academic research that lifts
the veil of secrecy from our fraternity and reveals the influential role we
have played and continue to play in the history of countries and societies
around the world.”
With this framework, the Grand Lodge of California in collaboration
with UCLA’s History Department formed a working relationship in 2009
to foster the academic study of Freemasonry and civil societies. Why
UCLA? It is the home to the largest and most prestigious university
history department in the world, and within it ranks was a true champion
to spearhead the partnership. Dr. Margaret Jacob, Distinguished Professor
of History and one of the world’s foremost Masonic scholars, was selected
to develop, organize and lead the program.
The program is multifaceted, with components that include Annual
International Academic Conferences; Undergraduate/Graduate Course
development and offerings; Research by Post-Doctoral Fellows and
Graduate Fellows; Continuing Education-Public Interest course offerings;
and a Research Depository website that provides academic resources for
those who are interested in the origins and influences of Freemasonry
within a framework of historical places and periods.
Seven international conferences on Freemasonry have been held on the
UCLA campus since 2009. I know many of you in this room have attended
one or more of them and I thank you for your interest and support.
Those conferences have yielded 37 published research papers; brought
forward 30 academic scholars from 13 different countries; 27 professors
from 22 different universities from around the world. Most importantly

30

31

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

of all, these conferences have attracted over 1,500 attendees, among them
Masons, college faculty, Masonic-affiliated organizations, students and the
public at-large, all of whom have learned of our Fraternity’s contributions
to civil societies all over the world.

grand lodge to have implemented an ongoing university, educational
and research partnership.

Five undergraduate courses were developed and taught covering the
subject of Freemasonry and civil society in the United States, Europe,
Mexico and Latin America. Four of those were taught at the university
each academic year between 2009 and 2017.
Additionally, undergraduate and graduate seminars were developed
which specifically focused on Freemasonry’s influence on social and
political history of Mexico and Mexican society.
Most importantly, over 800 students received first-hand educational
insight into Freemasonry in an academic setting and not from the
fantasies of a Hollywood movie.
From 2009 through 2017, the program retained three post-doctoral
fellows and lecturers, and three graduate research and teaching fellows,
who produced numerous published papers in academic journals.
In 2010, we added an extension component to the program that ran for
three years, with over 300 participants from throughout the state. Courses
were taught in both northern and southern California and included
such topics as: Freemasonry and American Democracy; Freemasonry’s
Impact on European History; Freemasonry and Civil Society in 19th
Century Latin America; and Freemasonry, Civil Society and Democracy
Worldwide.
As we have completed our first decade of this innovative program, we
must ask ourselves, “What have we achieved by our efforts?” First and
foremost, as a grand lodge we have established a strong partnership
with academic scholars of Masonic research from around the world.
We have certainly positioned California Freemasonry as the leader
in supporting scholarly research within higher education. Next, we
accomplished one of the original motivations for beginning this endeavor:
we have established a pool of independent resources for addressing and
responding to “Masonic Truths.” Five post-doctoral and graduate fellows
have carried their coursework to other universities, where they are now
teaching them in other states. We have also established a repository
for academic research on Freemasonry. Finally, we are the only U.S

However, with all that has been accomplished, as we enter this next
decade we are faced with significant challenges to the continuation of
the program.
When we began the program you, California Masons, with your lodges
and donors, most graciously contributed over $600,000 to the California
Masonic Foundation to fund and support this effort. Unfortunately, the
program has a price tag and the original funding has come to an end. The
second significant challenge facing the program is the Program Chair, our
champion, Dr. Margaret Jacob, who has formally retired from teaching.
The university has not shown a willingness to continue to support the
partnership in future years.
Our Deputy Grand Master and the Executive Committee are strong
proponents for the continuation of our commitments to this program. As
such, they have formed a special taskforce to explore and recommend a
new relationship with other institutions, and find a new champion that
will allow the program to continue. Most Worshipfuls Cooper, Heisner,
(Steve) Doan and I, along with Very Worshipful Casalou and Doug
Ismail have been tasked with the responsibility of finding paths for the
program’s long-term sustainability. We will be evaluating the potential for
broader participation among other Masonic entities. We will also try to
identify potential funding sources and determine potential opportunities
to move the program to another university. We will continue to explore
participation by other grand lodges with an eye to expanding the program
nationwide in the future.
My brothers, this program has elevated California Freemasonry to a
leadership role in Masonic scholarly research and study. Let us not take
a step backward by letting this vanish. Rather, let us move to ensure that
our position remains for our next generation of Masons. Let me conclude
by thanking our Grand Master for the time and opportunity to share the
update with you and to Most Worshipfuls Cooper, Steve Doan and Very
Worshipful Casalou who have worked with me since the inception to
bring this program into existence. I would also like to thank the California
Masonic Foundation for managing the funding over the past decade.
With success comes future challenges, with challenges we see
innovation and with your support will come continued success. I thank

you my brothers for your attention.
Respectfully Submitted,
Larry Adamson, Past Grand Master- 2008/2009.

Presentation of the Joe Jackson Lodge Outreach Award

This year, the Masonic Homes of California and our Grand Lodge were
pleased to present an award in memory of our late brother, Joe Jackson.
Joe Jackson, a Mason for 60 years and Hiram Award recipient, served
Joseph L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837 and Heartland Lodge No. 576 for
17 years as secretary, assistant secretary, treasurer and chaplain.
Through his tireless efforts and determination to improve and grow
Masonic outreach, Joe was a catalyst for launching the successful Lodge
Outreach Strategic Initiative in Division IX. Joe passed away in 2012,
leaving a legacy that set the foundation for extending Masonic relief.
The Grand Master went on to explain that the Joe Jackson Lodge
Outreach Award is given to a lodge that has demonstrated excellence in
outreach to their members and widows. The Joe Jackson Lodge Outreach
Award was presented to Barstow Boron Lodge No. 682 in Barstow and
Victorville Lodge No. 634 in Victorville, for their extraordinary outreach
efforts this year.

“Honoring our Past, Shaping our Future.” There is no theme more fitting
for the Masonic family. In the few months that I have been Miss California
Job’s Daughter, I have seen how the adult Masonic bodies honor the past.
I have seen and experienced how the masonic family shapes the future
through Job’s Daughters as well as the other youth organizations.
Speaking of the past, we as Job’s Daughters are celebrating our 98th
anniversary. Job’s Daughters was founded in 1920 by Ethel T. Wead Mick.
This was the same year that the 19th amendment, which granted women
the right to vote, was ratified. Mother Mick experienced first-hand what
happens when empowered women put their minds together, so she
created Job’s Daughters. The organization strives to shape young women
into strong leaders, confident public speakers, respectful and respectable
young women, as well as patriotic youth.
Job’s Daughters encourages young women to be philanthropic. Job’s
Daughters International supports HIKE, the Hearing Improvement
Kids Endowment. HIKE provides hearing devices to those in need from
newborn to twenty years old. So many children have been helped by

46

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

HIKE and will be able to live more normal lives and go onto greater
things. This year, the Job’s Daughters of California have been supporting
Project Piece by Piece in partnership with ACT Today! to provide grants
to families who have children with autism. These grants can be used in
so many ways, like building a fence for the child’s safety or purchasing
an iPad to enable the child to communicate easier.

DeMolay teaches young men lessons in leadership, community service,
and brotherhood. It builds their confidence through experiencing these
values in action. Our members plan our own events; we host mini golf
tournaments in order to raise thousands of dollars for charity; we practice
public speaking by reciting ritual; we enjoy each others’ company every
summer at camp. If our values sound familiar, it’s because they’re based
on the values of Masonry. From Truth, Relief, and Brotherly Love came
Filial Love, Reverence, Courtesy, Comradeship, Fidelity, Cleanness, and
Patriotism, thanks to our founder Frank S. Land, a devoted member of
Scottish Rite in Kansas City, Missouri. To this day, DeMolay is steadfastly
supported by Masonry; so, thank you. Thank you to every Mason, who
exemplifies what it means to be a man of good character, in order to serve
as role models for members of DeMolay and all young people. I must also
give a special thanks to the Masons who serve as DeMolay Advisors in
our chapters. You are paving the way for the leaders of the future, and
you are creating new Masons by doing so. I became a Mason because of
my incredible Masonic idols in DeMolay. And finally, thank you to the
Grand Lodge of California, for supporting Northern California DeMolay
in its endeavors to raise prominent leaders in our communities. Your
continued support is greatly appreciated.

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Grand Lodge Officers, distinguished
and honored guests and friends of California Rainbow: Good morning!
Thank you for inviting me to speak on behalf of the International Order
of the Rainbow for Girls in California!
In 2022, Rainbow will celebrate 100 years of sisterhood and service—
just four short years away. This is a huge milestone for any organization
and this would not have been possible without the help of our sponsoring
orders. Masonry, which just celebrated their 300th anniversary, has
always been one of our greatest supporters. Rainbow’s roots are found in
Freemasonry. We have built our order off the values important to Masons
and our members are informed of this fact from the very beginning of
their Rainbow careers.
When I was initiated into the International Order of the Rainbow
for Girls, I received a miniature lambskin apron as a reminder that
Masons had sponsored our assembly and had helped to preserve our
ceremonies and traditions. Every girl who joins Rainbow receives a
miniature lambskin apron as part of her initiation and she is told to keep
it always. It ties our order to yours, and each year at our Grand Assembly,
our State Rainbow Dad, who is a Mason, gives a lambskin apron lecture
in order to inform our new sisters and to remind our older members of
its deep meaning and symbolism. We have adopted many lessons and
symbols from Masonry and the lambskin apron is just one of them.
Our order would not have a history if it were not for Freemasonry
and Reverend W. Mark Sexson. Reverend Sexson served as the Most
Worshipful Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Oklahoma and founded
the International Order of the Rainbow for Girls when he noted that an
order for Girls setting forth the truths of Freemasonry was necessary. As
Rainbow Girls, we are eternally grateful for the support of our Masons
and this is reflected in our ceremonies and floor work. Just as your order
has the seven liberal arts and sciences on which Freemasonry is founded,
symbolized by the seven sides of the lambskin apron, Rainbow has seven
lessons, symbolized by the colors of the Rainbow, which we consider our
cardinal truths. The vows and commitments we make to these values not
only connect us to members of our own orders, but they connect us to
each other. Furthermore, during an initiation, once our sister has taken
her obligation at the altar, we create the shape of a lambskin apron in

50

51

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

our floor work, which further symbolizes that our new sister has joined
in the fraternal organization of our Masonic family. The lambskin apron
has become a priceless connection between our two orders and is just
one example of how our history as an order is linked with Freemasonry.

Our orders’ histories have been intertwined ever since our inception
in 1922. The lambskin apron, which is an emblem of innocence and the
badge of a mason to you, and a symbol of our fraternal organization to us,
is only one of the many ties that unify our Masonic family. This unity can
be utilize to strengthen the relationship between all Masonic orders, as
well as attract prospective members, so that we can continue to celebrate
our orders’ anniversaries for hundreds of years to come. Thank you

Rainbow, like all Masonic orders, would not have a history without our
sponsoring orders. Rainbow, Job’s and DeMolay are often portrayed as
gateways to introduce the youth of today to our Masonic family. And a
good portion of our membership does join the ranks of an adult Masonic
organization. We enjoy and appreciate the fact that these orders provide
the same sisterhoods or brotherhoods and have the same goal of service
that we have experienced in our youth orders. But some of our youth
orders are facing a membership drought, and diminished membership
for our orders may result in a diminished membership in your orders in
a couple of years. The future of our Masonic family can be directly tied to
the vitality and strength of the youth orders. In the past 100 years, society
has changed dramatically. The demands and expectations placed upon
our youth is much greater than it has been in the past and it has become
harder for our orders to stay relevant. While membership continues to
be a challenge for all of us, an investment in our youth orders would
not only ensure the longevity of our orders but also that of our lessons.
The youth groups were created after Masonry had accumulated over
200 of successful history and that history may be the key to secure our
future. When our members join in our ranks, they are not only joining
an organization, they are also joining a history. This is what makes our
Masonic family so unique and sets us apart from other organizations
with similar goals. The lessons that our orders teach, and the history
behind them, are what have helped us stand the test of time and are what
will help us prevail in the years to come. By sharing our values and our
histories with the world, we can draw in more membership. People are
always searching for a sense of belonging and have a desire to be a part
to of something bigger, which is what our rich history allows us to provide.

Mr. Alex Farris, Master Councilor
Southern California, DeMolay International

The story of my parents’ honeymoon is an example of how amazing
our family in California Freemasonry really is. My parents had known
each other for many years before getting married. Most of their early
interactions were through Masonic events; my father being a DeMolay,
and my mother being a Jobs Daughter and a DeMolay sweetheart. They
married in March of 1997. For their honeymoon, they decided to go up
and down the Pacific Coast Highway and stop at every Masonic lodge
possible. One lodge was having a practice for the Third Degree of Masonry.
The Master of the Lodge asked what brought them there and my parents
told them they were on their honeymoon. The Master was thrilled for
them and offered to have them stay at his house so they didn’t have to
pay for a hotel.

Most Worshipful Galloway, Grand Lodge Officers, Masonic Family,
Ladies, & Gentlemen.
Thank you for your hospitality and inviting your youth groups to
participate in today’s activities. Joining me in representing the Southern
California Jurisdiction, Order of DeMolay, are brother Kenneth Gonzalez,
our Deputy Master Councilor, brother John Logan, our Congress Secretary,
and Ms. Erin Phillips, our Jurisdiction Sweetheart.
Almost 100 years ago, a Mason from Kansa City, Missouri had a dream to
develop and prepare young men for the future that eagerly awaits them.
To give the young men of the early 1920’s a chance to pull themselves
up from the tragedies of war back to the prosperity of a peaceful future.
Frank Sherman Land dedicated his life to training young men to be the
leaders of a better tomorrow. Today I stand before you as a product of
that Mason’s dream.
I am here to thank you and tell you that because of your concern for
the future, DeMolay continues to lead that better tomorrow. In March,
DeMolay will celebrate our centennial, 100 years of building tomorrow’s
leaders.
I am honored to be here, and thank you so much for inviting me to
speak. As I thought about the message of my speech, I asked for input
from people close to me. My friends, DeMolays, senior DeMolays, Advisors,
Master Masons, and my family. But, when I began to write, I was thinking
about what this event represents, and I started to think about the people
who attend. To someone on the outside, it might look like we’re all a part
of a fraternity and therefore are good friends. But, when you are a part
of the fraternity, you realize that we aren’t just friends, we’re a family.
Family is about relationships. It’s about the respect and understanding,
trusting and confiding, and the love and affection we show to each other.
Overall, however, it’s about helping. It is about giving and receiving moral
support in times of trouble and need. It is about sharing a joy—a joy that
has no meaning of solitude. That is exactly what our Masonic family does.

My parents’ story taught me from very early on that wherever I go, I
have people to call friends, brothers, and family. That is one of the many
reasons why I have turned in my petition to Golden Trowel Lodge No.
273. I want to follow in the footsteps of my father, both grandfathers, and
Dad Frank S. Land. In light of Most worshipful Galloway’s theme for the
year, “Honoring Our Past, Shaping Our Future,” our purpose is fixed on
building that better future. Focused on repairing the world by improving
ourselves and those around us.

63

Grand Master’s Message
Members of the Grand Lodge – my brethren all,
Welcome to the 169th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of California. Welcome not only to the members of the Grand Lodge of
California, but also to the many guests who are joining us from other
jurisdictions. We hope that you enjoy your stay in this beautiful city and
we offer any assistance you may need to make your time in San Francisco
memorable and enjoyable.
I particularly want to thank Most Worshipful James L. Morgan for
speaking on behalf of the visiting Grand Masters. Most Worshipful Jim
is the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Oregon. We have spent time
together in many jurisdictions in the past few years and his friendship
means a great deal to me.
It is my privilege today to speak to you about all of my official acts
during the year, the general condition of Masonry in the Jurisdiction, and
my recommendations for legislation. It hardly seems possible, but it was
a year ago that I stood here and told you that my theme as Grand Master
would be “Honoring Our Past – Shaping Our Future.” Nearly everything
done this year has been based on shaping our future. I’m pleased with
the initiatives we completed and am happy that those begun will continue
as ongoing priorities.
Our past is what distinguishes us. It grounds us as Masons, so allow
me to briefly reflect on our past and how we honored it this year. One
event, of course, stands out.
I had the privilege and honor of representing the Grand Lodge of
California at Masonry’s 300th anniversary celebration in London in late
October. Gay and I were invited guests of the United Grand Lodge of
England. They were very gracious hosts. Grand Masters from all over the
world attended. It was the largest gathering ever of Grand Masters—there
were 136 present. It was a rare opportunity to talk with the leaders of
Freemasonry from all parts of the world.
As you might imagine, everything about the event was spectacular. Each
visiting Grand Master met, and briefly spoke, with the Grand Master of
the United Grand Lodge of England. He is the Duke of Kent, and he has
been Grand Master for 50 years. We presented the United Grand Lodge of

64

65

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

England a gift of fine china. The pattern was symbolic of both the United
Grand Lodge of England and the Grand Lodge of California.

Finally, I had the privilege and honor to celebrate, along with many
Grand Lodge Officers, the history of eight lodges. Eight lodges celebrated
anniversaries of their founding this year: one honoring 100 years, two
honoring 125 years, and five honoring 150 years. It is amazing to listen
to the history of our early lodges and see the pride that members have
in their lodges and their heritage. It was also wonderful to see that these
celebrations were also community events as well.

The finale of our time there was a grand production in Royal Albert Hall,
where 4,000 masons were in attendance and the events were streamed to
several other locations. A grand feast followed, just as it did 300 years ago.
Through our symposia this year, California Masons focused on our
past. I am grateful to Most Worshipful R. Stephen Doan, Most Worshipful
John L. Cooper, Worshipful Brian Bezner, and Worshipful Adam Kendall
for outstanding Masonic symposia again this year. As you know, some of
our lodges are now in their 170th year. I asked that the symposia reflect
upon our past. The subject this year was California’s Masonic Pioneers.
I was honored this year to be able to join in the celebration of the past
honors of some of our very distinguished brothers. I presented six Golden
Veterans Awards. One was to Most Worshipful Howard Kirkpatrick, a good
friend and member of my own lodge. The other awardees were friends
and mentors, some of whom were present when I was raised to Master
Mason many years ago.
I was truly privileged this year to present six Diamond Jubilee Awards
for 75 years of continuous service. One award was given to a Past Master
of Reading Lodge #254, who was Master in 1951 and is now 104 years old.
Unfortunately, the presentation had to be made at his home since he had
fallen several weeks before and had some difficulty getting around. I am
pleased to say that all the other award ceremonies took place in lodges or
public venues. I am proud to report that in every case, the lodges made the
event truly memorable. Attendance was outstanding, and each ceremony
was a very special occasion for our brother, his family and his lodge.
One presentation was particularly memorable and emotional. It was
to Jack O. Miller, a brother living in Santa Rosa. He is 99 years old and
his wife is only a couple of years younger. As you know, parts of Santa
Rosa were devastated by fire last year. The Millers lost their home, and
only just made it out themselves when a fireman helped them evacuate
at 3:00 a.m. The Miller’s entire family attended the ceremony, from their
daughter to great grandchildren. Long time friends and neighbors were
there, as well as firemen. I knew that Jack had lost his lambskin apron and
his Masonic Bible to the fire. So, after the presentation of the Diamond
Jubilee Award, I presented Jack a new lambskin apron and Masonic Bible.
It was an emotional afternoon.

Too often I believe we dream about the future, and while hope of
immortality ends in fruition, hope for our future and the future of our
lodges requires planning. We can let the future happen unaided, or we
can shape it. A few years ago, our Fraternity Plan was developed with
input and participation from a large percentage of our members. The
2020 Fraternity Plan this year has been the basis for nearly all of our
planning and activities. It is based on four strategic initiatives:
Rewarding Member Experience
Memorable and Meaningful Degrees
Positive Impact on Society
Strong Lodges and Halls
These initiatives have been the foundation of our outstanding leadership
retreats: the Master & Wardens Retreats and the Secretary & Treasurer
Retreats. Again this year, the four Master & Wardens Retreats and both of
the Secretary & Treasurer Retreats were well attended and well received.
Attendees received valuable information that they can use to become
effective lodge leaders. They received tools that they can use to shape the
future of their lodges. Importantly it gave them the opportunity to discuss
with other leaders those things that members say are most important to
them: making true friends, having an opportunity to improve themselves,
and having a positive impact on society.
The feedback on the leadership retreats has been positive and
attendance continues to grow.

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

I am also pleased that there have been very positive results on our
strategic initiatives this year. One initiative that has received attention
for several years now has truly emerged as a success: the creation of
new lodges.

These are conversations that all lodges should have: who should lead
us; what should our experience be like; and who are we as a lodge? You
don’t have to be a new lodge to have these conversations.

66

When we started the 2020 Plan, we knew that we wanted to have the
strongest lodges possible here in California. Uniformly, the strongest
lodges in the world are made of a small group of men with close
friendships, and are places where each member has a meaningful way
of engaging with the lodge.
Half the towns and communities in California do not have a Masonic
lodge. Yet, we know that the towns and communities where Freemasonry
does exist are stronger for it, and benefit from the presence of Masons
in their communities.
In the past two years, we have formed 20 new lodges across the state.
These new lodges are expanding our presence, both in towns and
communities where Masonry has existed for generations, and in places
where the Fraternity has never been.
At our last Annual Communication, we granted charters to seven new
lodges, and one of my first acts as Grand Master was to perform the
Ceremony of Constitution on those lodges. Five such ceremonies were
conducted in one weekend alone. It was rewarding to see the enthusiasm
of the officers and members. Each new lodge is distinctive and each has
determined who they are and what makes them relevant to their members
and Freemasonry in California.
We have learned a lot from this experience. One lesson we learned is
that many of the men who are making up these new lodges are men who
were not otherwise active in their old lodges. By giving the opportunity
for new lodges to form, we are helping brothers who have not been
regularly attending their old lodges—either due to distance or because
they were not finding something meaningful to do there. We are helping
them find a new home in Masonry.
New and renewed lodges are a lot alike and can learn a great deal
from one another. New lodges spend a great deal of time thinking about
the right men to lead their lodges and about where to meet—because
where we meet sets the tone for how we meet. Lodge identity takes up
the majority of the conversation for new lodges.

67

One of the first issues faced by brothers wishing to form a new lodge is
determining where they will meet. In many ways, this is a natural question
to ask. In fact, I would guess that the first time you came to the beautiful
facility in which we are meeting today, you wondered where the lodge
room was. All visitors ask that question. The California Masonic Memorial
Temple was built in 1958 as the third headquarters of our Fraternity.
At that time, we still retained the second Grand Lodge building at Van
Ness Avenue and Market Street, where many San Francisco lodges met.
Because of this, the architects did not see the need to build a lodge room
in the California Masonic Memorial Temple. Instead, they focused on the
auditorium for the Annual Communication and accessory spaces for that
purpose, as well as offices for our staff, and spaces for a memorial to those
Freemasons who lost their lives in the defense of freedom.
Freemasonry, mirroring society, moved to the suburbs in the 1960s and
1970s. Today, the center of San Francisco is a thriving city, with more
prospects than lodges can handle.
There are four young lodges in downtown San Francisco and there are
more needed to meet the demand. To help further Masonry in our state,
and to answer a demand that has evolved since the construction of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple, this year the board that governs
this edifice enacted plans to construct the very first lodge facilities in
the building.
Freemasons Hall is a 5,000 square-foot project that is currently
underway on the Exhibition Hall level. It will provide a meeting location—
as well as social and meeting spaces—for those lodges, and possibly
others, in downtown San Francisco.
The project is moving quickly, but unfortunately not quickly enough
to be able to have tours this weekend. As you are in the Exhibition Hall,
however, you will be able to see where this new space will be.
This was an outstanding year for our continuing support of our youth
orders. It was a year that brought about further participation by all of
the adult concordant and appendant bodies. I would like to congratulate
Most Worshipful Larry Adamson, the chairman of the Youth Orders

69

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Committee, and all of the committee members. This year, they developed
and implemented a multi-year strategic plan.

At our last Annual Communication, the Let’s Write the Future campaign
was introduced. It asked each of us to consider the role we play in
addressing our obligations to each other. It also encouraged us to consider
our history of supporting public education and the needs of some of
the most vulnerable among us. The campaign has captured the desire
of individual brothers and lodges to make a positive impact on society.

68

I had the privilege of attending the annual meetings of each of the
youth orders and was pleased to present checks for the support of their
leadership training programs. I’m proud to say that the scholarships
awarded to our youth order leaders this year totaled $120,000. There
are few better ways to shape our future than to help shape the future
of our youth.
Towards that end, several years ago, under the leadership of Most
Worshipful Perry, a scholarship program was envisioned and implemented
for highly qualified leaders of all four of our youth orders. These
scholarships were to be given to young men and women who gave so
much of their time, some even postponing college for a year as they served
in statewide leadership positions. On Sunday, I will have the privilege
to award this year’s scholarships to very deserving youth order leaders.
Cornerstone ceremonies are excellent opportunities to bring
Freemasonry before the public; to reveal some of our symbolism and
our past. They are a signal of optimism for the future and serve as events
that bring community leaders and the leaders of our local lodges together.
This year, 10 cornerstones were declared well formed, true and trusty.
In nearly every case, there was front-page coverage of the event in
the local newspaper. In several instances, television reporter attended
the event in person. We also conducted three cornerstone rededication
ceremonies. A highlight of the year was the groundbreaking ceremony
for the new skilled nursing and memory care building at our Masonic
Home in Covina.
There was one very unusual ceremony that involved Grand Lodge
Officers, local Masons, community leaders, and the relatives of an early
Past Master of King David’s Lodge in San Luis Obispo. In this ceremony,
we sealed a large stone pyramid in the cemetery—the Past Master’s
resting place. I can now say that I am an operative Mason as well as a
speculative Mason.

I would like to thank members of our Let’s Write the Future Leadership
Committee, as well as the board of trustees of the California Masonic
Foundation for undertaking this critical campaign. I particularly want
to thank those Pace Setter lodges and individuals who stepped in and
expressed their support this year. Thank you also for the generosity of
Masonic brethren over these many decades. With their help, we continue
to meet our promise to extend relief with dignity and the highest quality
of health care.
Our Commitment to Addressing Advanced Care
in our Masonic Homes
We have always risen to the occasion as a Fraternity, and today is no
different. In our Masonic Homes, as our members live longer and their
healthcare needs continue to be more complex, we often see that the
needs of spouses are on separate paths. The good news is that they are
living longer. Unfortunately, our campuses are not currently equipped
with the facilities necessary to keep them together with their loved
ones and communities of support. In too many occasions, we have had
to separate spouses in order to provide the level of care that they need
and deserve.
We know that diseases like Alzheimer’s and dementia can place an
unbearable burden on a relationship. We also know that separating
couples during that most vulnerable time of their lives is not consistent
with our values or principles. Our Let’s Write the Future campaign will
help ensure that those in our care do not have to lose the support, love
and safety provided by those who care the most about them. To address
this reality, we are building and expanding facilities both on our Union
City and Covina campuses that will fulfill our promise and address the
needs of the most vulnerable in our Masonic family.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

We Believe in Strong Families and Access
to a High Quality Education

we face issues every day, we constantly look forward to the future. Our
position is to anticipate change and to try to shape it rather than react to it.

Few issues are more important to the development of our democratic
society than that of providing access to education. We repeatedly see
proof that our freedoms and our way of life are connected to our ability
to ensure that each member of our society has the opportunity to learn
and think.

I have seen a number of outstanding degrees and ceremonies this
year, and I want to thank our retiring Grand Lecturer, Very Worshipful
Jack Rose. It has been my honor to serve with Jack for many years. He
has been instrumental in making our Ritual meaningful and memorable.

Freemasonry has understood this concept since our earliest days.
American Freemasonry has a long and proud tradition of supporting
public education. There are countless examples of Masons leading the
way in the struggle to provide equal access to all. This is a bedrock tenet
of our Craft.
Today, evidence shows that building strong reading habits at home
not only helps strengthen the family unit, but also builds vocabularies;
increases reading scores; and provides a meaningful and important
tool to engage entire families in the academic performance of our most
vulnerable children. By partnering with Raising A Reader—a relationship
now in its eighth year—we have brought the gift of high-quality books
to thousands of families in California who otherwise might never have
had one book in their homes. We have trained parents to use reading
together with their children as a tool to bond and to help them learn and
become more curious about the world.
The Let’s Write the Future campaign will allow us to install this
evidence-tested program in 1,000 of California’s lowest performing
classrooms. More than 100,000 children will ultimately benefit from
this effort. This is a remarkable accomplishment. This is also a gift to our
families, our schools and our communities. We can only speculate how
many lives we have affected, even saved, because of this amazing project.
I am incredibly proud of the progress we have made thus far, and we
are not done. We are, however, more than halfway to our goals. I have
asked throughout the year for you to help shape our future. Let’s Write the
Future is a call to action. Remember, my brothers, our Masonic heritage
will forever be linked to Charity. It is a virtue that shows the world what
it means to be a Freemason. Thank you for ensuring that this tradition
remains strong in California.
I am pleased to report that Masonry in California is strong. While

Lodges have plans and programs in place to ensure rewarding member
experiences. Plans have been developed based on values and the
distinctive attributes of individual lodges.
Most lodges and halls are functioning very well, and while some
struggle, in most cases it is because they choose to ignore or violate
provisions of the California Masonic Code, or fail to take advantage of
the help available to them. I was pleased to be able to return the charter
to East San Diego Lodge No. 561. They are once again a well-functioning
lodge. It gave me no pleasure to suspend the charter of Maya Lodge No.
793, but a flagrant disregard of our code and specific instructions from
me could not be ignored.
Support for our lodges and halls is outstanding, and I am pleased to say
that a high, and growing, percentage of our lodges and halls are taking
advantage of the resources available to them.
Lodges, and individual members, continue to do amazing things in
their communities. In addition to supporting the Let’s Write the Future
campaign, they also do many things locally that truly have an impact
on society.
The Grand Lodge of California continues to enjoy excellent relationships
with other grand lodges. While addressing our lodges, I nearly always
point out that we are pleased to share our jurisdiction with the Most
Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California and the Grand Lodge
of Iran in Exile. We are also pleased with our close association with the
Grand Lodge of Baja California and the Grand Lodge of Baja California
Sur.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Several of our Grand Masters and our Grand Secretary have developed
a close working relationship with the United Grand Lodge of England.
That relationship allowed us to facilitate a meeting this year between
the Grand Chancellor of the United Grand Lodge of England and the
leadership of the Grand Lodge of Baja California. The result is that the
United Grand Lodge of England now recognizes them as the rightful
Grand Lodge of Baja California.

GRAND MASTER’S CALENDAR

Just saying thank you to all that have helped me this year is inadequate
to convey how much I truly appreciate your friendship and willingness
to help and serve our wonderful Fraternity.
The Past Grand Masters share a special relationship with the Grand
Master, one that I truly value. They have been supportive and willing to
assist any time I asked. Thank you!
The Grand Lodge staff is perhaps the most dedicated and helpful
group with whom I have ever worked. Each year they support a new
Grand Master and new Grand Lodge Officers. Their skills and desire
to support the business of Grand Lodge is amazing. They have become
good friends. Thank you!
Thanks to this year’s Grand Lodge Officers and their wives. They
traveled the state and represented California Masonry well. I know
every Grand Master believes he had the best Grand Family. I know I do.
Finally, I want to thank Gay, my wonderful wife of more years than she
would want me to say. Not only has she been supportive this year, but she
has encouraged and supported me my entire time as a Mason. Actually,
supportive does not really describe what she has done. She has been an
ambassador for California Masonry. She has cheerfully interacted with
Masons and their ladies wherever we have gone.
Finally, I will say to you what I have said to Masons of California
throughout the year.
I am proud to be a Mason!
I am proud to be a California Mason!
I am honored that you asked me to serve as your Grand Master!
Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Bruce R. Galloway, Grand Master

Report of the Deputy Grand Master
2018-19 Grand Lodge Budget
Stuart A. Wright, Deputy Grand Master
Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
At the last Annual Communication, the brethren representing our
lodges adopted the per capita proposal I presented as Senior Grand
Warden. I am grateful for the support and it has allowed me to present
the following budget for the 2018-2019 Grand Lodge Year.
Revenue for the year is expected to be slightly higher than the current
year, although income from per capita is relatively flat. Expenses align
with the revenue, including expenses for iMember 2.0 and additional
lodge accounting support. The budget is balanced with a small surplus.
This budget will allow us to continue the programs and services that
our members and lodges rely upon and which aid us in providing a
rewarding membership experience; meaningful and memorable degrees;
strong lodges and halls; and a positive impact on society. Programs and
services supported by this budget include:
• Financial services to lodges and halls, including accounting
services, tax return services, and tax-exempt status restoration.
• New lodge development efforts that have already resulted in the
creation of 18 new lodges throughout the state.
• Leadership training events, including the Masters and Wardens
Retreats, Secretaries and Treasurers Retreats, Inspectors Retreats,
the Inspector Development Academy, and the Lodge Management
Certification Program
• Masonic education including support for events like the
International Conference on Freemasonry at UCLA, the Annual
Symposium, and the Candidate Learning Center
• Technology and data, including iMember, the Member Center,
and the Vault.

90

Proceedings of the

• Ritual education and training, including Ritual Conferences for
Inspectors, Officers Coaches, and Lodge Officers and the annual
Ritual Competition
• Communications to Masons, widows, and the public including
the lodge app; new lodge website templates; the bimonthly
publication of the California Freemason magazine; the monthly
electronic newsletter The Leader sent to all Lodge Officers; allmember emails; as well as the maintenance of seven websites
and all of the social media outlets.
• Community outreach that includes grand lodge events at
community libraries, courthouses, fire stations, and schools
throughout the state.
• Information and service requests
• Real estate services and support, including support and
consultation for building improvements, leases, sales, and
purchases.
Expenses exclusive of depreciation for the next fiscal year are
estimated to be $3,312,411. These expenses are divided between fraternal,
appropriations, programs and general and administrative expenses. The
projected net revenue after expenses is $19,928. The Executive Committee
and Finance Committee closely monitor the budget and we seek the
assistance of the Executive Committee, Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary,
and the Finance Committee to see that we operate according to it.
As Deputy Grand Master, I am excited about the future of Freemasonry
in California. I believe in our future and more importantly, I believe in
you. Working together, our lodges and the grand lodge can continue to
inspire this generation and future generations to join and engage in
our work as Freemasons. Let’s use our work together to raise the level
of enthusiasm even higher and show the world how proud we are to be
Masons in all that we do. It can be done, and you will make a difference!

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

I appreciate your past support on the per capita proposal I made as
Senior Grand Warden, and I thank you for your support now as we
position Freemasonry as a relevant and respected Fraternity for the next
decade and beyond!

Respectfully submitted by,
Stuart A. Wright, Deputy Grand Master

Proceedings of the

Installation Address

My goals are simple:

Stuart A. Wright, Grand Master

1.

To raise the level of excitement within our Craft

This long history of success with our grand lodge stems from Grand
Masters of the past who are no longer with us, as well as those currently
with us and sitting on my right.

2.

To raise the level of enthusiasm in each lodge

3.

To increase the commitment of everyone

4.

To ensure fun exists outside of Ritual

Most Worshipful Sirs, I salute each and every one of you and thank
you for the great leadership you provided to this grand lodge. Let’s offer
a big hand for their constant mentorship.
For the benefit of our non-Masonic friends, let me offer a short
explanation that may be helpful.
After a man asks to be a member, Freemasonry affects—indeed
changes—his whole circle of life.
He becomes more tolerant, more humble, more forgiving, more
benevolent, more understanding, more patient, and more committed
because of the impact of the lessons he learns in his three degrees. These
lessons use tools of a stonemason like the square, compass, level, plumb
and so on to explain the values and tenants to him.
During his Masonic career, and by applying these lessons, he becomes
a better father, son, neighbor and member of the community. He comes
a better man.
Freemasonry… the difference is you.
I selected this theme because in actual fact, each of you have affected
Masonry, one way or another, from the time you knocked on the door until
right now. Many who are no longer with us, also made a difference and
in some cases, they made a huge one. Our Past Grand Master’s themes,
when read, had “you” in mind.
The greatest man of a hundred years ago can do nothing now, but each
of you are here in the living spirt.

101

In each of these goals, I parallel the 2020 plan. The four strategic goals
from the 2020 plan include rewarding member experience; providing
memorable and meaningful degrees; creating strong lodges and halls;
and having a positive impact on society. All four of these will continue
in place and intertwine with the four goals I cited above.
Those action pins you get that say “I make a difference,” are designed
to stimulate conversation. Ask each other what difference he or she has
made. Answers can actually encourage each of us and should increase
the enthusiasm and the excitement that we say we desire.
This upcoming year, we will celebrate a couple of anniversaries:
First, our youth order, DeMolay, will celebrate 100 years. We will be
emphasizing this in the California Freemason magazine, and this very
topic will be the subject of the symposia in San Francisco and Long
Beach. The Northern California Jurisdiction of DeMolay plans to place
a statue and time capsule at the Masonic Homes in Union City, as well
as establish a new lodge composed of Senior DeMolays.
The Southern California Jurisdiction of DeMolay will have a time
capsule placed on the grounds of the Masonic Homes in Covina. There
is also a national celebration in Kansas City, Missouri in June of 2019,
at which I will represent our grand lodge. We are very honored that our
own Avery Brinkley was elected International Master Councilor from
the Southern California Jurisdiction.
Let me just say that for approximately two years, the planning for
grand lodge to support the 100th Anniversary of DeMolay has been
accomplished by the persistence and skills of Very Worshipful Glenn
Woody. Thank you so very much. “You have to have the ball to score” …
Right!

102

103

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Secondly, our own California Masonic Foundation will celebrate 50 years
in 2019. To celebrate the occasion and the great works that the Foundation
has performed in that time, we are planning a very special black-tie festive
board on June 22, 2019. More about this huge event later.

My sincere thanks to all those here today, both in the audience and
behind the scenes.

We have six lodges to constitute within 90 days from this communication—
in accordance with our California Masonic Code—and all have been
scheduled. Once completed, this will bring the number of new lodges to 21
since the last communication. This is the envy of many other grand lodges
and we need to be proud of this accomplishment and all those involved.

Each of you now have the opportunity to expand your difference in
your own life, the life of others, in your lodges and in your communities.

Our committee structure is under review as we gear up for the future.
Your Executive Committee is looking at long-range planning in all areas
with the forecasts to be centered on 2050. This is an ongoing process and
requires time and creative thinking. We hope you will be excited as we
move forward.
Branding has always been a concern to me, since we always hang our
worldwide Square and Compass for all to see, but we never get around
to communicating the values it stands for—values that are needed so
dearly in society today.
We are exploring statewide opportunities to explain these values to
the greater public through a variety of means. Our Foundation is an
important way our square and compass extends into the community.
Public School’s Month events and Masons Night at the ballparks are
important events that have a broad reach into the greater communities.
I urge you to attend and raise awareness for these efforts in your own
communities and beyond. Lodge Open House month will be another
opportunity to introduce members of the public who may not be familiar
with our Craft and give them a chance to see how we live and strive to
deepen our values. Lodge Open House month will be in September of
2019, and we will roll out resources you can use for this event over the
course of the year. Our robust digital marketing channels will also be
leveraged to build interest among younger, would-be Masons, throughout
the state and beyond.

Freemasonry… the difference is you.

You can make a profound difference.
Thank you.

Report of the Senior Grand Warden
Per Capita Recommendation for 2018-19
John E. Trauner, Senior Grand Warden
Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
I am pleased to present this proposal for the per capita assessment
that will be collected in 2019 to fund the fiscal year operations of Grand
Lodge for the period of November 1, 2019 through October 31, 2020.
I have worked for the last two years in preparing a draft budget for the
2020 fiscal year. Earlier this year, I shared these plans with the Masters
and Wardens who attended our spring leadership retreats. I appreciate
your input.
In preparing a draft budget for the FY2019, I have considered the
factors that will increase per capita, as well as those that will reduce
any increase.
The major factors that will increase the per capita are:
• Membership decline. We project a total loss of 1,504 billable
members. This represents a loss in revenue of $73,320 or $1.76
in per capita.
• Expenses. I have been careful to keep expenses to a necessary
minimum. Total expenses are only 2% over the previous year.
The total impact on increased expenses represents an increase
in per capita of $1.61.
These factors together would require an increase in per capita of $3.37.
However, a number of factors will reduce per capita. These include an
increased dividend from the Nob Hill Masonic Center of $20,000, and
increases in revenue from investments and all other sources that total
$22,692. With these factors, the necessary per capita increase can be
lowered by $1.37 to $2.00.
Therefore, the per capita I am proposing for FY2020 is $50.75.

108

Proceedings of the

At this per capita rate, we are projecting the total amount of per capita
collected will be $2,104,806, which is less than one-half of one percent
more than in the previous year.
I believe Freemasonry provides us with a golden opportunity. With your
support of this proposal, we can continue the programs and services that
make it possible to take advantage of these opportunities. Whether it is
the Masonic education or leadership training programs, the technology
and data services, or the important financial services to lodges and halls,
we are all working together today harder than ever to provide a bright
future for our Fraternity. I appreciate your support for this proposal and
I look forward to working with you in the years ahead.

Respectfully submitted,
John E. Trauner, Senior Grand Warden

Report of the Grand Treasurer
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren All:
In this, my third address to you as your Grand Treasurer, I am pleased
to report to you that the financial health of our Grand Lodge and related
entities remains strong. We benefit from the efforts and expertise of
so many brothers who volunteer their time as board members and
Committee Members. We also benefit from the expertise of our entire
Grand Lodge financial team led by: Tom Boyer, our CFO; Maribel Pasamic,
our Controller; Khalil Sweidy, our Director of Financial Planning; and of
course, Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, our Grand Secretary.
The Audit Committee, led by Worshipful Tony Garcia, has again chosen
to engage Moss Adams as our outside auditor, to ensure that our financial
statement audits for all of our Grand Lodge entities continue to go
smoothly. As of our last fiscal year ending October 31, 2017, each of our
entities once again received a clean audit opinion and were informed
that our internal controls remain effective and that our model for
shared service costs is not only appropriate but consistent with industry
standards.
The Finance Committee, led by Worshipful David Von Bima, continues
to work with our Deputy Grand Master and Senior Grand Warden each
year to provide wise and timely counsel in the preparation of their annual
budgets and per-capita determinations.
The Insurance Committee, led by Worshipful David Forsyth, continues
their tireless work in their detailed review of our complex insurance
needs for not only our Grand Lodge entities but also for our lodges and
hall associations. This includes an ongoing review of claims to ensure
an optimal result for the benefit of the Craft, and to look for ways to do
all of this in the most cost-efficient manner.
The Investments Committee, led by Worshipful Eric Hatfield, is deeply
immersed in their ongoing efforts to monitor the economic factors that
impact our portfolio. In their evaluation of our investment policies, they
continue to recommend that 4.5 percent of our investment portfolio be
distributed to fund operating budgets, which will also work to preserve
and grow our overall portfolio for future use. Their relationship with
NEPC as our investment advisory firm, which began during the last Grand
Lodge year, has brought forth a fresh perspective on our various fund

I have reported the various changes to the investments of each of our
entities but it is also noteworthy that in aggregate our Master Trust has
increased $8,891,636 or 0.8% net of distributions for the operations for
all of our entities. The Master Trust now stands at $1,063,159,164 as of
July 31, 2018.
Master Trust Allocation:

The breakdown of the Master Trust per entity is as follows:
• Masonic Homes in the amount of $985,535,103 or 92.7 percent
• California Masonic Foundation in the amount of $35,661,162 or
3.4 percent
• Acacia Creek in the amount of $23,548,961 or 2.2 percent
• California Masonic Memorial Temple in the amount of $6,321,595
or 0.6%
• Grand Lodge in the amount of $5,888,646 or 0.5%
• Lodge Investment Program in the amount of $3,888,314 or 0.4%
• Lodge Life Membership Program in the amount of $1,665,071
or 0.2%
• Nob Hill Masonic Center in the amount of $650,312 or far less
than 1/10 of a percent

The return on investment for the year to date is 1.8 percent and since
inception of our Master Trust in 1995 it remains at 7.7 percent.
As we marvel at the size our Master Trust has grown to, we must
remember that these funds are not available simply to withdraw to cover
all of the expenses of each of our entities. As I previously mentioned, we
are limited to draw 4.5 percent of the five-year average of the investments
for each entity to support the operations. This means that in the example
of our Masonic homes, with a current operating budget of approximately
$57 million and an investment distribution of approximately $35 million,
we have a delta of approximately $22 million dollars that needs to be
made up from other sources. Such sources can include fees for certain
services as well as each of our annual contributions in fulfillment of our
ongoing obligations to each other.
In 1992, our Grand Lodge created the Endowment Fund, which was to
be funded each year by the budget surpluses of each Grand Master. Since
that time, the Endowment Fund has grown to $2,548,011 as of July 31,
2018. It will be increased once again by the surplus from Most Worshipful
Galloway. This same Endowment Fund will now provide $104,356 for
the budget of Right Worshipful Wright in the fiscal year ending October
31, 2019 compared to the amount of $100,894 for the current fiscal year.
