As previously mentioned, our participation in the Grand Lodge Life
Membership Funds and the Grand Lodge General Investments Fund has
increased over the last year, thereby providing lodges a much needed
option in their investment strategies. As of July 31, 2018, we have 42
lodges participating in the Life Membership Master Fund with a value of
$1,665,071. We also have 14 lodges participating in the Lodge Investments
Master Fund with a value of $3,888,314.

Lastly, I would like to thank all of you for the opportunity to continue
to serve you as Grand Treasurer. I enjoy working on your behalf with so
many caring and dedicated individuals. I would especially like to thank
my friend, Very Worshipful Allan Casalou. His business knowledge and
tireless efforts continue to bring increased efficiency and professionalism
into the operations of our Grand Lodge and related entities for the benefit
of all California Masons.

Lodge Investment and Life Membership Programs:
Respectfully submitted,
Arthur L. Salazar, Jr., Grand Treasurer

Unfortunately, we continue to have lodges and hall associations
experiencing challenges with budgets, investments, payroll matters, tax
filings, and general accounting matters. I encourage all of our Lodge
Officers and hall association directors to take advantage of the many
resources available to you through our Grand Lodge, including Intacct
training, tax preparation services, payroll services, investment guidance,
audit guidance, real estate matters, and many others. In utilizing these
services and the expertise of our Grand Lodge staff, you will be able to
focus more of your attention on practicing Masonry within your lodge
and your community.
I would also like to encourage you to begin your budget discussions
as early as possible, with all of the key people in your lodge, like your
prospective Wardens, Treasurer, Secretary, Trustees, Hall Association
Directors, and those with experience in such matters. Discuss your
budgets openly and frequently so that the finances of your lodge do not
become one of the mysteries of Freemasonry.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

125

Report of the Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
In my 11th report as your Grand Secretary, I am pleased to state that
Masonry in California is thriving, and poised to maintain and grow its
reputation as a relevant and respected fraternity in the 21st century.
MEMBERSHIP INFORMATION
Current Membership Statistics
As of June 30, 2018, we had 46,443 active Masons, including 2,887
Entered Apprentice Masons and 903 Fellow Crafts. More than 2,000 are
newly initiated, affiliated, or restored brothers. This is offset by 3,485
losses, which lowers our total membership by 3 percent since last year.
Nearly 1,200 brothers were suspended for nonpayment of dues over
the past year – constituting 80 percent of the net membership decline.
Withdrawals were up in 2018 at 878 compared to 714 in 2017.
Our California Masonic family also includes 24,539 widows, slightly
more than last year. Widows receive our communications throughout the
year, including California Freemason magazine. I often receive grateful
responses in return, and I encourage every lodge to contact their widows
to offer fellowship and support.
Please refer to my written report for detailed membership activity, bylaw amendments, life memberships, and veterans’ awards.
Historic Trends
From 1944 to 1953, nearly 115,000 men were made Masons in California
lodges, nearly doubling our membership in a single decade. Unfortunately,
this growth proved to be unsustainable. Some men joined without truly
appreciating Freemasonry as a lifelong brotherhood. In other situations,
lodges grew too quickly to provide the meaningful experience that had
attracted members in the first place. In response, many of these brothers
left our fraternity over a period of time that has spanned decades.
This decline has continued as the brothers from this generation who
maintained membership have gradually passed away. For many years,
withdrawals and deaths surpassed new memberships by two and three

126

127

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

times. We are now reaching the conclusion of this era. Of the 1,444
brothers who ascended to the Celestial Grand Lodge this year, only 184
were initiated during that time.

Our Member Services team provides core support to lodges and
members. They processed nearly 7,200 requests this year, completing
more than 90 percent on the first day with an average completion time
of 90 minutes. They handled nearly 1,200 background checks and 1,300
awards and recognitions.

Our lodges have followed the same pattern, experiencing a period of
expansion and growth followed by many consolidations, which greatly
reduce our ability to make Masons. Between 1989 and 1998, 141 lodges
were lost to consolidation – an average of 14 per year. From 1999 to 2008,
there were 74 consolidations, about seven per year. In the last 10 years,
there have been 22 consolidations, an average of two per year; and, in
2018, there was only one.
Looking Forward
With the significant losses and consolidations behind us, turning
around a 50-year membership decline is today within our grasp. It won’t
happen on its own, but with some emphasis, our Fraternity can stabilize
and grow again.
If, next year, every California lodge achieves two more gains and two
fewer losses, our membership will likely stabilize. That is to say, if every
lodge in 2019 initiates, affiliates, or restores just two more brothers and
suspends or demits just two fewer brothers, our total membership should
remain essentially the same. From there, we will be in a solid position
for growth.
When we created our 2020 Fraternity Plan, we chose to prioritize
the quality of member experience over a numerical gain in brothers.
Articulating this was a cultural shift from the Fraternity of yesterday,
and it was a concept born of our belief that only strong lodges can make
good Masons who in turn elevate our Fraternity and inspire others to
follow their example. This must continue to be our priority as we look
towards the future.
PROGRAMS AND SERVICES
Led by the 2020 Fraternity Plan, we are guiding lodges in creating
sound administrative, financial, and operating plans; creating strong
new lodges; and supporting lodge leadership. More than ever before, we
are helping lodges to reduce administrative burdens and prioritize the
member experience.
Membership Services

Leadership retreat attendance reached over 1,100 participants, with
520 officers attending the Master and Wardens Retreats alone. Member
Services administered these and other statewide events, processing more
than 3,200 registrations.
iMember 2.0
This year we began developing iMember 2.0, an integrated membership
system that facilitates the duties of lodge secretaries while improving all
brethren’s experience. This system will launch next year.
New Lodge Development
Our efforts in new lodge development continue to grow. Since 2016, we
have created 20 new lodges. Six were instituted this year, one institution
is already planned for next year, and three are preparing to submit letters
of intent. New lodges have evolved in communities that have never had a
Masonic lodge, as well as in those where lodges have closed. New lodges
have also evolved in larger cities where there is rising demand and not
enough supply. I will give a full report on charters tomorrow.
Financial Services
The Financial Services team provides accounting, budgeting, reporting,
and audit support for Grand Lodge and our related entities. Additionally,
they provide a variety of supportive programs and resources for lodges
and halls.
This year, Financial Services prepared and filed 414 tax returns for
lodges, hall associations, and Masonic Homes residents. Nearly 70 percent
of our lodges are now using Intacct, which reduces the administrative
workload of lodge financial accounting and reporting. A dedicated Intacct
hotline also makes it easy for brothers to receive support.
Lodges not using these services are a minority and some of these lodges
have found themselves with serious financial and tax problems that could
have been avoided if we had been working more closely together. If your

128

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Proceedings of the

lodge or hall is not using these services, I strongly encourage you to look
closely at the services being offered and take full advantage of them.
Communications
Our Communications team executes a comprehensive communications
strategy for our Fraternity through websites, social media, email, a
monthly leadership e-newsletter, and California Freemason magazine,
which once again received national awards in the publishing industry.
Association Media & Publishing awarded last year’s 300th anniversary
commemorative edition a Silver Excel Award, and the magazine is a
finalist in seven categories of the Folio Awards, a prestigious editorial,
design, and marketing competition.
In 2017, we welcomed brothers Dago Rodriquez, Emanuel Rose, Russ
Hennings, Ian Laurelin, and James Tucker to a new California Freemason
Publication Committee, which now guides the strategic direction of our
magazine. This year, they created greeting cards with artwork from the
magazine for Masons to share with their brothers, family, and friends.
Purchase yours at the Communications booth in the lobby.
More than 200 lodges and 5,000 brothers are using the lodge app,
which connects members on a secure mobile platform. Many lodges
collect payments through the app, collectively processing thousands of
dollars each month. We have now created website templates for more
than 70 lodges, as well as halls, thereby providing them with a turnkey,
professional online presence. To learn more about these services, visit
the Communications booth.
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
It is my responsibility to inform the Grand Master of matters pertaining
to foreign grand lodge recognition and to present to you, in the form of
a motion, the recognition of certain grand lodges that meet our criteria.

129

Mexico
In Mexico, two grand lodges operate on a national or regional basis.
Each of Mexico’s 31 states also has a grand lodge. The state grand lodges
participate in a conference called the Confederation of Regular Grand
Lodges of the United States of Mexico, which is similar to our Conference
of Grand Masters of Masons in North America. Our Grand Lodge currently
recognizes 13 of these state grand lodges, and we have received requests
for recognition from two others:
1.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of the State of Tlaxcala
Ancient F. & A.M. was established in 2014 by a warrant from the Grand
Lodge of the State of Nayarit. It has been a member of the Confederation
of Regular Grand Lodges of the United States of Mexico since 2015.
2.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge Ancient F. & A.M. “Guadalupe
Victoria” of the State of Durango was founded on July 8, 1923 by the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge “Benito Juarez” Ancient F. & A.M. of the State
of Coahuila. It is a longtime member of the Confederation of Regular
Grand Lodges of the United States of Mexico.
In 2004, the Commission on Information for Recognition determined
that the grand lodges of the Confederation of Regular Grand Lodges
of the United States of Mexico were regular and met the standards of
recognition. In reviewing their applications, we also find that they are
regular and meet the standards of recognition of our grand lodge.
Therefore, Most Worshipful, I move that the Grand Lodge of California
approve the petitions and grant mutual recognition with the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of the State of Tlaxcala Ancient F. & A.M. and
the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge Ancient F. & A.M. “Guadalupe Victoria”
of the State of Durango.
Prince Hall
The Grand Lodge of California extended an offer of mutual recognition
to all Prince Hall grand lodges in the U.S. that maintain mutual recognition
with a grand lodge in their jurisdiction that is already recognized by the
Grand Lodge of California. In 2017, the Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of the
State of Alabama and the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge
of Alabama F. & A.M. entered into an agreement of mutual recognition.
Therefore, Most Worshipful, I move that our Grand Lodge extend an

130

Proceedings of the

offer of mutual recognition to the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand
Lodge of Alabama F. & A.M.
In 1849, Prince Hall grand lodges organized a North American
conference to perpetuate harmony among all Prince Hall grand lodges
in this region. All of the Prince Hall grand lodges that we recognize in
the U.S. are members of this conference. There are four Prince Hall grand
lodges outside the U.S. that are also members of this conference, with
which we have not offered mutual recognition:
1. Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge F. & A.M. Province
of Ontario and its jurisdiction was formed in 1856. It maintains
mutual recognition with the Grand Lodge Ancient F. & A.M. of
Canada in the Province of Ontario.
2. Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge F. & A.M. Province
of Alberta and its jurisdiction was formed in 1997. It maintains
mutual recognition with the Grand Lodge of Alberta Ancient F.
& A.M.
3. Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of the
Caribbean and its jurisdiction was formed in 1993.
4. Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of the
Commonwealth of the Bahamas was founded in 1950.
The United Grand Lodge of England, which has lodges in the Caribbean
and Bahamas, recognizes each of these grand lodges.
Therefore, Most Worshipful, I move that the Grand Lodge of California
extend an offer of mutual recognition to these four Prince Hall grand
lodges, which are members of the Conference of Grand Masters Prince
Hall Masons, Inc.

APPRECIATION
As I conclude my report, I wish to extend my sincere gratitude to the
lodge Secretaries and Assistant Secretaries whose dedicated work is the
backbone of our jurisdiction. I also wish to thank our Assistant Grand
Lecturers and District Inspectors who, in addition to their ritual duties,
provide invaluable administrative support throughout the year.
I wish to thank Worshipful Brother David Von Bima who will retire
from the Finance Committee after five years as chairman, and Worshipful
Brother Shay Maghame who retires after five years as chairman of the
Masonic Properties Committee.
I also extend my congratulations and appreciation to Very Worshipful
Brother Jack Rose who will retire as Grand Lecturer. For many years, Jack
and his wife, Robin, have been ardent supporters of our Grand Lodge
and they both deserve our lasting gratitude.
I am blessed to work with our Grand Treasurer, Very Worshipful Brother
Art Salazar, Jr., who is a great friend and colleague. We are thankful for
the team of true professionals in our Grand Lodge office, all of whom
care deeply about our Fraternity and support our mission with their
dedicated service. I thank them all for their commitment and good work.
Finally, I wish to extend my deep appreciation to our Grand Master.
Most Worshipful Galloway is a model leader, gentleman, and Freemason.
While guiding our Grand Lodge, he communicated clear priorities and
earned the respect and admiration of brothers throughout our jurisdiction.
Despite his hectic schedule, he modeled the upmost gentlemanly conduct,
often expressing his gratitude for those who worked alongside him in
the form of handwritten notes and other highly personal courtesies. And,
foremost, he has exemplified the true traits of Freemasonry to which
we all aspire – seeking truth, giving back to those in need, and behaving
honorably and fairly. Thank you, Most Worshipful, for your leadership,
friendship, and service to our Craft.
And thank you, my brothers, for the opportunity to serve and work
with you.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary

Report of the Grand Lecturer
Most Worshipful and Members of the Grand Lodge:
This afternoon, I present to you my seventh and final report as your
Grand Lecturer. With this report I will conclude my term as a Grand
Lodge Officer; a commitment that has spanned more than a quarter of
a century. I began in 1989 as a Grand Lodge Committeeman, became an
Inspector in 1991, the Grand Pursuivant in 1996, the Assistant Grand
Tiler in 1997, the Grand Tiler in 1999, the Assistant Grand Lecturer in
2001, and finally your Grand Lecturer in 2011.
This decision to not seek re-election was made of my own free will
and accord. The time has come for me to step aside and allow another
brother the opportunity to serve you as your custodian of our Ritual. This
will also allow me the opportunity to return to, and serve, my own lodge,
something I have been longing to do.
The California Masonic Codes requires that I provide you with a
detailed accounting of the past year’s activities and the status of the
Ritual in our jurisdiction. Additionally, I will also provide you with a
summary of the accomplishments of the Ritual Committee during my
tenure as Grand Lecturer.
RITUAL ACTIVITIES
I was again invited to, and attended, the Executive Committee Meetings
where I provided my insight relative to administrative and Ritual matters.
During this past Grand Lodge term, I continued to hold monthly
conference calls with the Assistant Grand Lecturers, which included
conversations with the Grand Secretary and his staff on relevant
administrative matters.
I held five Ritual examinations of the lodges within Divisions 2, 4, 6
and 8, which covered all three degrees, as well as two Inspectors’ Ritual
conferences that also included all three degrees as well as the ceremonial
ritual associated with the opening of the Grand Lodge of California.

In keeping with the Fraternity’s 300th Anniversary and the Grand
Master’s theme of “Honoring our past, Shaping our future,” I accepted an
invitation from Conejo Valley Lodge to speak at their educational night
about the history and development of our Craft Ritual over the past 300
years. Prior to the start of the event, the Lodge Master, Worshipful Frank
Shapiro, recognizing that I enjoyed daily walks, presented me with a very
special handmade walking stick, which I will always cherish.
The Ritual Committee held a Ritual competition for individuals and teams
in the delivery of the Marshal’s Interrogations and the Perambulations
in all three degrees. Sixteen members competed in the individual
competitions and nine teams competed in the team competitions. The
following are the competition results.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

I was disappointed with how fewer Masons participated in this year’s
competitions compared to last year’s. It is my hope that next year’s
competition, which will be the Master’s long-form lecture of the third
degree, will inspire greater attention and participation. The competition
will allow an individual and a team of two brethren to compete in the
delivery of the lecture.

“Let us accept the fact that Masonic Ritual should never be used as a
means to embarrass anyone. Masonic Ritual is an excellent method to
develop poise and composure when addressing groups. One who has
overcome the tensions of rendering a portion of Ritual, where every word
is known by most listeners, has the ability to speak at ease to a group of
listeners who do not know what words are to be used.”

STATUS OF THE RITUAL
Based on my personal observations and the reports I received from my
Assistant Grand Lecturers, our Ritual is in good hands. As I have reported
in the past, there remain some lodges whose Ritual work strays from the
standard. I continue to be concerned about the small number of lodges
where the perambulations and charges are being read and where they
are having difficulty finding brethren willing to present our lectures in
a meaningful manner.
Overall, because of the dedication of our officers’ coaches and Inspectors
as well as those members who truly understand and present our Ritual with
meaning, California Ritual still stands tall among all other jurisdictions.
FUTURE OF THE RITUAL
The future of our Ritual depends on our ability to continue the
development of that very special bond that is created between the new
member and his coach; between the new officer and his coach; between
the officers and the members of the degree team; and lastly, between the
lodge Master with his executive team. Our Ritual is a progressive system
by which a student is taught and, once enlightened, becomes the teacher.
In this way, the bond grows with each new teacher.
I am reminded of the words of Most Worshipful Kenneth Aldridge of
the Grand Lodge of Quebec when he said the following:
“Our Ritual is an important element of our Craft and one deserving
of flawless presentation. Let us also understand, however, that we are
all capable of error. When we are compelled to draw attention to some
apparent departure from the proper form, the occasion should be used as
a vehicle to promote brotherhood. This means that, except for corrections
made in rehearsals, all other corrections should be made in private and
in a supportive manner so that the erring brother senses a feeling of
kind assistance rather than unyielding criticism.”

“Even if it is necessary for a brother to be prompted on each word,
for valid reasons other than a lack of preparation, he should be able to
experience the marvelous feeling of support flowing to him as he makes
his way through that part as all others have done before him. Help the
ritualist grow in poise, composure and intellect, then surround him with
fraternal love and affection for he will then be your brother. Such is the
integral part of Ritual.”
NEEDS OF THE FUTURE
TOLERANCE – May we always remember that it is our Ritual that unites
our diverse Craft. As we journey into the future in order to honor our
past, we should remember that “Our individual faiths form the foundation
upon which we place and build upon our individual cornerstones of
Freemasonry.” As we shape our future, we should remember our core
values and be tolerant of the contributions of every religion, race, ethnic
background and nationality. You should also remember to, “let your
individual spirit be your guide and … your diversity of thought be the
cornerstone of the enlightened mind.”
FUNERALS - I strongly encourage our brethren to adopt a resolution
that requires our lodge Chaplains, before they can be installed, become
qualified to deliver the Masonic funeral service. There are just too many
times when lodges are unable to find a qualified funeral master to honor
a departed brother and we desperately need to develop a pool of qualified
brethren to deliver our funeral services.
In order to make it easier to learn and teach the lodge room funeral
service, the Ritual Committee developed 11 diagrams in support of the
written instructions that will be added to the funeral book.

172

Proceedings of the

MASONIC WIDOWS - I also strongly encourage the committee for the
Masonic Homes Board of California to work with our lodges throughout
the state to ensure that OUR Masonic widows are regularly remembered.
Furthermore, the Masonic Widow’s Pin and Widow’s Identification Card,
should be routinely made available to every Masonic Widow. Each item’s
significance should also be thoroughly explained.
MORE FUN - I predict a resurgence of the festive gatherings of our
Craft similar to the festive boards of our ancient brethren, where they
balanced Ritual with having a “jolly good time.”
EDUCATIONAL ADVANCES - I predict that technical advances,
especially in the area of virtual reality, will dramatically change the way
Ritual is experienced, taught, retained and presented in the future. We
must be ever mindful that no matter how useful technology may be to
our Fraternity, it can never replace the personal relationship a brother
has with his coach.
I foresee an increase in the use of the tracing boards in support of our
Master’s lectures; in fact, I predict an increased use of in-lodge monitors
in the East to present our degree slides in support of our lectures.
I foresee the day when our online current teaching modules will include
virtual reality systems that will allow a candidate to participate in the
Chamber of Reflection experience without the need to prepare a separate
room. I foresee candidates being able to re-experience the lessons of each
degree while walking alongside our ancient brethren in the temples of old.
Can you imagine a candidate actually walking up a flight of winding
stairs while his coach explains its meaning in more detail? I foresee
candidates and mentors both wearing virtual reality equipment and
sharing the lessons of Masonry together.
VIRTUAL TRAVELER - I foresee the time when our ill brethren will
be able to attend their lodges remotely through biometrically secured
computers.
As proof of the diversity of California Freemasonry, I foresee a time
when California will have lodges performing California Ritual in every
language. I also foresee the use of interpretive technology, where an
earpiece will allow brethren of all languages the ability to attend any
foreign language lodge and be able to understand the language being
spoken.

ADMINISTRATIVE DUTIES
Shortly after being elected Grand Lecturer, I was tasked with updating
every ritual and ceremonial document. I am proud to state that as of this
writing, every document was appropriately updated. (There were 53
documents – The details of which will be included in the printed version
of the Proceedings.)
The affected documents were as follows:
• Cipher Ritual
• Cipher Supplement, including the addition of balloting instructions
with diagrams.
• Floor Work and Best Practices Manual
• Monitor and Officer’s Manual
• Discontinued the Stated Meeting Flip Book and moved its data

Additionally, the Ritual Committee changed the format for the MastersElect and the Wardens-Elect advancement questions. Instead of making
them search the many resources available for an answer to a particular
question, the questions themselves now provide them with the resource
and ask them to answer the questions, “What is the intent of this resource”
and “How does it apply to the office to which he was aspiring?”

First, whenever a brother said the phrase “duegarden sign” instead
of “due-guard and sign,” he would gleefully display a sign, which was
specially made for him, that said “Duegarden” and declare that what he
held was the only “Duegarden” sign in the world and that the proper
phrase to be used in our Ritual was “due-guard and sign.”

In evaluating their responses, the Inspectors were asked to verify
that the officer understood the intent of the involved resource and how
it would apply to his future office. Should the response indicate a lack
of understanding, the Inspectors were told to use this opportunity to
continue a dialogue with the officer in order to mentor them so they
would have every opportunity to progress and become an effective leader.
Additionally, the Masters-Elect and Wardens-Elect questions include
an essay question having to do with civility relative to resolving conflict
situations.

As I was preparing this message, I learned the Lord had called
Worshipful Christopher Putnam to labor as His Organist in the Celestial
Lodge above, where Christopher’s music will live on with our departed
brethren and will play forever in our hearts.
Music has always been integral to Freemasonry from at least 1723. Early
lodge music generally took the form of singing, either unaccompanied
or with portable instruments, as the lodges were meeting in the private
rooms of inns and taverns, which had to be cleared at the end of a meeting.
During the 19th century, dedicated Masonic halls were built and a
pipe organ was often installed. When Worshipful Steve and Worshipful
Christopher played their music, they honored our past while shaping
the future of music in the California Grand Lodge. Their music created
harmony and contentment within our grand lodge, and it sent a message
as well—one specifically related to each officer of the grand lodge.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

183

Music adds a special dimension to our Rituals and ceremonies and
oftentimes “fills otherwise empty space” with music that sets the tone
prior to and after an event.
On the topic of music, it is my hope that our future lodge Masters will
appoint a brother to be the lodge organist, not to play the organ (it would
be great if he could) but to work with the Officers’ Coach to operate an
iPad or CD player with suitable speakers and play background music to
accompany the non-verbal portions of our Ritual. We have gone far too
long without music in our lodge rooms and this needs to change. We must
give the same attention to music as we give to memory and floor work.
Therefore, the Ritual Committee is preparing an iPad program that
contains music to accompany our Ritual. The iPad, which can be connected
to a wireless speaker, will contain music specific to each portion of each
degree along with music on a continual loop that can be started and
stopped and/or the volume turned up and down to accompany the Ritual.

of New Zealand, and specifically Worshipful Brother Peter C Howie, Past

Grand Chaplain
Inspirational Message
Today, you will be visited by three ghosts.
The first will show you a picture of where you come from; your past,
your heritage and the multitude of choices and moments that have
shaped who you are. The second will show you scenes depicting the
world we share today; your present, the world around you and how you
are perceived by those you know and love—your family and friends. The
last will bring to light the future you are shaping — a future that may or
may not include you but is a direct product of your actions, behaviors,
and relationships you make today.
Some of you might now be thinking, “This sounds a lot like the famous
story by Charles Dickens, ‘A Christmas Carol.’” You might next ask, “Why
in the world is a Jewish man choosing today to tell me a Christmas story?”
Because inside this story is a timeless message and a premise that will
compel you forward into a future you have the power to shape.
Our Grand Master’s theme, “Honoring our Past, Shaping our Future,”
is a perfect parallel to this classic story, in which choices and behaviors
come under self-examination and in which we see the full shape and
shadow of a spiritual building.
The Past
Who are you, and where did you come from? A challenge and a question.
Rabbi Nachman of Breslev says, “The day you were born was the day
God decided that the world could not exist without you.”
Our Great Architect has blessed us all with a pure and beautiful
soul, each of us a unique expression of the Divine imbued with the
foundational plans for a useful life. Our parents have lovingly handed
down a collection of values, culture, and community — a heritage that
creates an infrastructure to support your personal monument, with
your unique design. No one else has ever had the opportunity to be you.
The miraculous ingredients that came together to make you will never
happen again.

189

No matter your background or how you came to be, we all share two
truths from which there is no escape: we are all born and we all, sadly,
will die. God gave us all the power of choice, so what you chose to do with
the time between those two pillars is up to you. This is the only time this
life can be lived; it is not a rehearsal, and you get only one. In fact, you
are the only you you can ever be.
The Present
Who do you choose to be, right now? How are you defining yourself in
this world and preparing for the next? Who have you chosen to surround
yourself with? Are you happy with the life you’ve built? Are your actions
in alignment with your core beliefs? St. Francis of Assisi was quoted as
saying, “Preach the gospel, and when necessary, use words.” What!? Did
you think I was only going to quote Rabbis? “Preach the gospel, and
when necessary, use words.”
I have good news: you’re in the right place. You have chosen today
to associate yourself with the right people; people who are working
on themselves, and making each other better—repairing the world by
improving themselves. They’re breaking off their rough and superfluous
parts. Go ahead, name another place where you will routinely see grown
men — regardless of their religion, profession, political leaning, sexualorientation, race, age, or station — wearing aprons and embracing, crying,
praying for each other and their families, and genuinely saying to one
another, “I love you, my brother.”
Name another place where women are honored, loved, and respected –
not reduced solely to the decorative parts of our buildings, but treated like
integral parts of the foundation, structure, and function. They’re treated
like wise and trusted partners. I know my lady is all those things for me.
Name another place where young men are being taught integrity and
reverence for sacred things; taught to be respectful to women (including
a special ceremony honoring their mothers); and to see women as
equal partners in leading. Name another place where assemblies of
young women are being taught lessons of true womanhood, sisterhood,
patriotism, faith, and what it really means to keep a promise. Name
another place where our Bethels teach daughters to honor their parents,
to do at least one useful act each day, and to rock a tiara/cape combo like
a boss on their way to being the fairest in the land. You can’t name any
other place like this—including the other concordant and appendant

190

191

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

organizations present here today. There is nowhere else on Earth like
this. We are assembled as a Masonic family here today not by something
so accidental as blood — but by choice.

Our spiritual buildings are all monuments to God’s love, an honor to
the generations that came before us and to your own personal work.
When someone tells you that they love you, they are essentially saying
something nice about your building — “I love what you’ve done with the
place.” If God loves you, then your family loves you—your friends and
mentors love you. I have a bit of a scary question to ask. Do you love you?

The Future
What if all of this was gone? What would happen if this miraculous
mixture were just to stop? I can assure you that, as Rosa Parks said,
“Memories of our lives, of our works and our deeds will continue in
others.” But, what if all of this just became a memory?
Ebenezer Scrooge’s Ghost of the Future shows a dark version of where
his current path will lead him. He is shown how his present attitudes and
actions will lead to a very sad future. He has a choice to make: continue
on his current path or change; or as we Masons say, “Break off his rough
and superfluous parts.”
Start Song – Lake Street Dive, I Can Change
What does Scrooge do? He changes.
How do we as a Fraternity make good on the promise we make to our
world and the world we will someday leave behind? How do we rise
and build for a better tomorrow? How do we work together to build
a future for those who come after us? When Scrooge finally sees that
he must make a change in himself in order to make this world a better
place, he sparks a previously speechless young boy to say the innocent
words, “God bless us, every one.” That line has ended every prayer I’ve
written this year. As a call to all of us — a call to action, a call to “shape
our future”—we have to start with us.
You alone have the power to align yourself, in every moment to choose,
and to change — to make choices that bring you closer to your best you.
This voyage isn’t easy, and it takes no shortage of patient introspection
or bravery. The good news is that you are not alone. We are doing this
together. We’re celebrating each other’s successes and helping each other
grow from our mistakes. We’re building each other up, being champions
for a person in need. We’re making real God’s plan for our world, one
person at a time, through service and love.

Your ability to really love someone else starts with you. Now, this might
be a bit uncomfortable to say, because in polite society, humility is much
more the accepted practice. However, real love starts somewhere that
isn’t easy to say at parties. Repeat after me: “I love me.” I know it feels
strange to say, but in order to grow and make real change, you have to be
gentle with yourself, to be as forgiving as you would be with someone you
love. You have to forgive yourself when you make a mistake. You have to
love yourself when you have been unlovable. You are the most important
person that you can love. It feels really strange to say out loud, but let’s
say it again. “I love me.”
If God loves you, how dare you not love what he created — you!
If the generations that came before you love you — how dare you
shrink!
If you love your community, how can you not contribute your verse to
this powerful play?
If you love you, how can you not joyfully make your unique dent in
the universe?
In honor of our past, present, and the future we are shaping here today,
God bless us, every one.

Respectfully submitted,
Jeffrey M. Schimsky, Grand Chaplain

Grand Oration
Most Worshipful Sir, our honored Past Grand Masters, distinguished
guests and visitors, and members of the Grand Lodge of California, my
brothers all in Freemasonry.

It has been a high honor to serve this past year, with these Grand
Officers and with you, the members of this grand lodge. Together,
we have worked to further the building of the Temple of California
Freemasonry. I pay homage to our Grand Master, Most Worshipful
Bruce R. Galloway for his leadership and guidance that we have been
privileged to witness. Our Grand Master and his lady, Gay, have served
us well as worthy ambassadors of California Freemasonry to the world.
To call him friend and brother is indeed an honor.
Through his many, many visitations, presentations, and ceremonies
along with thousands and thousands of miles traveled to every corner
of our jurisdiction and beyond, Most Worshipful Bruce has, in his wellordered and kindly and manner, carried the principles of Freemasonry
to the brethren. He’s done this not by precept alone, but more so
by example. His contribution to the cause of Freemasonry will long
endure, and the fruits of his labors will be harvested in all the years
to come, for the good deeds a man performs live long after he is gone
to that Bourne from which no traveler returns. On your behalf I say
to our Grand Master, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant of
Freemasonry.”
While growing up in a small rural town in the central valley of
this golden state, my sister and I would sneak up to the pulpit of
the Presbyterian Church on many a Sunday morning and count the
number of pages in the homily for that day so we might know how
long the sermon was going to last. Of course, we lost count unless we
paid attention, so the mischief worked to the advantage of both the
minister and us kids. Well, just so you know, today’s oration is six pages
long—so start counting.
I have had the opportunity to speak several times this year. On one
occasion, I asked our Grand Marshal to wake up the brother who had
fallen to sleep in the front row. The Worshipful Brother suggested I
should wake him myself, as I was the one who put him to sleep in the
first place. But I digress. . .

196

197

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Whatever I say to you today is merely giving back to Masonry a very
small part of what Masonry has given me. If I am led to impart to you
something of inspiration, something that will invigorate your thought,
I am only reflecting meagerly the inspiration that has been given me
by my beloved Craft through you, my brothers. Each time I return to
my home lodge or to this magnificent hall, I have counted it a privilege,
for the associations I have acquired and the riches that have flowed
from them is of incalculable value and will remain with me as a crown
of rejoicing that shall continue when time shall be no more. And so, in
the spirit of sincerest humility, I stand before you today blessed with
the great honor of addressing this Annual Communication upon such
matters appertaining to the Craft.

We need these standards to serve as guards for our Fraternity to
ensure its continuance. King Solomon posted guards at the entrance
to his temple for protection from without. The lodge Tiler dismisses
the unqualified. Our Masonic shields must protect us from having
unworthy thoughts or deeds and to keep our consciences pure before
God and man.

The first inquiry presented to the Entered Apprentice is, “Whence
Came You and Whither Are You Going?” If this question was placed
before me today I’d most likely respond “I came from the past and I’m
moving towards the future.” Philosopher Soren Kierkegaard wrote,
“Life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forward.”
The reality of time demands that we always remember that we must
live in the present because the past is behind us and the future is
unsure.
The next question put forth to each new initiate is, “What came
you here to do?” The universal response is, “to learn; to subdue my
passions; and to improve myself in Masonry”. Advancing through the
degrees we learn the Landmarks of Freemasonry. We learn to practice
outside of the lodge those great moral precepts that are instilled in it.
We learn to be good men; to be true and faithful; to honor others with
civility and respect—civility and respect being the key ingredients of
the cement central to building true and trusting relationships.
As our lodge officers advance through the various chairs and
stations, many life skills are imparted. Lodge Stewards learn servitude;
he Marshal, protocol; the Junior Deacon, etiquette; and the Senior
Deacon, Ritual. The Junior Warden develops management and the
Senior Warden charity. The Lodge Master demonstrates leadership.
We learn that temperance is an important virtue. That without
morality, righteousness and the great light of Masonry, our world
would unravel.

One night the Tiler asked a brother who had not attended lodge for
quite some time, in fact for many years, where he’d been. The absent
brother’s response: “I’ve been learning to subdue my passions.”
When we learn the lessons symbolically illustrated through our
degrees and have learned them well, we will have prepared ourselves
to teach them to all mankind. However, we must, by example, bring
these teachings into the twenty-first century for them to be welcomed
by generations to come.
Is the value of Freemasonry gauged by the structure of initiation
fees or the annual cost of dues? Or can it be measured by the esteem
with which we are regarded in our local communities? Would your
lodge be missed in the community if it were to cease tomorrow? The
reputation of the Fraternity resides with each individual brother.
It is the content of your character that holds importance, not the
content of your biography. Your character, actions and reputation
will determine if Masonry will remain a vibrant force in today’s
world. This isn’t the responsibility of the Grand Master; it isn’t just
the responsibility of grand lodge, or even the responsibility of your
lodge. It is the personal responsibility of each of us. It is within the
power of every brother to glorify or nullify the institution. From time
immemorial, our Craft has exercised an influence over our society that
has been due to the unchallenged, fundamental principles of human
conduct. The foundations of Freemasonry laid long ago still support
the superstructure of our civil society.
However, new opportunities are being presented on the tracing
table. Opportunities that challenge our curiosity and reasoning. This
is the time that the individual’s consciousness of the basic principles,
upon which our institution was founded, need to be invigorated. Our
local communities, our school boards, our state and federal governing
bodies are crying out for the leadership that is exhibited in our beloved
Craft. Let us give that leadership light. Let us practice out of the lodge
those great moral precepts which we have been taught in it; and by
amiable, discreet and virtuous conduct, convince the world of the
goodness that resides in all mankind.

198

199

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

At this time, with all of the strife and tragedy occurring in our public
schools, community halls and town centers, one could rightfully ask,
“How could God let these events happen?” When God is no longer
allowed in our schools, public hallways or government squares, we
cannot expect God to give us His blessing and His protection while
at the same time we demand He leave us alone.

It is time—for us as Masons—to honor our past and shape the future.
In every social organization, before every civic club, in every business
plan, and at each everyday activity, each of us has the opportunity
to bring to the treatment of every problem, challenge and obstacle
an application of the sound principles which masonry has instilled
into the consciousness and into the impulses of our life. Here, in the
everyday world, my brethren, is the opportunity to return the world
to that Masonry of action and spirit, which is the very heartbeat of
civilization.

Students no longer pledge allegiance to our great country in schools
and our children’s heroes protest civility by denigrating the honor
our country deserves. As patriotism is demeaned in our public places
and social activities, we must be sure that loyalty is not shunned and
discarded to the dung heap of hypocrisy. My brothers, we have each
pledged our patriotic allegiance to our constitutions and country at
the altar of Masonry. We must exhibit that same allegiance in our
everyday life, or face losing the freedoms our forefathers fought for so
vigilantly. When we move outside of our Compasses, we lose morality.
When we don’t meet upon the Square, we lose our integrity; and my
brothers, when we remove the Great Architect of the Universe from
our lives, we become Godless!
Today this country is being challenged with the supreme test of our
spiritual, moral, mental and physical strength. It is a test to determine
whether free men are fitted to govern themselves or whether despots,
zealots and insignificant minorities shall direct the destinies of
mankind. It is a conflict between a totally materialistic philosophy
and one that is based upon the principle that materialism must be
guided and controlled by moral law. It is not a new conflict. It extends
back to the very beginning of human relations and over time has
been fought in many forms. But today’s technological and scientific
achievements have given man the power to destroy our civil society
and place these two opposing ways of life in a real fight for survival.
We must recognize that we Masons must meet our adversaries on
all fronts, wherever and whenever our free way of life is challenged.
The great Light of the teachings and practices of Freemasonry gives
us the tools for this battle. When we study our country’s early history,
we realize that Masonry was the great unifying force, the catalyst that
welded together the colonies with their diverse economies, political
philosophies, predominant religions, and geographical barriers into
one great nation. As Masons, we must recognize our responsibility as
citizens in maintaining for all the people those principles of freedom,
equality of opportunity, and justice, for which our early brethren
worked, and lived, and died so that they might pass on to future
generations a brighter and better world.

We need to have the backbone that our founding fathers had when
they created our great country. We need to have the determination
our ancestors had when they came west to settle this great state, and
the vision to see what we need to do. We need to stand shoulder to
shoulder across our great country and say we have a toleration for
different religions, different opinions, and conflicting beliefs, but that
no person, special interest group, organization or government has
the right to remove the constitutional rights from our lives. No one
has the right to depress the thoughts or the words of our fellow man.
We must stop the atheist, madman, and fool from promulgating the
untrue, the divisive and destructive among the less informed.
As Masonic leaders of today, in meeting the challenge we face, we
must have a set of clearly defined goals and arrange a program that
will be effective in meeting the needs of the members. Our duty is clear.
If Masonry is to prosper, we must convince the world by our actions
that we are better men; that we are actively engaged in the industry of
spreading useful knowledge, practicing charity and inculcating good
will among men. It is to the everlasting credit of Freemasons that we
have taken these great principles, the Brotherhood of Man and the
Fatherhood of God, as our foundation and put them into practice in
daily life. Masons are principled men. To be a Mason is to be a friend
to any man in need, regardless of his race or creed. We believe in the
values of Temperance, Fortitude, Prudence and Justice. We stand before
the pillars of Wisdom, Strength and Beauty. We cherish the sanctity
of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth.
Remember, I am only ONE Mason, but I AM one Mason. I can’t do
everything, but I CAN do something. And what I CAN do, I MUST do.
And with the help of the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe, I
WILL do.

2018 GRAND LODGE LEGISLATION
GRAND MASTER’S DECISIONS AND
RECOMMENDATIONS
GRAND MASTER GALLOWAY’S DECISION NO. 1
LODGE BUSINESS
I have been asked whether a lodge may hold a special meeting for the
purpose of presenting the Hiram Award, the Golden Veteran Award or
the Diamond Jubilee Award. CMC Section 807.010 limits the business that
may be conducted at a special meeting. None of these presentations is
on the list. In addition, under CMC 807.020.B, all business of the lodge
must be conducted in a lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons, with
certain exceptions, none of which includes these presentations. If these
presentations are considered business for these purposes, then they may
not be conducted in a tiled meeting other than at a lodge stated meeting.
The real question is then: what is business? If a lodge holds a tiled
meeting to transact business, then such business must be those activities
that can only be conducted at, or in conjunction with, a tiled meeting.
Thus, business would include such lodge actions as approving minutes,
receiving reports of investigating committees, balloting, receiving
applications for the degrees, paying and authorizing lodge expenditures,
conferring degrees, conducting examinations in the candidate’s lectures
and the like. While a funeral service may be conducted without a lodge
opening, the Funeral Service Ritual requires a lodge opening if the
service will be held in a lodge room. While our Installation Ceremony for
Constituent Lodges is conducted in an untiled setting, the Installation
Ritual requires a lodge opening before the ceremony. I note that our law
does limit activities at tiled meetings to those that must be conducted at,
or in conjunction with, a tiled meeting. For example, Masonic education
is encouraged at tiled meetings but may also be held in untiled settings,
if the content is appropriate for non-Masons.
There is no requirement in our law or usage that the presentation of the
Hiram Award, the Golden Veteran Award or the Diamond Jubilee Award
must be conducted at, or in conjunction with, a tiled meeting. Therefore,
it is my decision that these presentations are not business for purposes
of the various code limitations on the conduct of lodge business at stated
and special meetings and may be done at a special meeting of the lodge,

206

207

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

open in any degree. By like measure, a lodge may hold a special meeting
open in any degree that is then called to refreshment when any one or
more of these presentations may be conducted.

aspects of Masonry. In stark contrast, the Hiram Award, the Golden
Veteran Award, and the Diamond Jubilee Award are public ceremonies
intended to celebrate and appreciate a Brother in the presence of his
friends and family: no confidentiality is intended and these ceremonies
are not esoteric.

If you agree with this interpretation of our law, I ask you to vote “yes” for
Grand Master’s Decision No. 1.
If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added to the
appendix of the California Masonic Code in which the Grand Master’s
interpretative decisions are recorded:
Interpretation of Section 807.010 of the California Masonic Code.
Lodge Business
(2018 G.M. Decision No. 1)
The restrictions on the conduct of business at a special meeting apply
only to activities which must be conducted at, or in conjunction with,
a tiled meeting. There is no requirement in our law or usage that the
presentation of the Hiram Award, the Golden Veteran Award or the
Diamond Jubilee Award must be conducted at, or in conjunction with,
a tiled meeting. Therefore, these presentations are not business for
purposes of this section and may be conducted at a special meeting of
the lodge open in any degree.

Report from Legislative Analysis Committee
This Grand Master’s Decision clarifies that a Lodge may hold a Special
Meeting for the purpose of presenting the Hiram Award, the Golden
Veteran Award, or the Diamond Jubilee Award. Further, that these
ceremonies may be conducted while a Lodge is at refreshment. This
decision is based on the rationale that these activities are not “business”
that is required to be performed during a Stated Meeting.
As this decision points out, business required to be performed during
a Stated Meeting includes: approving minutes, receiving reports of
investigating committees, balloting, receiving applications for degrees,
authorizing and paying Lodge bills, conferring degrees, conducting
candidate examinations, etc. These activities require a certain level of
confidentiality, as they deal with internal Lodge functions or esoteric

This Grand Master Decision is a reasonable interpretation of the
California Masonic Code and clarifies an ambiguity that is likely to affect
most Lodges.
Decision: PASSED

GRAND MASTER GALLOWAY’S RECOMMENDATION NO. 1
ALLOWS A LODGE TO INVEST IN A BUILDING
ASSOCIATION OWNED BY GRAND LODGE
A challenge facing some lodges today is ownership of a lodge building.
Having a proper meeting place is of fundamental importance to every
lodge.
Over the last number of years, certain lodges have surrendered or
lost their charter. Some of these lodges owned a lodge building, which
the Grand Lodge has maintained through an incorporated building
association so that other lodges and perhaps new lodges in the future
may meet there.
From time to time, certain lodges have asked if they could invest funds
into such a building association and become a minority shareholder in it,
while the Grand Lodge maintains the majority share or membership. This
is appealing to the lodge because a minority interest would give them a
sense of having a permanent home and would allow them representation
on the board of directors that oversees the building. The building usually
needs improvements after decades of deferred maintenance by the
previous lodge owner. The investment of funds by a lodge could be used
to make those improvements. I see this as a win-win situation for the
Fraternity.
The California Masonic Code currently requires a lodge to use an
incorporated Masonic Hall Association, wherein a lodge or lodges
collectively hold a majority of memberships or shares. I recommend that
we add a provision to the code that would also allow a lodge or lodges
to invest in a building association, wherein the Grand Lodge holds a
majority of membership or shares.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following provision would be
added to the end of Section §809.130 of the Code:
With the consent of the Grand Master, a lodge or lodges may invest
in a building association, wherein the Grand Lodge holds a majority of
memberships or shares, upon such terms as the Grand Master may direct.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

209

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The Grand Master recommends California Masonic Code section
809.130 be amended to allow Lodges to invest in a building association,
wherein the Grand Lodge holds a majority of membership or shares. This
recommendation is intended to allow Lodges to become minority owners
in buildings currently under the stewardship of the Grand Lodge, which
were placed there after the Lodge that owned the building surrendered
or lost their charters.
This is a common-sense approach to allow newer Lodges to take an
ownership role in older Masonic properties they currently use.
Report from Masonic Properties Committee
The Grand Master’s Recommendation No.1 proposes to allow a Lodge to
invest in a building association owned by Grand Lodge.
Over the years due to financial limitations and other constrains, a few
Lodges have either surrendered or lost their charters. Some of these
Lodges owned Lodge buildings titles to which were held by Masonic Hall
Associations duly formed pursuant to relevant regulations of the CMC.
By surrendering or losing their charter the Masonic hall association
had ceased to exist as a Masonic entity. In some of these cases Grand
Lodge through a duly formed building association has taken title to these
buildings and has been maintaining said buildings for possible future
use. None of these buildings can be characterized as a Masonic hall
association or Masonic building association as defined in the relevant
section of the CMC.

211

210

GRAND MASTER GALLOWAY’S RECOMMENDATION NO. 2
§809.140. INVESTMENT IN MASONIC HALL ASSOCIATION states:
“A Lodge, after first obtaining the consent of the Grand Lodge
Committee on Masonic Properties may also invest its funds in or
maintain an investment in:
A. Membership or shares in a Masonic Association wherein a Lodge
or Lodges collectively hold a majority of membership or shares or
when controlling interest is acquired by such investment.”
Since buildings described above and now owned by Grand Lodge are not
Masonic hall association, §809.140 (A) does not on its face apply to Grand
Master’s Recommendation No 1. Nor does §809.140 (A) explicitly allows
a Lodge to invest in a building association as a minority shareholder if
the investment is for Masonic purposes.
§809.130. LODGE INVESTMENTS describe where and how Lodge funds
can be invested. Subsection (B) Tier 3 (Growth Assets) lists 9 areas where
up to 80% of the Lodge assets can be invested. Although none clearly
describes the issue at hand article 9 in part states: “Such other prudent
and appropriate investment as may be approved from time to time by the
Grand Master………”. Section 809.130(B)(9) clearly envisions other areas
where a Lodge may want to invest its funds subject to approval of the
Grand Master. Investing in a building association where majority interest
is held by Grand Lodge could easily fall within extended definition of
“Growth Assets”. Such investments will help preserve valuable Masonic
assets, give members a sense of ownership and perhaps encourages
potential new members to join the fraternity. Adding the proposed
language as suggested in the recommendation will clearly define the
additional investment area.
The Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Properties recommend a YES
vote.
Recommendation: PASSED

ELIMINATES THE LODGE SUPPORT COMMITTEE
AS A STANDING COMMITTEE
The California Masonic Code identifies two types of Grand Lodge
committees – standing committees and special committees. The newly
installed Grand Master must appoint standing committees before the
close of the Annual Communication, and the duties and size of standing
committees are prescribed in the code. A special committee may be
created and members appointed by the Grand Master at any time during
his term of office. The duties and size of a special committee may be at
the discretion of the Grand Master, unless otherwise directed by Grand
Lodge. Currently there are 14 standing committees and eight special
committees.
Lodge Support is a standing committee of not less than 11, nor more
than 20, members. The duties of the committee are to provide assistance
to lodges in developing and executing various programs and to undertake
such other duties as the Grand Master may assign to it. These duties
are broad and, in practice, the Grand Master and Executive Committee
provide direction to the committee each year about the types of assistance
to be provided to lodges.
After working with the Lodge Support Committee for a number of
years, I have concluded the committee actually functions like a special
committee and I recommend the code be amended to reflect this reality.
If this recommendation is adopted, future Grand Masters will be able
to appoint the committee and provide direction to it as Grand Masters
have done previously, yet he will also have the flexibility to appoint the
appropriate number of members based on the duties assigned.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made
to the code. Section 406.005 of the code would be amended to read as
marked:
§406.005. STANDING COMMITTEES.
The members of standing committees (other than those who serve exofficio) shall be appointed by the newly installed Grand Master at each
Annual Communication before the close thereof. A member ceases to be
a standing committee member by death, removal by the Grand Master

a successor for the balance of the current term. All standing committee
appointments (other than those who serve ex-officio) shall expire at the

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The Grand Master recommends California Masonic Code (CMC)
sections 406.005 and 805.120 be amended, and section 406.055 be
deleted, in order to reclassify the Committee on Lodge Support from
a Standing Committee to a Special Committee.
Generally, the difference between a Standing Committee and a Special
Committee is that Standing Committees are created by the CMC
and perform the duties specified in the CMC. By contrast, Special
Committees are created by the Grand Master and perform the duties
specified by the Grand Master.
In practice, the Committee on Lodge Support receives direction from the
Grand Master and Executive Committee about the types of assistance
it is to provide to Lodges. In this manner, it already operates more like
a Special Committee than Standing Committee.
If the Committee on Lodge Support were reclassified as a Special
Committee, the Grand Master would have more flexibility in the size
of the committee. The scope would not change, as the Grand Master
already has vast discretion in directing the activities of the committee.

214

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

This recommendation would conform the CMC to reflect how the
Committee on Lodge Support has been and is used in practice.

Resolution No. 17-01
Modifies Position of Candidate’s Hands
During Third Degree Obligation
The proponents of this Resolution seek to modify the position of the
candidate’s hands during the third degree obligation so that it more
closely aligns with the current third-degree due-guard.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, in ancient times, the position of the candidate’s hands
while taking the third degree obligation was different from that which
is practiced in California today; and
WHEREAS, the due-guard more accurately represents what should be
the position of the candidate’s hands during the third degree obligation;
and
WHEREAS, it is the proponents desire to return the candidate’s hands
during his obligation to the ancient position to conform them to the
current due-guard; and
WHEREAS, as this resolution contains reference to our esoteric
work, any questions about this resolution can be addressed by either
the proponents or members of the Ritual Committee who have been so
advised and are prepared to explain and/or demonstrate the intent of
the esoteric portions of this resolution.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Ritual be amended to
provide that the position of the candidate’s hands during his obligation be
that which will be displayed by the proponents on the overhead screens
during the Annual Communication.

216

Proceedings of the

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to clarify a candidate’s hand
placement during the obligation of the Master Mason Degree. The
Ritual Committee will be showing slides illustrating the proposed hand
placement.
It has been the custom of The Grand Lodge of California to not make
changes to Ritual, unless there are strong reasons to do so, and it is
unclear whether this is an actual change or an affirmation of proper
practice. Due to the esoteric nature of this subject, there is little to no
documentation on the historical placement of hands during the obligation
and there is no apparent uniformity from jurisdiction to jurisdiction.
Passage of this resolution would provide clarity and uniformity on a
matter where currently there exists different practices among Lodges and
would establish the consensus of this Grand Lodge on hand placement
during the Master Mason obligation.
If adopted, the Inspectors would, under the direction of the Grand
Lecturer and Assistant Grand Lecturers, be in charge of teaching the
proposed hand placement in their schools of instruction.
Report from the Ritual Committee
The proponents of Resolution 2018-05 seek to modify the Installation
Ritual for ceremony for Constituent Lodges to allow the Installing Officer
to gavel the brethren of the lodge up prior to giving the lodge membership
present their instructions.
The Master is given his admonitions while standing in front of the east
to convey the importance of the instructions given by the Installing Officer
relative to the Master’s actions and attitude towards peace and harmony,
and placing the will and pleasure of the lodge as a whole, above his own.
The Wardens are given their instructions in like manner. Their instructions
are equally important to assisting the Master in the government of the lodge
and in their readiness to serve in the Master’s absence.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

217

The gaveling up of the brethren instills the importance of the
instructions that is not adequately conveyed while the brethren remained
seated. The words of instruction given to the standing members of the
lodge conveys a sense of responsibility to the brethren that they are just
as responsible for the keeping of the peace and harmony of the lodge as
the Master and Wardens are charged to do.
This resolution does not take anything from the Ritual of the installation.
On the contrary, it enhances our Installation Ritual and gives more
meaning to it. The Ritual Committee is unanimous in urging a YES vote.
Resolution: PASSED

221

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

If Grand Lodge grants the petition and orders the issuance of a charter
to the lodge, the lodge’s dispensation shall be revived and the Grand
Secretary shall return it, together with the bylaws, books of records and
returns to the lodge that presented them. The lodge may then proceed
to work under the revived dispensation, unless legally revoked, until
duly constituted.

The CMC, since its creation in 1931 had separate sections governing
lodges under dispensation, newly chartered and Constituent Lodges.
In 1885, Grand Master Hines made a decision that was approved by
Grand Lodge regarding qualification certificates for only the Master and
Wardens of a newly constituted lodge. A certificate did not need to be
presented at the ceremony if the officers were the same as those listed
on the charter, as the granting of the charter required their qualification,
so it served as the qualification certificate. The decision stated that this
was consistent with long standing policy of Grand Lodge. In 1903 Grand
Lodge approved a decision that a lodge under dispensation did not
have to do degree work to get a charter, if the Master and Wardens
were qualified to do the work. This decision appears as a section in
the CMCs published in 1931, 1956 and 1975. It was incorporated into
the section on the requirements for issuing a new charter in the 1991
code. Both decisions demonstrate that for more than 132 years, that
Grand Lodge has maintained separate treatments of the Senior Deacon
qualification for Lodges under dispensation and newly Chartered then
those of Constituent Lodges.

If grand lodge does not order the issuance of the charter, it may in the
alternative continue the consideration of the petition one time to the
next Annual Communication, in which event the dispensation shall be
revived and the Grand Secretary shall return it, together with the bylaws,
books of records and returns to the lodge which presented them. The
lodge may then proceed to work under the revived dispensation, unless
legally revoked, until the first day of the next Annual Communication.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The intent of this resolution is to require the Senior Deacon of a lodge
under dispensation and a newly chartered lodge to qualify in the Ritual
work of his office. Currently, the California Masonic Code requires that
a Senior Deacon of a Constituent Lodges must qualify before he can be
installed in his office. There is no similar requirement for a lodge under
dispensation or being instituted after receiving its charter. While both
ceremonies are similar to an installation of officers of a Constituent
Lodge, they are treated differently under our code.
It has been the policy of the Grand Lodge of California for the Master,
Wardens and Senior Deacon of Constituent Lodges to qualify in the Ritual
Work before they are installed. Since the first CMC was published in 1931
it has contained sections requiring these qualifications. In reviewing the
proceedings of the Grand Lodge prior to publishing of the first CMC
in 1931 it is clear that these qualifications had been required for quite
some time.
It has also been the policy of the Grand Lodge to only require that the
Master and Wardens be qualified in the Ritual of their offices before a
dispensation should be granted by the Grand Master or a Charter issued
by Grand Lodge. There has never been a requirement for the Senior
Deacon to do so.

It has always been the policy of the Grand Lodge that all work in this
Jurisdiction, including each degree conferred and all lectures, must be in
conformity with the Ritual, and such must be adhered to by all Lodges
and Masons in this Jurisdiction. The practice of not requiring the Senior
Deacon to qualify in a lodge under dispensation or newly chartered does
not change that policy. It allows a lodge under dispensation or newly
chartered to use any qualified Master Mason to be the Senior Deacon
for degrees, regardless of whether they are a member of the lodge. The
only requirement is that they are qualified to do the work.
Currently all Lodges under dispensation and newly Chartered are closely
monitored by an Inspector assigned by Grand Lodge which includes
making sure that all degree work is performed in accordance with the
CMC. This resolution would add a formal verification of the qualification
of the Senior Deacon before a dispensation or a charter can issued. It
would require that the Senior Deacon be a member of the lodge or in the
case of a dispensation would join the lodge if chartered.
The resolution, if passed will require as part of the conditions for a
dispensation or a charter to be granted that a Senior Deacon qualify in
the Ritual work of his office. No qualified Senior Deacon, no dispensation

222

or charter. The California Masonic Code requires all officers be installed as
soon as is practical after their election or appointment. It does not mandate
which officers have to be installed for a lodge to operate. Therefore,
a chartered lodge can install its officers without installing a Senior
Deacon. This resolution will place stricter requirements on lodges under
dispensation or newly chartered than we place on Constituent Lodges.
If this resolution passes, Lodges granted Charters during this annual

resolution. Which means they will cease all operations until the Grand

a new dispensation.

§807.020. ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS APPLICABLE TO
MEETINGS.
A. Sunday Meetings. No stated or special meetings of a lodge shall
be held on Sunday except for the annual Installation of Officers
or funeral services. If the stated meeting of a lunar lodge falls on a
Sunday, the stated meeting shall be held on the following day.
B. Lodge in Which Work May Be Done. Examinations in the candidate’s
lecture of a degree and the conferring of that degree shall be done
in a lodge of that degree. All other business may be conducted in a
lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons, a lodge of Fellow Craft Masons
or a lodge of Master Masons at the option of the presiding officer. At
the discretion of the presiding officer, a lodge of Entered Apprentice
Masons may be called up to a lodge of Fellow Craft Masons and then
to a lodge of Master Masons for any purpose but shall thereafter
similarly be called down to a lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons

before closing. At the discretion of the presiding officer, a lodge
of Fellow Craft Masons may be called down to a lodge of Entered
Apprentice Masons or called up to a lodge of Master Masons for any
purpose but shall thereafter be back to a lodge of Fellow Craft Masons
before closing. At the discretion of the presiding officer, a lodge of
Master Masons may be called down to a lodge of Fellow Craft Masons
and then to a lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons for any purpose
but shall thereafter similarly be called up to a lodge of Master Masons
before closing. Work to be Done in lodge of Entered Apprentice

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The intent of this resolution is to allow the presiding officer of a Lodge
to conduct business on any degree and to be able to call the Lodge up
or down for any purpose.

226

227

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Prior to the passage of Resolution 11-06 in 2012, Stated Meetings for all
Lodges in California were conducted on the Master Mason Degree. A
Lodge could not be called up to a higher degree for any purpose and could
be called down to a lower degree only for the purpose of examination.

This resolution does not require that the presiding officer open on a degree
that accommodates all Brethren wishing to attend the Stated Meeting.
It is possible that a presiding officer might choose to always open on
the 3rd degree with the result of excluding all Entered Apprentices and
Fellowcrafts from attending the Stated Meeting. This, however, must be
reconciled with CMC 804.860, which states that all Entered Apprentices
and Fellowcrafts have the right to speak on any matter coming before
the Lodge. This could be interpreted as requiring that if any Entered
Apprentices desire to attend the Stated Meeting, then it must be opened
on the 1st degree. If none are present, then the presiding officer could
open on a higher degree. Similarly, the presence of a Fellowcraft would
prevent opening a Stated Meeting on the 3rd degree.

Resolution 11-06 changed the California Masonic Code to require all
Stated Meetings to be held on the Entered Apprentice Degree. Entered
Apprentices and Fellowcrafts were allowed to sit in the Stated Meeting
but not to vote. Currently, a Lodge can be called up to a higher degree or
down to a lower degree only for the purpose of examination.
If adopted, Resolution 17-06 would grant the presiding officer of a Lodge
the power to determine on which degree a Stated Meeting will be opened.
The choice of degree would be at the discretion of the presiding officer.
This would permit a Lodge to open a Stated Meeting on the 3rd degree
with just five officers and the Tiler instead of seven officers and the Tiler
as required in the 1st degree opening. It would also allow the presiding
officer to vary the degree opened upon to improve the Lodge’s proficiency
in the three different openings.
It would also permit a Lodge to conduct Masonic Education on topics
pertaining to the higher degrees at a Stated Meeting. Currently a
Lodge can only discuss topics pertaining to the 1st degree at a Stated
Meeting, since the Lodge is only allowed to call up to a higher degree for
examination. This resolution would permit the presiding officer to open
on the 1st degree for the business portion of the meeting, then calling
up to a higher degree for Masonic Education in the 2nd or 3rd degree,
then calling down to the 1st degree for closing.
Additionally, there would be no restrictions on the purposes for which a
Lodge could be called up or called down. The only requirements are that
degrees and examinations must be conducted in the appropriate degree
and that the Lodge be closed on the same degree that it was opened on.
It would be permitted, for example, to open on the 1st degree, call up to
the 2nd degree for a Fellowcraft proficiency, call up to the 3rd degree for a
Master Mason conferral, and then call down to the 1st degree for closing.
It would also be permitted to open on the 3rd degree, call down to the 1st
degree for conferral of the Entered Apprentice degree, then call back up
to the 3rd degree for closing (after dismissing the candidate).

Another issue is that of an Entered Apprentice or Fellowcraft who arrives
late to a Stated Meeting that has been opened on a higher degree. Would
the presiding officer be required to call down to a degree that would
permit them to attend the business portion of the meeting?
If this resolution is adopted, a decision by the Grand Master as to the
restrictions on the choice of degree by the presiding officer for conducting
a Stated Meeting may be necessary.
Resolution: FAILED
