Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

229

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to modify the opening Ritual in all
three degrees to include mandatory recognition of Past Masters, Golden
Veteran recipients, and Hiram Award recipients. Additionally, they seek
to add an option for the Senior Deacon to call any “first time” visitors
west of the altar to present them with a Lodge Visitors Card, if it is the
Lodge’s practice to do so.
It has been the custom of this Grand Lodge and its Constituent Lodges
to recognize certain groups within our fraternity during dinners and
social gatherings. This is usually done by way of introductions; either
individual or in groups. Despite this being common practice, it has not
been a requirement. Each individual lodge has the discretion of how and
when introductions or recognitions are done.
Lodges currently have the option to recognize members whenever deemed
appropriate, including during their meetings. Some do so at dinner prior
to meetings. This resolution would require certain introductions during
opening, and thus some Lodges would have to decide whether to make
certain introductions multiple times in a single evening or forego public
introductions. Further, it is likely the same people would be recognized
at nearly every meeting as these groups would not change greatly from
week to week.
Recognition and appreciation is given to members many different
ways throughout our jurisdiction. Historically, the opening Ritual of
our Lodges has not been intended to be one of them. Lodges open for
specific purposes, such as Stated Meeting, degrees, and proficiencies: to
name a few. The Ritual is designed as a mechanism to facilitate these
specific functions. Sitting Masters and Past Masters are invited to seats in
the East during opening because they have been in the unique position
of governing a Lodge. It is considered a sign of respect to offer them a
position near the presiding Master in case he asks for advice or guidance
during the meeting.

230

231

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

The second part of this resolution, adding an option for the Senior Deacon
to call first time visitors west of the altar. This practice is not prohibited
by the California Masonic Code and thus codifying it is unnecessary.

We recognize that each lodge has many opportunities and means by
which its distinguished Brothers can be recognized and honored. Such
recognition or introductions during a meeting have traditionally been a
matter of lodge custom and culture. This Resolution would seek to make
law matters of protocol that have always been subject to lodge tradition
and custom, and are at the discretion of the Worshipful Master. It is these
very traditions and customs that serve to define each lodge, and are a
part of its distinctive character. By requiring lodges to observe certain
traditions, we diminish each lodge’s ability and opportunity to express
its own character and values.

To protect the autonomy of our Lodges has been important to this Grand
Lodge since its formation. Just because something is right for one Lodge,
does not mean it is right for every Lodge unless there is an overlying
legal or other compelling reason to standardize them. Lodges already
have the discretion to recognize its members at Stated Meetings and this
resolution may be seen as an unnecessary imposition on Lodges that
choose to recognize their members and visitors in other ways.

This Resolution seeks to require the introduction of Past Masters, Golden
Veteran Award recipients and Hiram Award recipients at all tiled lodge
meetings and to provide for a formal presentation of a lodge visitors card.

Further, there is currently nothing legal or Ritual that would prohibit
a lodge Master from making such introductions or recognitions at the
point specified in the Resolution, or at any other appropriate time. As
there currently exist frequent opportunities for lodges to recognize
distinguished Brothers, both within and without a tiled lodge, there is
no necessity for providing a Ritual requirement to do so.

In the past, the Grand Lodge has made such changes to our Ritual as
may be required for reasons of Ritual consistency, safety, compliance
with lawful authority, or other necessity. In considering this Resolution,
the Committee has applied these four tests.

The provision requiring the Senior Deacon to introduce any first time
visitors “just before the closing of the lodge” removes from the Worshipful
Master the option to make such introductions at some other point during
the evening where he may believe it more appropriate or timely.

First, introductions, honors, and recognitions a matter of protocol and
have never been, a part of our Ritual, or ceremonies. The invitation to
Masters and Past Masters to sit in the East is a Ritual courtesy extended
to those who currently, or have in the past, sat in the East. This courtesy
is not intended to be all inclusive. Nor is it a recognition or introduction
of any individual or group. Therefore, it cannot serve as a precedent for
the necessity of requiring the Worshipful Master to make introductions
or recognitions at this point in the Ritual. As such, there is no issue of
Ritual consistency to consider.

Additionally, this Resolution also provides, “any first time visitors may
be called West of the Altar and presented with a Lodge Visitors Card by
the Master, if it is the practice of the Lodge to present these cards.” This
is currently accepted practice throughout the jurisdiction and provides
nothing new. It is therefore unnecessary.

Second, this Resolution does not address any issues of safety or compliance
with any requirement of the Jurisdiction or other lawful authority.

The information contained in the Monitor and Officers Manual is
not esoteric, but it is Ritual in the same manner as the Ceremony of
Installation and the Lodge Funeral Service are Ritual. It contains nonesoteric work from all three degrees, plus balloting, election of officers,
calling up and down, presentation of Grand officers and the Flag of Our
Country, among others. Amending the Monitor and Officers Manual to
implement the requirements of this Resolution will effectively add to our

Report from the Ritual Committee

Last is the issue of necessity. Does this Resolution meet any clear and
pressing need of the Fraternity or its constituent lodges?

Lastly, this Resolution also provides that the Monitor and Officers Manual
be amended by the Ritual Committee with the consent of the Grand
Master to implement the foregoing resolutions.

While the Committee agrees that we should do all we can to recognize
and honor those of our Brethren who have served our Craft long and

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
Public Law No. 110-118 (approved on January 28, 2008, Statute 138-139)
states that members of the Armed Forces and veterans who are present
but not in uniform may render the military salute to the flag of our
country. However, this law does not specifically address whether those
persons should or should not remove their headdress.
The Proponents of Resolution 18-02 seek to allow Lodge Masters who are
members of the military or veterans the option of rendering the military
salute while remaining covered at all Masonic presentations of the US
Flag. This Resolution would also apply to Past Grand Masters and other
authorized members of the fraternity who are also members of the Armed
Forces or veterans while wearing the Master’s hat.
The California Masonic Code does not specify how the Master should
salute the flag as this is considered part of the Ritual. The Monitor and
Officers’ Manual indicates that the Master “removes his hat with his right
hand, holding the hat at his left shoulder, the hand being over the heart”.

Report from the Ritual Committee
The proponents of Resolution 2018-02 seek to change our Ritual by
allowing Lodge Masters, and others who wear the top hat during our
meetings and who are military veterans, the option of rendering a military
hand salute while remaining covered during flag presentations.
First, the Ritual committee honors, respects and thanks all those who
currently serve or have served in the military in defense of our Country.
Secondly, the Ritual committee is not in favor of adding options to
our Ritual. Allowing portions of our Ritual to be “optional” introduces
inconsistency throughout the State and makes learning our Ritual even
more difficult for new members. Currently, our Ritual has 14 options and
adding additional options only introduces further confusion and more
inconsistency.

Military regulations notwithstanding, we should remember that the
Master is the only brother authorized to wear a hat during our meetings
(unless the Grand Master is also present, then both may wear the top
hat). We should also remember that as the Master of the lodge, at the
moment he is installed, ceases to be his own Mason. He is no longer a
representative of himself and his own journey in the fraternity, but is
instead a single-being encapsulation of his lodge, his community and
the fraternity.
During our Installations, the Master is shown the Compass and told that
it teaches us to limit our desires in every station, and never to suffer our
passions or our prejudices to become the masters of our judgment.
If performing his duties appropriately, he no longer enjoys many privileges
of membership. He is no longer able to assert his opinion regarding
things before the lodge, as he must strive to balance the desires of the
lodge. He no longer provides a vote in most motions, because he is now
voting only to break a tie in order that peace and harmony of the lodge
might prevail. And while he can enjoy being his own person during the
dinner before our meeting, the moment he places that hat on his head,
he is now the chosen representative of us all, considering all of us and
entrusted to care for us all.

Additionally, the Ritual Committee is not in favor of changing a practice
that has not proven to be a burden to the Fraternity in general or the lodge
in particular over the years. The Ritual Committee is in favor of Ritual
amendments that allows us to remain relevant and improves member
experience without jeopardizing our teachings, traditions and heritage.

By taking a personal privilege, instead of following the currently
prescribed Ritual of the placement of the hat-holding hand over the heart
with the hat near the shoulder, the Master would be leaving behind his
brothers who are not Veterans and taking a moment of personal privilege
from the very place with which he received the trust of his lodge to set
aside his own desires for a season and serve.

Regarding this resolution, current law prohibits the Master, who is a
veteran, from rendering a military hand salute while wearing the Master’s
hat when he leads the Pledge of Allegiance. If the Master is active military
and in civilian attire or a veteran, he is required to remove the civilian
Masonic top hat during the Pledge of Allegiance.

A Master of the Lodge considers his duties above all else. And the way he
balances his democratic election to an autocratic position is by constantly
reminding himself that he is a servant first. This should be apparent
in all he does from the first time the jewel hits his chest to the time he
removes it from around his neck for the last time.

236

237

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Therefore, the Ritual committee does not believe the current Ritual used
by the master when saluting the flag of our country, to be a burden to the
Fraternity in general or the lodge in particular, but instead reinforces
the master’s neutrality in all matters before the lodge.

Does not amend the Constitution, Ordinances or Ritual. Simple majority
affirmative vote required for adoption.
Charles L. Schubert and Rogelio Bulanadi are authorized to represent
and act for the Resolution.

The Ritual Committee does not support this resolution.

Resolution No. 18-03
Allows California Masons to Belong to the Operatives
The proponents of this resolution seek to allow California Masons to
belong to the Worshipful Society of Free Masons, Rough Masons, Wallers,
Slaters, Paviors, Plasterers and Bricklayers.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, under Section 1200.015 of the California Masonic Code,
a Mason residing in the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California
shall not be, become or remain a member of any Masonic organization
with activities in this jurisdiction and a ritual other than the Ritual of
this jurisdiction, unless such Masonic organization was established or

Annual Communication; and

bylaws of the operatives are hereby approved under Section 1200.015B
of the California Masonic Code thereby permitting any Mason residing
in this jurisdiction to become a member of such organization.

of Free Masons, Rough Masons, Wallers, Slaters, Paviors, Plaisterers

California. The Operatives exists to perpetuate or preserve a memorial
of the practices of operative Free Masons existing prior to, or continuing
independently of, modern Speculative Freemasonry and consists of
seven grades commemorating a lifetime, or “forty years”, of operative
craft Rituals:
Iº

Indentured Apprentice

IIº

Fellow of the Craft

IIIº

Fitter and Marker

IVº
Vº

Setter Erector
Intendent, Overseer, Super Intendent and Warden

VIº

Passed Master (Note: Not “Past Master”)

VIIº Master Mason, or Grand Master Mason Honoris Causa, of whom
three are the Grand Master Masons
While the names of The Operatives’ degrees may seem similar to those
of the Speculative Craft, The Operatives do not purport to confer the first
three degrees of Speculative Freemasonry, nor alternatives to these. The
requirements for membership presume that all candidates for Indenture
have already received the first three Speculative Craft degrees. To be
considered for membership in The Operatives, one must be a member
of a Craft Lodge in a Jurisdiction recognized by the United Grand Lodge
of England, a Mark Master Mason, and a Royal Arch Mason. Each of the
degrees are conferred in a separate Lodge within each Assemblages.

238

Proceedings of the

The Society has members scattered throughout the world with
Assemblages in England & Wales, Australia, New Zealand, India, Spain,
France, Canada, Belgium, South America, and the United States. All of the
Assemblages retain allegiance to Grand Assemblage in London and adopt
an “English” practice of Freemasonry within The Operatives. No matter
where they are being worked, they are always conducted in English and
the first toast at the luncheon or dinner which follows the meeting is,
whenever possible, always to the Monarch of the United Kingdom.
There are nine Assemblages in the United States that constitute the
United States of America Region (USAM Region) that is overseen by
a Deputy Grand Master Mason. The nine Assemblages are located in
Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Texas (2), New York, Virginia (2) and Utah.
Although one can apply directly to join The Operatives in the UK, in the
USAM Region The Operatives can be thought of as a “semi-invitational”
body of Freemasonry with some Assemblages being more open and
some being more strictly invitational. In all cases, candidates must be
proposed by two members of the Society, supported by an additional five
members of the Assemblage to which they have been invited to apply, and
approved by the membership according to the established procedures.
The Indenture Fee required of all candidates in the USAM Region is $500.
Annual Dues vary by Assemblage and range from $50 to $150.
According to the USAM Region, membership in The Operatives is
considered most suitable for Masons experienced in the Speculative Craft
who seek a deeper experience of its operative origins. Commitment to
attendance and participation are reasonable expectations of membership
and are required for advancement. The founding members of the first
Assemblage of The Operatives constituted in the United States, spent
more than six years traveling to Canada and the UK in order to achieve
sufficient advancement to qualify as founders. As with our Operative
predecessors, travel to the work is considered an opportunity and not
a hardship. Advancement within The Operatives is slow by American
usage. It may take two years or more to reach the IVº, which is the “full
membership” degree of the Society. Advancement beyond the Iº and IIº
is dependent upon participation and attendance.
The proponents state that their Assemblage will be invitational, that it
will meet in the Long Beach or Garden Grove up to 3 or 4 times a year

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

239

and that it will cost $500 to join with dues of $75. They plan on an 18 to
24 month start up period to raise the $5,000 to $10,000 to make all of
the equipment, regalia and furniture needed for each Assemblage and
to get the 15 to 20 members necessary to effectively operate the new
Assemblage. They currently have four members in California with two
more that will be members before the end of 2018.

Resolution No. 18-04
Removes Restrictions on Holding a Tiled Meeting on a Sunday
The proponents of this resolution seek to removes restrictions on
conferring degrees and/or holding a stated or tiled special meeting on
a Sunday.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, by definition, California Freemasonry does not require a
member to be a Christian, only that he profess his belief in a Supreme
Being and a future existence; and
WHEREAS, men of different faiths with different days of worship are
members of our great Fraternal body, so how can we favor one person’s
Sabbath observation over another if we truly consider every man and
his faith to be equal; and
WHEREAS, there are concordant bodies that require its members
practice Christianity that hold their tiled meetings and degrees on
Sundays, so it is logical that the symbolic or blue lodges who do not
have Christianity as a prerequisite should not have a restriction against
meeting on Sundays; and
WHEREAS, the time restraints of today’s young masons are far
different that those of our fathers and grandfathers; and
WHEREAS, lodges of young members with demanding employment
and family obligations need the flexibility to meet at a time that is most
practical for the majority of its members; and
WHEREAS, removing the Sunday restriction allows more flexibility
when scheduling lodge meetings and degrees.

established in its bylaws. The foregoing notwithstanding, lodges whose
bylaws provide for meetings fixed by the phase of the moon shall hold a
stated meeting for the transaction of business once in each lunar month,
and Mountain Range Lodge No. 18, Harmony Lodge No. 164, Truckee

711 shall only be required to hold a stated meeting for the transaction of
business once in each of 10 calendar months during the year, as it may
provide in its bylaws.
A lodge may be opened for a stated meeting prior to the time fixed in
its bylaws. However, no business shall be transacted prior to such time.
The Inspector or Grand Master may grant a dispensation to change
the date of a stated meeting, as provided Section 405.060 of this code.
In the event that the Master of a lodge determines that inclement
weather, including ice, snow, and flood conditions, existing on the day
established in the bylaws of the lodge for its stated meeting, makes it
hazardous for members of the lodge to attend the meeting, he may, with
the consent of the Inspector of the district to which the lodge is assigned,
postpone the stated meeting to the same day of the week next following
the week scheduled for the stated meeting. The Master shall notify, to the
extent possible, all members of the lodge residing within 50 miles of the
meeting place of the lodge of the date of the postponed stated meeting.
Should a stated meeting be postponed, the business transacted at the
postponed stated meeting shall be limited to the reading of the minutes of
the last stated and subsequent special meetings, action thereon, payment

done or business transacted, except by, or in the presence of,

Warden, the Grand Master or the Grand Master’s designated
representative. No lodge shall transact any business with fewer

D.C. Presence of Charter. No meeting shall be conducted by a lodge
unless the charter of the lodge (or, in the case of a lodge under

charter may be made under the direction of the Grand Secretary

No Adjourned Meetings. There shall be no adjourned meeting.
Each meeting of a lodge must be closed when the business
proposed for transaction has been concluded, but in no event
later than the close of the day on which it was opened.

H.G. Good Standing Requirement. No member may make a motion,
second a motion, speak on a motion, vote on a motion, recommend
anyone for membership or ballot on membership at a lodge
meeting unless he is then a member in good standing of that
lodge. He must present a current dues receipt to the Tiler to
demonstrate that he is a member of the lodge in good standing
or be verified by the Master, Senior Warden, Junior Warden,
Secretary or Assistant Secretary as a member of the lodge in good
standing. If a member is present who is not in good standing,
any question or action to be decided hereunder by a majority
or greater vote of the members present shall be decided by a
majority or greater vote of the members present who are in good
standing.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this legislation wish to remove the restriction on
conferring degrees or holding tiled meetings on Sunday. The Grand
Lodge of California was formed nearly 170 years ago. It was formed by
Mason who were primarily Christian. As such, Sunday was reserved as
a day of worship.
California Masonry does not require a man to be of any particular religion.
We only require that he believes in a Supreme Being and future existence.
While the majority of the members of the fraternity are Christian, we have
embraced members from a vast array of religions. This has strengthened
our fraternity in many ways. Many of these religions have a Holy day
other than Sunday, or no specific Holy day day at all. California Masonry
is very accepting of different cultures and religious beliefs.
Time is a precious commodity. Having the flexibility to hold meetings
and degrees at a time that is convenient for the members of the Lodge
is extremely important. Removing this restriction would give Lodges the
option to expand their calendars.
This legislation, if adopted, would remove a bias in our law towards a
specific religious belief. That would lead to a more inclusive organization.

Resolution No. 18-05
Modifies the Installation Ceremony
The proponents of this resolution seek to modify the Installation
Ceremony for Constituent Lodges to allow the Installing Officer to invite
all lodge members to rise.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, when the Installing Officer addresses the Master-elect
and the Wardens-elect, they are standing; and
WHEREAS, when the Installing Officer addresses the members of the
lodge, they are seated; and
WHEREAS, the instructions given by the Installing Officer to the
lodge members carry the same level of importance as those given to the
Master-elect and Wardens-elect; and
WHEREAS, when the Installing Officer addresses the members of the
lodge, they too should be standing; and
WHEREAS, precedent for inviting the lodge members to stand may
be found in the ceremony for the institution of a new lodge where the
Grand Master, while addressing the lodge members, asks them to stand
along with the Master and Wardens.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Installation
Ceremony for Constituent Lodges be amended as marked:
I.O.

Brothers Senior and Junior Warden. You are too well acquainted
with the principles of Masonry to warrant any distrust that
you will be found wanting in the discharge of your respective
duties. Suffice it to say that what you have seen praiseworthy in
others, you should carefully imitate, and what in them may have
appeared defective, you should yourselves avoid. You should
be examples of discretion and propriety; for it is only by a due
regard for our laws and regulations as shown in your conduct,
that you can expect obedience to them from others. You are
assiduously to assist the Master in the discharge of his trust;
diffusing light and imparting knowledge to all whom he shall
place under your care.

247

In absence of the Master you will succeed to higher duties; your
acquirements must therefore be such as will insure proper
instruction to the Craft. From the spirit which you have hitherto
evinced, I entertain no doubt that your future conduct will be such
as will merit the applause of your Brethren, and the testimony
of a good conscience.
Senior and Junior Wardens will be seated when the I.O. states:
“Brethren of______________Lodge . . . etc. (No gavel – All remain
seated.)
Brethren of __________________ Lodge, No. _____ , please rise. My
Brethren, such is the nature of our Constitution, that as some
must of necessity rule and teach, so must others of course, learn
to submit and obey. Humility in both is an essential duty.
The officers who have been chosen to govern your Lodge are
sufficiently conversant with the rules of propriety and the laws
of the Institution to avoid exceeding the power with which they
are entrusted; and you are of too generous disposition to envy
their preferment. I therefore trust that you will have but one
aim — to please one another and unite in the grand design of
promoting happiness.
Finally, my Brethren, as this association has been formed and
perfected in so much unanimity and concord, so may it long
continue. May you long enjoy every satisfaction and delight which
friendship can afford. May kindness and brotherly affection
distinguish your conduct as men and as Masons.
Within your peaceful walls may your children’s children celebrate
with joy and gratitude, the annual recurrence of this auspicious
solemnity. And may the tenets of our profession be transmitted
through this Lodge, pure and unimpaired, from generation to
generation.
The Lodge Wardens and members may be seated.

gavel presentation.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of resolution 18-05 seek the option of having all the
members of a Lodge rise during the annual Installation ceremony
immediately after the Installing officer addresses the wardens near the
close of the Installation. After the members rise, the Installing officer
addresses them reminding them of their duties to the Lodge and partially
of their responsibilities to the master. This allows the members to feel a
part of the Installation ceremony.
This proposed change to the installation ceremony may clear-up a
perceived incongruity in the installation ceremony.
Report from the Ritual Committee
The proponents of Resolution 2018-05 seek to modify the Installation
Ritual for ceremony for Constituent Lodges to allow the Installing Officer
to gavel the brethren of the lodge up prior to giving the lodge membership
present their instructions.
The Master is given his admonitions while standing in front of the east to
convey the importance of the instructions given by the Installing Officer
relative to the Master’s actions and attitude towards peace and harmony,
and placing the will and pleasure of the lodge as a whole, above his own.
The Wardens are given their instructions in like manner. Their instructions
are equally important to assisting the Master in the government of the
lodge and in their readiness to serve in the Master’s absence.
The gaveling up of the brethren instills the importance of the instructions
that is not adequately conveyed while the brethren remained seated. The

250

Proceedings of the

words of instruction given to the standing members of the lodge conveys
a sense of responsibility to the brethren that they are just as responsible
for the keeping of the peace and harmony of the lodge as the Master and
Wardens are charged to do.
This resolution does not take anything from the Ritual of the installation.
On the contrary, it enhances our Installation Ritual and gives more
meaning to it. The Ritual Committee is unanimous in urging a YES vote.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to allow California Mason
to belong to the Masonic Order of Athelstan. Section 1200.015 of the
California Masonic Code (CMC) currently prohibits Masons residing in
this Jurisdiction from becoming or remaining a member of the Masonic
Order of Athelstan.
The Order of Athelstan was formed in 2005 in England. It is organized
into Courts and its teaching focus on monitorial symbolism found in Craft
Masonry, King Athelstan (the first King of England), and the Rosetta
Stone. It seeks to preserve and expand an “English” system of Masonry by
meeting only three or four times a year, holding short meetings of an hour
to an hour and a half, and holding social boards after every meeting. At
the social boards, the members join in a number of toasts, including toasts
to the President of the United States, the Queen of England, Officers of
the Court, new members, King Athelstan, and a silent toast. There is also
a focus on education and at least one paper must be prepared, approved,
and presented at the annual installation.
As a prerequisite to membership, candidates must be both Master

254

Proceedings of the

Masons and Royal Arch Masons. Courts may only induct two candidates
each meeting, although dispensation can be obtained to induct up to four
candidates per meeting. This is because Courts are intended to be small.
New courts require 20 candidates or members to start. Applications fees
vary from $300 to $350. These fees are intended to provide Courts with
adequate funds to purchase needed paraphernalia and officer jewels.

B. Past Grand Officers;

When deciding to authorize another appendant body, there are two
competing theories. One is that this Jurisdiction is having difficulty
supporting all the appendant bodies it already has. The other is that the
Brethren should be free to explore the Mysteries of Masonry however
they determine best.
Resolution: FAILED
Resolution No. 18-08
Requires Lodge to Designate the Voting Past Master at Grand Lodge
The proponents of this resolution seek to provide a procedure to
determine who shall cast the Past Masters collective vote at Grand Lodge
and to assure that only those with a vote may cast a vote.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, honest, legal and appropriate votes cast are a necessity
to any ballot cast; and
WHEREAS, each chartered lodge is entitled to four votes: one for each
of its Master, Senior Warden, Junior Warden and Past Masters collectively;
and
WHEREAS, any Past Master in good standing can demand the lodge’s
Past Masters’ collective ballot at the registration desk while checking in
at Annual Communication; an
WHEREAS, there is no procedure to assure that only those with the
vote are casting the vote.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 403.075 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

C. Masters, Senior Wardens and Junior Wardens of chartered lodges;
and
D. The Designated Past Master on behalf of the Past Masters
collectively of each chartered lodge.
If neither the Master nor either of the Wardens of a lodge has registered,
the elected representative of the lodge may cast the votes of Master and
Wardens of the lodge.
The Committee on Annual Communication Activities shall mark the
credential of each registered member of Grand Lodge entitled to vote
and the credential of each registered elected representative with the
vote or votes to which each is entitled. Only members with credentials
so marked may receive and cast ballots and then only in the number as
marked. The lodge Master with the attest of the lodge Secretary shall
certify to the Grand Secretary the lodge’s designated Past Master and
elected representative, if any. The designated Past Master may be chosen
by either those members of the lodge or by those Past Masters of the
lodge, present and voting at a stated meeting, as the lodge may determine.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to limit the distribution of the
collective ballot for the Past Masters to the one Past Master designated
by the Lodge.
Since its inception, the California Masonic Code has provided a vote
to the “Past Masters collectively of each chartered Lodge” (emphasis
added). It is not the vote of an individual person and is instead a vote to
be exercised collectively and in reliance upon the collegiality of the Past
Masters. The CMC does not mandate how this collegiality is achieved
and instead leaves this to the sound discretion of the Past Masters of

256

Proceedings of the

the Lodges. In the past, Past Masters of a particular Lodge would often
sit together during the Annual Communication to hear the arguments,
consider the merits, reach a consensus, and then cast the Past Masters
collective vote as the group had decided; and a number of Lodges still
follow this practice. Whatever method is used, the nature of the vote has
remained the same: it is a vote intended to be exercised collectively, and
the Past Masters of our constituent lodges have, for many years, exercised
their vote collectively in good faith.
This resolution would effectively change the nature of the Past Masters
vote. Instead of being a vote to be exercised collectively, the vote would,
in effect, be a vote exercised by an individual. If only the one designated
Past Master of a Lodge can collect and cast the Past Masters vote, then
that designated Past Master has no reason to consider the opinions of,
or be collegial with, the other Past Masters of his Lodge. While it could
be argued that the current provisions of the Code permit the Past Master
who first shows up at registration and collects the Past Masters vote
to behave likewise, this resolution, if adopted, does nothing to solve
that potential behavior. Instead, it gives the designated Past Master the
incentive to ignore the input of his fellow Past Masters, and the right to
cast the ballot as he, as an individual, sees fit, rather than casting the
ballot as the Past Masters, as a collective, may see fit.
In addition, this resolution stems from disharmony that took place at
a single lodge, which gave rise to the filing of Masonic Charges against
the Past Master who collected the Past Maters ballot for that lodge. Those
charges were ultimately dismissed; and this resolution is intended to
resolve the perceived problem at issue in those charges: namely, that
any Past Master of a Lodge may collect and cast the Past Masters ballot.
However, it has not been this Grand Lodge’s policy to resolve issues at
an individual lodge by way of a resolution that would affect all lodges.
Resolution: FAILED

Report of the Board of Trustees
Masonic Homes of California
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
In this annual report of the Masonic Homes of California, I am pleased
to share that we are close to completing the ambitious goals we defined
in the 2014 strategic plan, Roadmap 2020. In just four years, we have
achieved many important milestones, like developing and implementing
impactful programs for members of all ages, supporting more members
in need, and building plans for our future.
Over the past year, our Masonic Homes served more than 1,400 brothers
and their wives, widows, and families – more than 700 on our campuses
and communities, and an additional 694 clients through our Masonic
Center for Youth and Families (MCYAF). Through Masonic Outreach
Services (MOS), 399 elderly Masonic family members received support
in their communities, close to their lodges and families. Many of these
brothers, wives, and widows required financial assistance in order to
afford even basic necessities and housing. Service in the central valley
has doubled over the past year, and we will continue to expand services
in this and other previously underserved areas.
More than 300 Masons and their wives and widows live on our residential
campuses in Union City and Covina. These residents continue to thrive,
with six members in our 100+ Club. Our eldest resident celebrated her
105th birthday this month.
Over the past fraternal year, MOS handled more than 2,200 information
and referral calls and made more than 1,000 home visits. We expanded the
Lodge Outreach Program, which trains volunteer Masons to lead outreach
efforts locally, to all Masonic divisions. This important program extends
MOS’s reach while meaningfully engaging members and reconnecting
absent brothers with their lodges.
Another way that we are now supporting Masonic families statewide is
through the Masonic Value Network, which helps members conveniently
and independently research and access care in their own communities. In
2018, we added a prescription discount service and additional retirement
communities to the network.

260

261

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

In the year since the successful redesign of the campus waitlist, we
have reduced the time it takes to move into one of our Masonic Homes.
We can now provide on-campus care for those with the greatest need
within one to two months. For independent members whose needs we
can continue to meet in the community, the waitlist has been reduced to
an average of around 12 months; a reduction of more than 50 percent.
We now also offer direct admission into our skilled nursing program in
Union City, thereby serving those who require more advanced nursing
home care. For many families, knowing that their loved ones will be cared
for at the Masonic Home has been a godsend.

Yet another success in Covina has been MCYAF’s southern campus,
which quickly hit capacity after opening. MCYAF provides familycentered integrated mental health services for children and adolescents
experiencing emotional, academic, behavioral, or social difficulties, as
well as their families. In addition to supporting southern California
Masonic families, MCYAF partners with the Child Advocacy Center to
serve children who have been abused or have witnessed violent crime.
Together with its San Francisco center, MCYAF has grown its client
base by three-fold, and now serves almost six times as many Masons as
it did in 2015. Its telehealth counseling services will enable it to reach
even more Masonic families over the next year. It has also expanded its
reach to include members of the Masonic youth orders, adult caregivers,
and community members. It is also working to serve residents of the
Masonic Homes.

As Alzheimer’s disease and dementia statistics rise each year, memory
care remains a primary focus. The Stepping Stones Program, which
provides successive care strategies to address the progression of memory
loss, continues to yield positive outcomes. From the Brain Gym, where
residents sharpen memory through neurologist-designed computer
stimulation, to the innovative Compass Club daytime memory care, we
continue our commitment to preserving residents’ cognition as much as
possible. We have demonstrated that memory loss progression can be
slowed and, in some cases, even reversed. Our staff has been invited to
share our programs later this year at the national Leading Age conference
in Philadelphia – a testament to the success our programs.
We continue to provide state-of-the-art facilities and best-practicefocused care, and are working to expand southern California resources.
As skilled nursing and memory care are not currently offered on the
Covina campus, residents must move to off-campus facilities for advanced
care. Unfortunately, as a result, husbands and wives may be separated,
widows are taken from the community they have come to call home, and
brothers must spend their final days away from their Masonic community.
To address this issue, a new 32-bed skilled nursing center, which will
offer memory and long-term care, is currently under construction on the
Covina campus and will open by late 2019. The facility will vastly improve
the quality of life for elder members in Covina.
This year, we also opened a new Shared Housing Program on the Covina
campus for independent seniors who need safe, affordable housing. Two of
the formerly unused children’s homes have been remodeled to provide 14
bedroom and bathroom suites with common living and dining areas. This
innovative approach to shared senior living will provide opportunities
for clients to benefit from socialization with fellow housemates and
Masonic homes residents.

I am also pleased to announce that in Union City, we are embarking
on an ambitious plan to modernize our aging campus and add additional
capacity to meet the increasing demand for advanced care, particularly
quality memory care and high-level assisted living. Two 60-year-old
buildings are being completely renovated, allowing for additional capacity.
Moreover, a new state-of-the-art center for memory care and assisted
living is under construction. Union City will have a new “heart of the
campus” area, which will provide more outdoor space and activities for
residents to enjoy. Plans are in place to create a veterans’ memorial,
which will recognize residents who have served our country from the
Civil War to the present day.
Thanks to the success of our Let’s Write the Future capital campaign,
these programs will move forward, allowing us to uphold our commitment
to our brethren and their families and ensuring that the Masonic Homes
will be here when they are in need of relief.
Our greatest resource remains the dedicated Masonic homes
professional team, who continually strive to improve services for the most
vulnerable among our Masonic family and community. Our commitment
to person-centered care is exemplified through the Masonic Homes Way –
a culture of caring that has been successfully adopted by team members at
all levels. Our dedication to providing excellent care is reflected in the high
ratings our communities continue to receive. Transitions is consistently
named one of the best short-term, post-surgical rehabilitation programs
in the Tri-City area. The Lorber skilled nursing program was once again

262

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

awarded the coveted Five-Star Rating from Nursing Home Compare –
awarded to only 10 percent of nursing homes nationally. Moreover, our
Union City campus was recognized with the national Excellence in Action
Award for resident satisfaction. Our Lorber long-term care program was
recognized as a top performer in staffing by U.S. News and World Report.

Respectfully submitted,
John F. Lowe, PGM, Chairman
Michael J. Cornell, Vice Chairman
Gary L. Charland, President

Through a renewed commitment to our local communities, we have
actively engaged with the citizens surrounding our campuses, as well as
with Masonic family members statewide. This year, we sponsored more
than 100 on-campus community events, hosting more than 3,000 guests.
Many of these events have become annual traditions, like the holiday
tree lighting in Union City, which brings hundreds of neighbors to our
campus; an annual chili cook-off that honors local police and firemen;
and the Luminary Caregiver Awards, which recognize the contributions
and dedication of the people who make a difference in the lives of those
suffering from Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia.
Our SummerFest and HarvestFest events continue to be successful
Masonic family events. This year, more than 2,000 Masonic family
members gathered to share fun and fellowship. Next year, we hope that
the formal Masonic cornerstone ceremony for the new health center in
Covina will bring together families from throughout California to witness
this extraordinary addition to our campus.
Since 1898, the Masonic Homes of California has provided relief to our
brothers and their wives, widows, and children in need. This charitable
spirit carries on today. The Masonic Homes will be here when you need
us, and we are committed to serving you now and in the future. With
shorter waitlists; a direct-admit skilled nursing program; memory care
resources; statewide outreach programs; and support for youth, our
Masonic family can easily access the quality services they deserve in
their time of greatest need.

Report of the Board of Directors
Acacia Creek Retirement Community

This is accomplished through a leadership-level commitment to assessing
policies and procedures on an ongoing basis, and implementing changes
as needed to meet ever-evolving resident needs and best practices. Acacia
Creek demonstrates this commitment by ensuring its wellness program
provides a wide range of opportunities to address residents’ physical,
spiritual, social, and intellectual growth. Over the past year, we have
focused on training our team members and their families in the tenets
of successful aging, to promote their health and continued professional
development.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
Located on a picturesque hilltop setting adjacent to the Masonic Home
at Union City, our continuing care retirement community of Acacia Creek
is now in its eighth year of operation. It gives me great pleasure to report
on the community’s success over the past year.
Acacia Creek continues to remain above the national average for
occupancy in independent continuing care retirement communities
across the United States. Our marketing program is focused on reselling
apartments as they become available and expanding our waitlist to
quickly identify prospective residents as transitions occur. With very
few resident transitions, we project that our year-end occupancy rate
will be in the mid to high 90th percentile.
Acacia Creek’s success is driven by its current residents’ satisfaction
and happiness, which infuses the campus with a tangible vitality. These
important qualities were evaluated in this year’s Resident Survey, which
indicated an astounding 96.5 percent resident satisfaction rate. Residents’
joyful spirit is apparent to prospective buyers and visitors, whether they
are joining a resident for a delicious meal, touring the campus, or staying
overnight in one of our well-appointed guest apartments. Acacia Creek
residents demonstrate, through national data collection, that they enjoy
better health, nutrition, and physical activity than those at comparable
communities elsewhere in the country.
We have continued to partner with Masterpiece Living to continually
develop our successful aging culture. This national organization provides
us with education and programs of physical and mental wellness inspired
by the MacArthur Foundation’s 10-year study on aging. As a Masterpiece
Living community, Acacia Creek residents are empowered to pursue new
skills, physical activities, and personal fulfillment, as well as contribute to
the community by sharing their skills, knowledge, and life experiences.
Acacia Creek is proud to maintain its recognition as a Certified Center
for Successful Aging. Only 19 communities nationwide hold this highly
prestigious distinction, and Acacia Creek is the only one in Northern
California. This competitive certification is awarded to communities that
have cultivated a culture where residents can continue to grow and thrive.

Acacia Creek continues to benefit from the camaraderie between its
Masonic and non-Masonic residents. This year, an additional man became
a Master Mason after moving into our community, bringing the total
number of non-Masonic residents joining the Fraternity to 13 since
the community’s opening. Acacia Creek Masons are active in Siminoff
Daylight Lodge at the Masonic Home.
Acacia Creek team members, who follow a team management concept,
report a positive work environment. This is reflected in the community’s
low staff turnover. Employees are decision-makers who feel a sense of
ownership in the community’s operations. Reliable team members play
a vital role in making the community an ideal place to live.
When we established Acacia Creek, the Fraternity envisioned that it
would include all levels of healthcare, from independent and assisted
living to skilled nursing and memory care. The Acacia Creek community,
together with the boards of the Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek, are
collaborating to expand and improve services on both campuses to further
enhance the lives of current residents.
The board wishes to extend our sincere appreciation to Chuck
Major, president of Acacia Creek, and Martin Herter, vice president/
administrator who, together, have been responsible for maintaining the
high level of morale and staff accountability, as well as for executing
the strategic marketing program that has maintained Acacia Creek’s
occupancy stabilization at over 92 percent through 2018.
I want to thank the members of the Grand Lodge Executive Committee,
the Grand Lodge staff, the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees, and the
Acacia Creek Board of Directors for their expertise, vision, and passion.
We are excited about our future, and together we look forward to ensuring
the continued success and support of the mission of Acacia Creek.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
This past year has been incredibly exciting for the Masons of California
and your California Masonic Foundation. With our revised role as overall
funding arm of the Fraternity firmly in place, we set out to markedly
improve our ability to touch the lives of our most vulnerable brethren, as
well as the underserved and most needy students within California. I am
proud to report that you, my brethren, have embraced a renewed spirit
of giving over the past year, cementing philanthropy as a cornerstone of
your Masonic experience.
We began this year by kicking off our Let’s Write the Future fundraising
campaign, the first such campaign in our jurisdiction in over 60 years, and
our largest ever. Our goal is to expand our capabilities to provide advanced
care to our elder members through the Masonic Homes of California, and
to double the number of students and classrooms supported by Raising
A Reader, our childhood literacy education partner.
We asked Most Worshipful R. Stephen Doan to serve as campaign
chairman and created two committees composed of board trustees
members, Grand Lodge staff, and dedicated members in the north and
south who could work directly with lodges and brethren. Chaired by
Worshipful Brothers Randy Brill and Bob Whitfield, and teamed with
Candler Gibson, Greg Cherry and others, these committees have made
visitations and presentations all over the state during this first, Pace
Setter, phase.
The response to their call has been nothing short of phenomenal!
More than 25 Pace Setter lodges have pledged major funds over the
next five years, while many brethren have made their own personal
multi-year pledges. Thanks to their generosity, we are well on our way to
achieving our goal. This amazing response demonstrates that a culture
of philanthropy has truly blossomed in our jurisdiction. Your trustees
are extremely appreciative to be a part of this campaign, and we look
forward to reaching out to every lodge and brother over the next two
years. You will be hearing much more about the overall campaign during
this Annual Communication.

We look forward to celebrating the 50th anniversary of our Foundation

remember that the impact we have achieved over the past half-century
has only been possible through the continued generosity of our brethren

brothers, community, Foundation, and this great Fraternity.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:

continues to serve on its Park and Security committees. CMMT was the
main sponsor of the annual Huntington Park Tree Lighting Ceremony
last December, which attracted hundreds of our Nob Hill neighbors and
was regarded as one of the most successful in recent years.

at CMMT this year has been the construction of Freemason’s Hall – the
first lodge hall to be built in the CMMT. Designed to suit the needs of a
smaller, more connected modern lodge, Freemason’s Hall incorporates

Report of the Board of Trustees of the
Nob Hill Masonic Center

To promote occupancy of the garage throughout the day, we are
continuing our relationship with car-sharing services such as ZipCar,
City Car Share, and Getaround, in addition to Scoot – a new, two-wheeled
vehicle company.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California, F. & A.M. of
California:
The Board of Trustees for the Nob Hill Masonic Center (NHMC) is
pleased to present this annual report to the Grand Lodge of California and
its members. As the Grand Lodge’s only for-profit entity, our primary ends
policy is to ensure the efficient and effective operation of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple garage in order to generate an annual profit
for the Grand Lodge of California, its stockholder. This revenue provides
the Grand Lodge with essential funding for ongoing operational activities.
This year, the NHMC parking operation continued to set new revenue
highs, extending the recent trends of continued growth in an increasingly
difficult and changing parking market. First and foremost, the NHMC
will again be able to match/exceed last year’s largest dividend payment
ever to the Grand Lodge of California in the amount of $380,000. We
have been able to achieve this success through thoughtful, strategic, and
well-planned infrastructure changes – including garage automation and
solar energy – and by recognizing modern and future parking trends and
capitalizing on the use of technology to effectively promote our garage
business. The solar energy installation, which was completed at the end
of last year’s fiscal year, has truly been a benefit to our bottom line, with
an 80 percent reduction in electricity expenses against our budget for
traditional power costs. Our bottom line has also benefited from the tax
incentives we received through the conversion to solar power.
Early this year, under the watchful eye and leadership of our Grand
Lodge staff, the garage operator, SP+ Management, introduced new
on-site leadership to better manage and market the Masonic garage.
This change has led to a new high in monthly parkers, which is the core
revenue stream for the garage. Our team has also worked hard with SP+
to increase efficiency in planning staffing needs during events, decreasing
overall labor costs.

In addition to our building signage and word-of-mouth advertising,
NHMC now markets the garage through a number of online channels.
Our main online presence is the online parking guide at SFMasonic.
ParkingGuide.com. This year, new marketing efforts within the online
digital space have increased brand awareness of our garage tenfold, with
ads on driving apps such as Waze Navigation, Yext, and Google Maps, as
well as online ads on LiveNation. Our online digital ads appear on Google,
Bing, Yelp, Foursquare, Facebook, and MapQuest. Such advertising helps
us to raise public awareness of the Masonic garage as a parking option
on Nob Hill, and allows riders to reserve a parking space in advance of
their visit to our venue or other destinations on and around Nob Hill.
We are also working on a partnership-linking program that will place
Masonic garage links on the websites of restaurants, hotels, and other
destinations. Businesses that are unable to provide parking for their
customers will allow the Masonic garage to place a parking widget on
their websites, thus providing a parking option that visitors may not
otherwise know about.
In summary, NHMC’s success throughout the past year has been due
to our ability to control costs, manage expenses, grow revenue via the
use of modern technology, and harness new and improved marketing
efforts through the various online digital channels.
As we close out our fiscal year, we would like to thank our Grand
Lodge staff for all their hard work. Thank you to our fellow colleagues on
the Board of Directors for the wisdom and counsel they have provided
throughout the year. The board is particularly grateful to Worshipful Jeff
Wilkins for his tremendous service during his nine-year tenure on the
board and leadership as former board president.
Most Worshipful Galloway, it has been an honor and privilege for
this year’s board to serve you and this Grand Lodge. We appreciate
your support and we pledge to continue to achieve our ends policy of
delivering the very best and highest dividend possible to the Grand
Lodge of California. Congratulations to you for a fantastic year and your
leadership and labors on behalf of our fraternity.

Report of the Committee
on Jurisprudence
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the
Grand Master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session.
The committee reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to
be considered at the next Annual Communication and prepares any
necessary legislation to carry out the intent of the proponents. At the
Annual Communication, it comments on the legality of the Grand Master’s
decisions and dispensations and on the legal effect of the proposed
recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual Communication,
it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect the
legislation that was adopted.
In the committee’s view, those of Grand Master Galloway’s decisions
and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his
discretion. In the committee’s view, the legislation posted by the Grand
Secretary to the California Grand Lodge website on July 27 of this year
is sufficient to carry out the intent of the proponents. Furthermore, the
legislation contained in Grand Master Galloway’s recommendations,
which he will present in his message, is sufficient to carry out his intent.
We believe that each piece of this legislation has the legal effect set forth
in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no
recommendations as to the action you should take with it. While the
committee has written the title and introductory explanation for each
resolution before you and assisted the proponents in drafting the code
changes required to effect their intent, the proponents’ arguments in
their whereas clauses are their own. The committee does not assist in
drafting the whereas clauses and makes no comments on them.
The legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge
website on July 27 of this year and the legislation contained in Grand
Master Galloway’s recommendations require no separate motion because
they are automatically before this Annual Communication. The presiding
officer will announce the vote required for the passage of each item before
discussion begins. Any legislation that does not amend the California
Masonic Code or the Ritual requires a simple majority only for adoption.
Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or the Ritual must be

292

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment receives a
simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries over
to the next Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative
vote is required for adoption.

Respectfully submitted,
R. Stephen Doan, P.G.M., Chairman

In addition to the foregoing responsibilities, the committee reviews
all charges and specifications of un-Masonic conduct, strikes out those
portions that are not supported by a clear and precise specification
of un-Masonic conduct and revises those portions that are incorrect,
ambiguous or insufficient. The committee may dismiss charges if all
the facts set forth in the specifications, even if true, would not warrant a
verdict of u-Masonic conduct. As part of its review, the committee provides
the parties with every essential factual element which must be proven
at trial for the accused to be found guilty of each charge. Since the last
Annual Communication, the committee has reviewed the charges and
specifications in 16 trials.
If a Mason under the disciplinary jurisdiction of the California Grand
Lodge has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere (no contest) to, or has been
convicted of, a crime of moral turpitude by a federal or state court, he
shall be deemed automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges
of Masonry without any further action of his lodge or Grand Lodge.
The committee reviews a certified copy of the record of conviction to
determine whether there has been an automatic expulsion. Since the
last Annual Communication, the committee has reviewed seven federal
or state court records to evaluate whether there has been an automatic
expulsion of the Mason involved in the proceeding. These matters are
summarized in the attached exhibit.
No person shall hold or be eligible for membership in any constituent
lodge who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been convicted
of, a crime involving a violation of the moral law unless, for the reason that
he did not commit the offense, he either has been pardoned or had his
judgment of conviction vacated or reversed. All applicants are subject to
background checks to determine compliance with this rule. Since the last
Annual Communication, the Grand Secretary has asked the committee to
review 12 federal or state court records to evaluate whether an applicant
is eligible for the degrees.
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity that he has given
us to serve this year.

Michael H. Anatole
John R. Heisner, PGM

Exhibit
Automatic Expulsions
October 13, 2017 to October 18, 2018
Trial No. 2774
In Trial No. 2774, the member pled no contest to a violation of each of
California Penal Code Sections 30305(a)(1), 22900 and 29825(b). It is the
judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence
that these crimes do not involve moral turpitude for purposes of Section
100.075 of the California Masonic Code. Automatic expulsion is not
appropriate unless the only activity for which there could have been
a conviction under the applicable statute involves moral turpitude.
Based on the court record, the member may have been convicted of
possession of a firearm or other weapon only, which is not a crime of
moral turpitude. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing
analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee
on Jurisprudence that the member has not pled guilty to, pled no contest
to, or been convicted of a crime of moral turpitude before a federal or state
court. Accordingly, the member has not been automatically expelled from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of
the California Masonic Code. However, the information set forth in the
court record should be sent to the lodge in which the member is a Mason
to determine whether the crimes involved un-Masonic conduct and
therefore whether charges of un-Masonic conduct should be preferred.
Trial No. 2818
In Trial No. 2818, the member was convicted of a violation of California
Penal Code Section 487, which is grand theft. Under Section 100.075 of
the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2,
grand theft involves moral turpitude. Therefore, based on the court record,
it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on
Jurisprudence that the member pled guilty to a crime of moral turpitude
before a state court. Accordingly, the member has been automatically
expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section
1404.820 of the California Masonic Code. His expulsion from Masonry
was effective on November 2, 2016, the date he entered his plea of guilty.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

295

Trial No. 2824
In Trial No. 2825, the member pled guilty to Second Degree Murder
with punishment as a Class B2 felon under North Carolina General
Statutes 14-17. Under Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code and
2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, murder involves moral turpitude. In
the committee’s opinion, the conduct described in North Carolina General
Statutes 14-17 involves murder. Therefore, based on the court record and
the foregoing analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members
of the Committee on Jurisprudence that the member pled guilty to a
crime of moral turpitude before a state court. Accordingly, the member
has been automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code.
His expulsion from Masonry was effective no later than February 13,
2017, the date of his conviction.
Trial No. 2825
In Trial No. 2825, the member was convicted of a violation of California
Penal Code Section 288(a). Under Section 100.075 of the California
Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, lewdness involves
moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the conduct described in
California Penal Code Section 288(a) involves lewdness. Therefore, based
on the court record and the foregoing analysis, it is the judgment of a
majority of the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence that the
member has been convicted of a crime of moral turpitude before a state
court. Accordingly, the member has been automatically expelled from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the
California Masonic Code. His expulsion from Masonry was effective no
later than November 29, 2007, the date of his conviction.
Trial No. 2826
In Trial No. 2826, the member pled no contest to vehicular
manslaughter, which is defined under California Penal Code Section
192(c)(1) as: driving a vehicle in the commission of an unlawful act, not
amounting to a felony, and with gross negligence; or driving a vehicle in
the commission of a lawful act which might produce death, in an unlawful
manner, and with gross negligence. It is the judgment of a majority of the
members of the Committee on Jurisprudence that vehicular manslaughter
(if the killing is not the result of recklessness) does not involve moral
turpitude for purposes of Section 100.075 of the California Masonic
Code. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing analysis,

296

297

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on
Jurisprudence that the member has not pled guilty to, pled no contest to,
or been convicted of a crime of moral turpitude before a federal or state
court. Accordingly, the member has not been automatically expelled from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820
of the California Masonic Code. However, the information set forth in
the court record should be sent to the lodge in which the member is a
Mason to determine whether the crime involves un-Masonic conduct and,
therefore, whether charges of un-Masonic conduct should be preferred.

In Crime No. 2, the member pled nolo contendere to a violation
of California Penal Code Section 496(a), which involves possession of
stolen property knowing it to have been stolen. Under Section 100.075
of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No.
2, possession of stolen property knowing it to have been stolen is a
crime of involving moral turpitude. Accordingly, the member has been
automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry
pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code. His
expulsion from Masonry was effective no later than March 24, 2015, the
date he was sentenced based on his plea of nolo contendere.

Trial No. 2827
Trial No. 2827 involved two crimes.
In Crime No. 1, the member pled no contest to a violation of California
Penal Code Section 273.5(a), which includes assault. Section 100.075
of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No.
2 provide guidance as to the meaning of the term moral turpitude. As
set forth in that decision, an assault without an evil intent or depraved
motive does not involve moral turpitude. For an assault to involve moral
turpitude, it must be with intent to kill; with intent to commit rape; with
intent to commit robbery; with intent to commit serious bodily harm; or
with a dangerous or deadly weapon. It is the judgment of a majority of
the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence that California Penal
Code Section 273.5(a) does not involve moral turpitude for purposes of
Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code. Automatic expulsion is
not appropriate unless the only activity for which there could have been
a conviction under the applicable statute involves moral turpitude. Based
on the court record, the member may have been convicted of assault
without an evil intent or depraved motive, which is not a crime of moral
turpitude. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing analysis,
it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on
Jurisprudence that the member has not pled guilty to, pled no contest to,
or been convicted of a crime of moral turpitude before a federal or state
court. Accordingly, the member has not been automatically expelled from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of
the California Masonic Code.

Trial No. 2830
Trial No. 2830 involved three crimes.
In Crime No. 1, the member pled no contest to a violation of California
Penal Code Section 273.5(a), which includes an assault. Section 100.075
of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No.
2 provide guidance as to the meaning of the term moral turpitude. As
set forth in that decision, an assault without an evil intent or depraved
motive does not involve moral turpitude. For an assault to involve moral
turpitude, it must be with intent to kill; with intent to commit rape; with
intent to commit robbery; with intent to commit serious bodily harm; or
with a dangerous or deadly weapon. It is the judgment of a majority of
the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence that the Crime No. 1
does not involve moral turpitude for purposes of Section 100.075 of the
California Masonic Code. Automatic expulsion is not appropriate unless
the only activity for which there could have been a conviction under the
applicable statute involves moral turpitude. Based on the court record for
Crime No. 1, the member may have been convicted of assault without an
evil intent or depraved motive, which is not a crime of moral turpitude.
Therefore, based on the court record for Crime No. 1 and the foregoing
analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee
on Jurisprudence that the member has not pled guilty to, pled no contest
to, or been convicted of a crime of moral turpitude before a federal or state
court. Accordingly, the member has not been automatically expelled from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of
the California Masonic Code as a result of Crime No. 1.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Insurance is responsible for reviewing the Grand
Lodge property, casualty, professional lines insurance policies, and other
related insurance programs. The committee is also responsible for working
with the broker selected by Grand Lodge and making recommendations
regarding coverage and other insurance related matters. The Committee
on Insurance reports to the Grand Secretary on all insurance matters
(except life and medical coverage and benefits for employees), who then
makes the final decision regarding the different coverages and limits
to purchase or renew. The committee also works closely with the Chief
Financial Officer (CFO) and the legal team on an ongoing basis.
Currently, the full committee meets three times each Masonic year, with
an additional meeting in December for just the Chairman, Vice Chairman,
the CFO, other Grand Lodge representatives, and the insurance broker
(Marsh).
The purpose of the December meeting is to advise the broker of any
changes to Grand Lodge activities or exposures to loss as well as to review
new programs being contemplated or that are under way. The broker
provides any information on changes in the insurance marketplace
regarding cost, coverage, and availability. The broker may also make new
recommendations regarding the insurance program.

Overview
The Investment Committee has been charged with the prudent
handling of California Grand Lodge investment funds. These funds
consist primarily of the General and Endowment funds for the Masonic
Homes of California, but also include the investment portfolios of the
California Masonic Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple,
the Grand Lodge Retirement plan and the Grand Lodge of California
itself. We take this charge very seriously. In its simplest terms, we manage
the investment funds with an eye to growing and preserving capital. We
strive to maintain an increasingly diversified portfolio that is designed
to generate the necessary funds for the continuing operation of Masonic
functions, as well as allowing for growth for future needs. In doing so, we
constantly scan the horizon in an attempt to take advantage of long-term
trends as well as near-term opportunities. The Grand Lodge Investment
Committee utilizes the services of professional investment management
firms to gain access to the capital markets. The funds are invested in
the domestic United States, international equity markets, fixed income
markets, and alternative strategies which strive to be non-correlated to
the traditional stock and bond markets.
The past year (ending June 30, 2018) yielded a return of 6.4 percent
on the invested funds. We recognize that not all years can be positive
years, and we remain committed to the process and to the structure of the
portfolio as constructed. We have spent a good deal of time finding ways to
balance risk and reward and analyzing the strategic allocation to various
asset classes in the portfolio with the help of our consultants (NEPC,
LLC). We have implemented a mix of traditional equity investments, as
well as fixed income and alternatives. A primary driver of the allocation
strategy is to assemble a collection of investments that do not share a
direct correlation in risk profile (so that all the assets do not react the
same to down market conditions).

potential for appreciation of assets after withdrawals are taken into

The Total Grand Lodge and Related Entities portfolio grew 6.4 percent
for the year ending June 30, 2018. The total fund policy benchmark
was up 7.0 percent. As of June 30, 2018, the market value of the Total
Grand Lodge and Related Entities portfolio was $1,044,633,771 compared
to $1,021,627,891 a year earlier. This represents a gain of $23,005,880.
For the three-year period ending June 30, 2018, the combined Grand
Lodge and related entities returned 5.7 percent versus 6.7 percent for
the benchmark. Since inception, our funds have returned 7.6 percent
annually versus 7.8 percent return of the benchmark.
Highlights of the year June 30, 2017-18:

The U.S. equity allocation of the portfolio was up 13.2 percent
compared to 14.8 percent for the Russell 3000 Market Index.

•

The Non-U.S. equity portfolio was up 10.9 percent compared to 7.3
percent for the MSCI All Country World ex-U.S. Index.

All returns are net of fees. Detailed entity performance can be found
in the tables attached to this report.
Year in Review Activity
You will find attached a YEAR IN REVIEW summary which outlines
all the activities within the committee over the past year. You can see it
was a busy year and the committee feels great about all we were able to
accomplish. A few highlights to call out are included below.
Investment Manager Changes: Within the asset categories, there were
many manager changes made to implement the revised asset allocation
developed with our new consultants (NEPC, Inc.) in 2017. You can see
the additions and subtractions in the attached report.

•

Global Equities were up 9.9 percent compared to 10.7 percent for
the MSCI All-Country World Index.

•

The fixed income portfolio was up 1.0 percent, compared to a 1.4
percent return for the Barclays Global Aggregate Bond Index.

In order to take advantage of investment opportunities that require
quick decision making, the Investment Committee decided to give our
consultants (NEPC, Inc.) discretionary authority to add and subtract
managers to the Private Markets portion of the portfolio. The managers
in that portion of the portfolio are reviewed with the committee so that
we are aware of what changes have been made and why.

•

Our Total Hedge Funds and GAA Hedge Funds were up 1.4 percent
compared to the HFRI Fund Weighted Index of 5.7 percent.

Grand Lodge Investment Management For the Year Ended June
30th, 2018

•

And our Total Private Markets were up 2.8 percent.

In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand
Lodge Investment Policy and Philosophy, the Investment Committee
meets quarterly with our investment consultant, NEPC, LLC. We also
meet with our individual portfolio managers as needed and review due
diligence reports from the consultants every quarter. We also monitor
respective performance of the managers compared to various indices
representing their objective. This process provides the Investment
Committee with the necessary data to evaluate each investment manager
on a timely basis, and to observe whether they continue to achieve the
objectives of their mandate.

A more detailed manager performance review can be found in the
tables attached to this report.
The Investment Committee does not attempt to take advantage of
perceived short-term anomalies in the markets by chasing the most
recent top performing asset class. Rather, it arrives at its recommended
allocation to stocks and bonds and other asset classes only after very
careful due diligence and consideration. The purpose of the funds, their
spending requirements, investment time horizon, and ability to assume
risk are all factored into these recommendations. The probability and
duration of potential losses are carefully weighed against the long-term
