Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Report on the Committee on Lodge Support

for leadership or ritual-related matters. For administrative matters, they
would directly contact the respective California Grand Lodge staff. Ad
hoc members may also be identified within each Masonic Division to
provide additional support, as required. The Inspector or AGL would
be able to direct the requesting brother or lodge to the appropriate ad
hoc member or Grand Lodge staff member if they were unable to help
resolve the issue at hand. Also envisioned are potential updates to the
California Grand Lodge website that provide case studies, lessons learned,
frequently asked questions, and potentially other interfaces for members
to access before they pick up the phone to their Inspector, the ad hoc
committee member, or the Grand Lodge staff member.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Lodge Support Task Force, formed by M:.W:. Bruce Galloway
and the Executive Committee, submitted their recommendation to the
Grand Master and the Executive Committee on 20 June, 2018 regarding
the future of the Lodge Support Committee.
The Task Force addressed a key question of “What is lodge support?”
and then looked at how it should be provided. In the past, the Lodge
Support Committee was ineffective for two reasons. The first was that it
was focused on the “Troubled Lodges” and there was a stigma associated
with the lodges receiving support. The second problem was with members
not being aware of the committee or of the California Grand Lodge staff
resources to provide support. The Lodge Support Committee needs to
transition from the one or two individuals traveling the Jurisdiction and
“fixing” lodges to a system where the lodges are relying on the Inspectors
within their division, the grand lodge staff, and ad hoc members identified
as having specific talents that could be used to support the lodge.
After several meetings, the Task Force has a consensus recommendation
that the Lodge Support Committee transition from a standing committee of
11 - 20 members to a special committee of three to six members. This special
committee would provide expertise and coordination in administrative or
leadership-related issues. These subject matter experts would coordinate
lodge support activity for the Craft by doing the following:
•

Create list of regional ad hoc members based on their talents
(conflict resolution, finance, taxes, etc.) as needed and ensure that
they were accessible from the California Grand Lodge website.

•

Provide input as to changes to Grand Lodge website and IT
infrastructure to support self-service, FAQ, best practice case
studies, and lessons learned.

The Special Committee would rely upon the AGL/Inspectors and
ad hoc members for direct support for the lodges. This support would
be for administrative (finance, tax, properties, etc.) related matters and
leadership (conflict resolution, cultural issues, membership development,
leadership development, community awareness programs, etc.) related
matters. The Craft would access support for their lodge by directly
contacting their respective Divisional Inspector or Inspector at Large

It is envisioned that the Lodge Support Committee would have a
dedicated budget, to be determined. Any regional support within the
Division/District would be covered by respective AGL/Inspector budgets.
The recommendation, options considered, and additional information
are outlined in the presentation sent via email on 16 May, 2018. For
implementation, this recommendation required a Grand Masters
Recommendation to change the CMC.
This recommendation became GRAND MASTER GALLOWAY’S
RECOMMENDATION NO. 2 ELIMINATES THE LODGE SUPPORT
COMMITTEE AS A STANDING COMMITTEE, which was passed during
the Annual Communication of the California Grand Lodge on 20 October,
2018 and made the standing committee, as required by our CMC, a special
committee. It will now be up to M:.W:. Wright to appoint members to the
now Special Committee for Lodge Support during the ensuing Masonic
year.
Fraternally,
Jeffery M. Wilkins, Chairman
Stuart A. Wright, DGM
Arthur H. Weiss, JGW

Proceedings of the

Report of the Committee on Trial Review
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Committee on Trial Review has carefully examined the records of all
trials completed during this Masonic year. In each of the following matters,
the Committee finds that there was compliance with the procedural
requirements of the California Masonic Code, and that the findings were
supported by substantial evidence except where otherwise noted.
The following cases were decided by the Trial Masters after investigation
either because the Accused failed to submit a plea or submitted a plea
of guilty or no contest:
1. In Case No. 2805, the Accused was charged with fraud, falsehood
and deceit by representing himself as an agent of the Accuser’s
business by preparing a bid for construction using the Accuser’s
company name, e-mail, telephone and contractor’s license number.
There was no dispute that the Accused did prepare said document,
but the Accused stated he had permission from the Accuser to do
so and the Accuser denied he gave any such permission. The Trial
Master found that this was a “he said vs he said” confrontation.
The Trial Master found nothing inherently unethical, fraudulent,
misleading or criminal about the bid. Based on the evidence,
inferences, and credibility of the witnesses, including that the
parties had worked together before on projects and had referred
each other to prospective clients, the Trial Master found that the
Accuser did not sustain the required burden of proof and found
the Accused not guilty.
2. In Case No. 2718, the Accused was charged with misrepresenting
a material fact by omission in an application for degrees and
violating a criminal law involving moral turpitude and the moral
law. The Trial Master found the Accused failed to disclose on his
application a conviction for a serious felony violation of RICO (or
the Federal Racketeering Act as well as his unlawful activities with
the Mongols, an outlaw motorcycle gang. The Trial Master reviewed
the application and the federal criminal case file and found the
Accused guilty of both charges and set the penalty at expulsion.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

319

3. In Case No. 2772, the Accused was charged with injuring a Mason
when he used physical force to bar the Accuser from entering the
Hall for dinner before a stated meeting. The Accused had been told
by the Master not to allow the Accuser into the room. The Accuser
tried to go around the Accused. The Accused ultimately pled guilty.
After interviewing the parties, the Trial Master found mitigating
factors including a handwritten apology and remorse by both
parties. The Accuser requested a reprimand and formal apology.
The Trial Master set the penalty at reprimand in open Lodge.
4. In Case No. 2820, the Accused was charged with committing theft
by false pretenses and, further, with engaging in conduct prohibited
by the federal Stolen Valor Act of 2013. In the first specification,
the Trial Master found that the Accused admitted to the defrauded
Applicant that he took and personally spent the Applicant’s Lodge
fees and never submitted the application. The Accused only repaid
the stolen money after his actions were discovered. In the second
specification, the Accused fraudulently posed as a “wounded
warrior” having received the military Silver Star, Purple Heart
and other combat medals which he did not earn. This was done
by the Accused to persuade and cause the Lodge and others in the
community to give him substantial sums of money and tangible
benefits on many occasions. The Trial Master set the penalty at
expulsion.
5. In Case No. 2793, the Accused, sitting as Junior Warden, was
charged with committing ballot fraud by removing cubes at a
stated meeting from the ballot box on three separate votes and
announcing that the ballot was “fair.” The Accused pled “No
Contest.” Ordinarily, the conduct would have warranted expulsion.
However, the Trial Master found numerous factors in mitigation,
including the fact that the Accused quickly accepted responsibility
for his actions and admitted that, though his own actions were
un-Masonic, they were intended to correct what he perceived
to be ongoing un-Masonic “black balling” of new members and
affiliates. This was part of a course of conduct which resulted
in the Grand Master removing the previous Master. The Junior
Warden was removed by the appointed Master, and ultimately the
lodge’s charter was temporarily suspended. The Trial Master set the
penalty at suspension for 9 months, and given the highly unusual
circumstances, the Committee reluctantly agrees.

320

Proceedings of the

6. In Case No. 2817, the Accused pled “No Contest” to two charges of
un-Masonic conduct: (1) embezzlement and (2) breach of fiduciary
duties as Treasurer of the Masonic Hall Association by making a
check for $4,000 payable to himself and cashing it for his own use.
When the missing funds were discovered several months later, the
Accused signed a note promising to repay same and then demitted
from the Lodge. After he demitted, an additional embezzlement of
$1720 was discovered. There were no mitigating circumstances, and
the Trial Master fixed the penalty at expulsion.
7. In Case No. 2813, the Accused was charged with embezzlement,
fraud and larceny by forging another brother’s name on lodge
checks, writing checks to cash for himself, and stealing lodge funds.
The Trial Master examined the transaction records and interviewed
several Lodge members who attested to the Accused’s admission
of the thefts. The Accused’s sister reimbursed the Lodge in full the
sum of almost $6,000. The Trial Master found the Accused guilty
and set the penalty at expulsion.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Numbers
2805, 2718, 2772, 2820, 2793, 2817, and 2813, the Trial Masters’ procedures,
findings and the penalties affixed be hereby affirmed.”
The following case was decided by the Trial Master after investigation
because the Accused submitted a plea of no contest:
8. In Case No. 2816, the Accused, while a member of the Masonic
Hall Association, embezzled approximately $2,976 in three
separate ATM withdrawals from the Hall Association funds for
his personal use without the knowledge or consent of the Lodge
or Hall Association. The Accused reimbursed $3000 to the Lodge
upon discovery of his actions seven months later, but four months
before charges were filed. The Accused pled “No Contest” to this
charge and the Trial Master, noting many mitigating factors, set the
penalty at suspension for a definite period of 12 months. However,
the Committee on review of the aggravating and mitigating factors
notes that there is a “bright line” in Masonry and that an act of
embezzling money from a lodge crosses that line. The Committee
therefore recommends that the penalty be modified to expulsion.
Although the Accused pled “No Contest” to the Second Specification
of improperly investing $3,000 of Hall funds in Bitcoins contrary
to his fiduciary duty and California Grand Lodge guidelines, the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

321

Trial Master found there was no damage to the Association as the
investment returned $3,200. Damage being a necessary element
in the offense, the Trial Master dismissed the second specification.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Number
2816, the Trial Masters’ procedures and findings are affirmed, but that
the penalty be modified to expulsion.
The following cases were settled by the parties with the approval
of the Trial Master:
9. In Case Nos. 2740, 2744, 2743, the three Accused, all from the
same Lodge, were charged with refusal to obey an edict of the
Grand Master to produce bank account numbers, type of accounts
and statements of their Lodge and Building Association. The Trial
Master found at a Settlement Conference that following the edict
one of the Accused, as the then Master, submitted a written letter
detailing his investigation, including a portfolio of bank records,
which were delivered to the then Assistant Grand Lecturer and
Inspector. None of the Accused had the ability as either a Lodge
officer or member of the Building Association to access any further
documents. The Trial Master noted that two of the Accused were the
Masons who had brought such financial concerns to the attention
of the Grand Master. The Accuser requested that the charges be
withdrawn. The Trial Master ordered same and dismissed the
charges.
10. In Case No. 2794, the Accused pled “Not Guilty” and then
changed his plea to “No Contest” to unmasonic charges that while
intoxicated, he made racially abusive comments to a Brother in
the presence of at least three Masons. In mitigation, the Accused
apologized within a couple of days to the Brother who accepted
the apology and wrote a letter of apology to the three witnesses.
The Trial Master set the penalty at reprimand in open Lodge.
11. In Case Nos. 2780 and 2781, both Accused were charged with
embezzlement of Hall Association funds. Each pled not guilty.
Following two pretrial conferences, the Trial Master concluded
their actions were the result of poor operations at the Hall
Association rather than intentional falsehood or embezzlement
and, accordingly, the charges could not be proven. The parties
agreed to settle the matter by pleading guilty to an amended

322

Proceedings of the

charge of failure to properly discharge duties as Hall Association
board members, accepting a reprimand in open Lodge, refunding
the $400 and $2000, respectively, demitting from the Lodge, and
agreeing not to serve as an officer of any Lodge or appendant or
concordant body for five years. Based on this agreement, the Trial
Master imposed the penalty of reprimand.
12. In Case No. 2814, the Accused was charged with falsely failing to
disclose that he had previously received his First Degree in another
recognized Lodge outside of California. The omission constituted
a misrepresentation of a material fact and a material breach of
his obligation not to cheat wrong or defraud. The Accused, now
residing outside of California, pled not guilty. As a result of a
settlement conference, he changed his plea to “No Contest.” He
sent an e-mail to the Lodge apologizing, taking responsibility for
his actions and accepting whatever punishment might be imposed.
The Trial Master fixed the penalty at indefinite suspension.
13. 
In Trial No. 2789, the Accused was charged with making
inappropriate comments to and touching the wife of a Master
Mason while intoxicated on multiple occasions. At the Pre-trial
Conference, the parties reached a settlement with terms agreeable
to the Trial Master. Pursuant to the settlement, the Accused pled
guilty to the charges, provided a lengthy and sincere letter to
the lady, enrolled in a substance abuse program, demitted from
the Lodge and was issued a penalty of definite suspension from
masonry for nine months.

The following case was remanded for further investigation by the
Trial Master following the 2017 Annual Communication:
14. In Case Nos. 2771 and 2768, the Accused were charged with
falsehood and deceit for making false statements that the Accuser
had been in a “knock down drag out fight” with his now ex-wife. One
of the Accused also was charged with having a sexual relationship
with the Accuser’s wife before the divorce. The Accuser failed
to appear and prosecute his case at a scheduled 2017 Trial, and
the Trial Master dismissed the charges without conducting the
required investigation. At the 2017 Annual Communication, the
matter was remanded. The Trial Master conducted the required
investigation. Both the Accuser’s ex-wife and Accused denied
any sexual relationship. Additionally, there was evidence that
there may have been abusive conduct by the Accuser. The Trial
Master concluded that the evidence did not support the charges
and dismissed the case.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the

2771 and 2768, the Trial Masters’ procedures, findings and the penalties
affixed be hereby affirmed.”
The following cases involved trial proceedings including the taking
of testimony:
15. In Case No. 2806, the Accused was charged with electioneering
arising from a widely disseminated e-mail in support of a
Resolution to restore an expelled Master Mason and knowingly
refusing to obey a Grand Master’s edict by providing false and
misleading responses to the Grand Master’s questions both in
writing and in person. The Trial Master and the Commissioners
agreed that the Accuser did not meet the required burden of proof
on the charge of electioneering. However, the Trial Master and
Commissioners found that the Accused was evasive, misleading
and incomplete in responding to the Grand Master and therefore
found him guilty of failing to obey the Grand Master’s edict. The
Trial Master set the penalty at a definite suspension of 12 months.

16. In Case No. 2807, the Accused was charged with electioneering by
sending e-mails to Master Masons and creating a public website in
which he attacked a Grand Master’s Recommendation to be heard
at the Annual Communication; refused to obey a Grand Master’s
edict by providing false and misleading answers to questions
directed to him in writing by the Grand Master; and defamed the
California Grand Lodge in articles on his website by claiming the
Grand Lodge was corrupt and had paid for protests outside of
the Masonic World Conference in San Francisco in 2015. Prior to
Trial, the Accused objected to the appointed Trial Commissioners.
Given the Accused’s objections, nearly one month before the trial,
the Trial Master informed the Accused in writing that he would
proceed with the trial without Trial Commissioners. Although on
timely notice of the Trial Master’s decision to proceed without
Trial Commissioners, the Accused through various statements
and other inaction directed toward the Trial Master in advance
of the trial, waived any objection to any error in the Trial Master’s
decision to proceed without Trial Commissioners. The Trial Master,
proceeding alone, heard the evidence presented by both parties
and found that the Accused continued to assert the positions he
had taken in the postings and e-mails including that the California
Grand Lodge was corrupt. The Trial Master accordingly found the
Accused guilty of all three specifications and set the penalty at
indefinite suspension. Having reviewed the evidence and actions
of the Accused, the Committee found that the Accused waived any
error in the decision to proceed without Trial Commissioners and
that the finding of guilt was not a miscarriage of justice which is
required for a reversal of the findings.

The following cases involved previously expelled members who have
requested restoration of their Masonic membership:
A request for restoration must address the factors enunciated in Grand
Master Adamson’s Decision No. 3, that is, whether his current standing,
conduct, character and reputation are such as would make him worthy
of membership in a Lodge, the nature of the conduct which gave rise to
his expulsion, the seriousness of the conduct, the passage of a suitable
length of time, the likelihood he will repeat the conduct, his acceptance
of responsibility, remorse and atonement, his efforts to make amends
for the consequences of his conduct and recommendations of concerned
and knowledgeable Masons and non-Masons.
17. Miranda and Pascua—Case Nos. 2639 and 2640: In 2013, Mr. Pascua
and Mr. Miranda were expelled from Masonry following trial for
striking and hazing a hoodwinked candidate while he was in the
preparation room prior to his third degree. The victim, despite
giving a written statement confirming the battery, later testified
at trial that nothing untoward happened in the preparation room.
The Accused were convicted and the victim was charged for lying
and suspended for one year. In 2015 and 2016 their requests for
restoration were denied by the California Grand Lodge because
of the seriousness of the offense and their failure to follow the
factors enunciated in Grand Master Adamson’s Decision No. 3.
I n March of this year, Mr. Pascua again filed a request for
restoration in which he apologized for his conduct and failure
toward his brethren, family, friends and fraternity. He stated he
has learned a valuable lesson. He provided a letter of apology to
the victim. The victim accepted the apology and requested that Mr.
Pascua be restored. Mr. Pascua also included supporting letters
from the Navy, YMCA, and from the non-profit Feeding San Diego.
I n July of this year, Mr. Miranda filed for restoration calling
his conduct “extremely inappropriate, immature and…lacking
respect.” He apologized for his conduct and for fighting the charges
at their inception, attributing it to a matter of ego. He notes that
he has volunteered in various capacities at his church, including

teaching children every Sunday. Mr. Miranda included supporting
letters from his parish and friends noting his work for the youth
in his church and attesting to his good character.
I n September 2018, their Lodge affirmatively voted for Miranda’s
and Pascua’s restoration.
 sufficient period of time has now passed, and the actions of these

and they have shown a track record of rehabilitation.
 he Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for

18. Montero and Reyes—Case Nos. 2737 and 2738. The facts of both
cases are factually linked as to the nature of the acts constituting
the expulsion and to the restoration petitions. Both Montero and
Reyes were acting as Stewards at a degree in 2016 during which
the candidate was battered while in the preparation room and
while hoodwinked. No one would take responsibility for the attack.
The Trial Master found after trial that: (1) Mr. Reyes, despite his
denials, battered the candidate; (2) Montero lied about Reyes’
presence in the preparation room during the attack; and (3) in
addition to his lying, Montero’s efforts and that of others to deny
that the incident occurred caused “mental injury or humiliation” to
the candidate. The Trial Master accordingly ordered that Montero
and Reyes be expelled, and Grand Lodge sustained the penalty.
 ast year both requested restoration. Their requests were denied
L
by vote of the California Grand Lodge. The present petitions
again fail to address the factors set forth in the 2009 Grand
Master Adamson’s Decision No. 3 governing restoration which,
in part, require “acceptance of responsibility, remorse and
atonement” for the conduct giving rise to the expulsion. Both
fail to accept any responsibility for their conduct in their letters
requesting restoration. Indeed, they seem to be laboring under
the misapprehension that they were expelled for leaving the
room and claim that someone else attacked the candidate. Neither
one of them considers the harm done to the candidate, to the
Lodge and to Freemasonry. Both claim a lack of intent calling their
acts negligent, which, to the Committee, constitutes a complete
denial of that of which they were convicted. While the Lodge

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

327

has approved their requests for restoration, their unwillingness
to accept responsibility points to a refusal to acknowledge the
severity of their conduct and makes them both prime candidates
to repeat the behavior.
Mr. Reyes’ request, while now thanking the Lodge for its support,
fails to address or apologize for his conduct or even to offer an
apology to the Lodge, to Masonry or more importantly, to the
candidate who was his victim.
Mr. Montero’s request notes his continued support of other
community charities and activities and states he is repentant
and remorseful. However, he fails to detail what he is remorseful
for or for the damage his conduct caused.
Battery is a crime under the California Penal Code, and the
California Grand Lodge should not forgive a criminal battery on
a helpless and blindfolded candidate so readily. That candidate
had entrusted his well-being to our care and in this case, during
the initiation, we let him down.
Until such time as they comply with 2009 Grand Master Adamson’s
Decision No. 3, restoration should be considered.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Bruce R. Galloway, and the
members of the Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California:
California Freemasonry has long understood the importance of
supporting the development and growth of the youth orders in our State.
Your Youth Orders Committee is charged with ensuring that our lodges
and members share in the commitment to our youth orders and provide
the adult leadership and support necessary to their success.
In our third year of the committee restructure and refocus plan,
significant advancement has occurred in the implementation of the
long-term strategic plan. The plan was presented to both the youth
orders leadership, the Grand Lodge Executive Committee and other
leaders of the concordant and appendant body’s leadership. The plan
was unanimously approved by all and the committee has begun work
on a wide array of goals and tasks identified in the plan. Two state-wide
surveys have been launched that will provide the baseline information
necessary for accessing the current state of involvement by our lodges
in support of the youth orders. Work has begun on expanding youth
order awareness and understanding in collaboration with the Grand
Lodge Office through a publication-wide awareness campaign and a
call for involvement by all lodges and our members. Additionally, youth
order awareness and understanding modules are being added to many
of our educational and training forums. Assessment and evaluation tools
are being established to better measure outcomes and to promote the
engagement of our lodges and members. A fifth initiative/pillar has
been added to the strategic plan that targets transitional engagement of
our youth orders members reaching majority and will streamline their
pathway into our adult organizations for those who wish to do so.
The committee again embraced its role as the facilitator of the MAYO
meetings throughout the year. The customary on-site meetings were held
in Burlingame at the NorCal DeMolay convention in November 2017;
in Fresno at the Grand Assembly in April 2018; and in Riverside at the
SoCal DeMolay conclave in September 2018. Additionally, one meeting
was held in July 2018 via video/teleconference. I am pleased that the
leadership of the York Rite joined with the other concordant bodies—
Scottish Rite, Eastern Star and Amaranth—to attend these meetings and
to offer their support.

The committee was successful in facilitating financial support for year
three of the Arts and Sciences Educational Project for our youth orders.
The project grew to over 250 youth participants this year. Special thanks
goes out to the California Scottish Rite Foundation and the Grand Lodge
of California for providing the financial support for the continuation of
this important youth project.

been my extreme honor to have served as chair of this committee for the

to our most precious asset – our youth.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
This committee is honored to have had the opportunity to provide
guidance and direction for California Freemason magazine, the flagship
publication of our Grand Lodge. This year, our committee provided
readers with engaging content that focused on the lived experiences
of modern Freemasonry. With topics ranging from fatherhood and the
prospect experience to the fraternal experience around the world, this
year’s issues covered themes that appealed to our broad audience and
resonated with members.
At the end of our last year, we explored the 300-year history of our
Fraternity through a historic commemorative issue, which was sold as a
collector’s edition. It has since sold over 700 copies and has been given
to grand lodge jurisdictions throughout the world.
We are very pleased to report that California Freemason magazine
was commended once again this year by the Association of Membership
Publishers EXCEL Awards.
EXCEL AWARD WINNER:
Silver Award, Special Report Category: 300 Year Commemorative Issue
The magazine was also nominated for several awards by Folio, a
national organization that for over 20 years has been recognizing excellent
publications across a variety of industries – including commercial, nonprofit, and membership publications. The Folio Awards is highly regarded
in the publishing field, and this year we are proud that California
Freemason received the following recognition:
FOLIO AWARD NOMINATIONS:
Instructional/How-To Category: Masonic DIY: Create a Perfect
Square (March/April 2018)
Cover Design: Sacred Geometry (March/April 2018)
Series of Articles: 300 Years of Freemasonry: Past, Present and
Future Series (300 Year Commemorative Issue)
Photography: A Big Spark (May/June 2018)

In the coming year, this committee looks forward to continuing
to inform and inspire our brethren through California Freemason. In
addition to meeting the interests and needs of our own brethren, we plan
to continue to improve our digital channels, with the goal of reaching
even more Masons and community members outside our jurisdiction.
As the reputation of California Freemasonry continues to grow across
the country, we are proud to serve on this committee, and we look forward

Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges 2018
The Grand Lodge of California recognizes all of the Grand Lodges in
the United States published in the 2018 List of Lodges Masonic, which
includes all 50 states and the District of Columbia. In addition, the Grand
Lodge of California recognizes a number of Prince Hall Grand Lodges and
foreign Grand Lodges around the world. The Grand Lodge of California
recognizes some, but not all, of the foreign Grand Lodges and Prince Hall
Grand Lodges in the 2018 List of Lodges Masonic as well as a number
of foreign Grand Lodges that are not listed therein.
For clarity, the foreign Grand Lodges that are recognized by the Grand
Lodge of California are listed below alphabetically by country. For those
that are published in the 2018 List of Lodges Masonic, the corresponding
page number is provided in parentheses. Recognized Grand Lodges that
are not published in the 2018 List of Lodges Masonic are marked with
an asterisk (*). The Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of California
is responsible for all correspondence with these Grand Lodges and the
lodges under their jurisdiction. Please contact this office for assistance.

Lodge of Andorra*; ARGENTINA: Grand Lodge of Argentina (123);
ARMENIA: Grand Lodge of Armenia (126); AUSTRALIA: United Grand
Lodge of New South Wales (127), United Grand Lodge of Queensland
(129), Grand Lodge of South Australia and the Northern Territory (132),
Grand Lodge of Tasmania (133), United Grand Lodge of Victoria (134),
Grand Lodge of Western Australia (136); AUSTRIA: Grand Lodge of
Austria (137); AZERBAIJAN: National Grand Lodge of Azerbaijan (138).

Lodge of Benin*; BOLIVIA: Grand Lodge of Bolivia (140); BOSNIA and

The Grand Lodge of California maintains mutual recognition with
the following Prince Hall Grand Lodges. For those that are published
in the 2018 List of Lodges Masonic, the corresponding page number is
provided in parentheses. Recognized Prince Hall grand lodges that are
not published in the 2018 List of Lodges Masonic are marked with an
asterisk (*). The terms of recognition are the same with each Prince Hall
grand lodge and are consistent with the agreement of mutual recognition
between the Grand Lodge of California and the Prince Hall Grand Lodge
of California, Inc. Dual membership in lodges under the two jurisdictions
is not allowed, but visitation may be had between members of lodges
of both jurisdictions. For these purposes, visitation means visiting tiled
meetings.
